116604.q: Which quantity alone determines the period of a body on an elliptical orbit around the same central body?
116604.e: According to Kepler’s third law, the period depends only on the semi-major axis. A highly eccentric ellipse and a circle with the same a have the same period.
116604.m: The period depends only on the semi-major axis.

116605.q: Which auxin occurs most commonly in plants naturally?
116605.e: Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) is the most important natural auxin. Gibberellic acid, zeatin and abscisic acid belong to other groups of hormones.
116605.m: The most important natural auxin is indole-3-acetic acid.

116606.q: Where is auxin mainly produced in a plant?
a: In shoot tips and young leaves
In the bark of the trunk
116606.e: Auxin is produced mainly in growing tissues at the shoot tip and in young leaves. From there it is transported downwards.
116606.m: Auxin is produced mainly in the shoot tips.

116607.q: Why does a seedling lit from one side bend towards the light?
a: Auxin moves to the shaded side and promotes elongation there
Auxin moves to the lit side and promotes elongation there
Light destroys the cell walls on the shaded side
Chlorophyll pulls the shoot tip towards the light
116607.e: When light comes from one side, auxin is moved to the shaded side. There the cells elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light.
116607.m: In phototropism, auxin stretches the shaded side of the shoot.

116608.q: Which researchers showed in 1880, using grass seedlings, that the tip senses the light stimulus?
116608.e: Charles Darwin and his son Francis covered the tips of coleoptiles and described the experiments in 1880 in “The Power of Movement in Plants”. Without a lit tip, the bending did not happen.
116608.m: The Darwins found that the seedling tip senses the light.

116609.q: Seedling tips are placed on small agar blocks, and the blocks are then put on decapitated seedlings. These grow again. What does this prove?
a: A chemical substance from the tip triggers growth
Agar naturally contains a plant hormone
Seedlings without tips always grow faster
116609.e: The substance from the tip had passed into the agar and kept working there. In this way Frits Went demonstrated auxin in the 1920s.
116609.m: Agar experiments proved that auxin is a chemical growth substance.

116610.q: Why are cuttings in horticulture often dipped in a powder containing synthetic auxin?
116610.e: Auxins such as indole-3-butyric acid stimulate the formation of adventitious roots at the cut. That is why rooting powders contain such substances.
116610.m: Rooting powder contains auxin so that cuttings form roots faster.

116611.q: Which synthetic auxin is used as a herbicide against broadleaf weeds in cereal crops?
116611.e: 2,4-D acts like an overdose of auxin and makes broadleaf plants grow uncontrollably until they die. Grasses such as cereals are less sensitive.
116611.m: The herbicide 2,4-D kills weeds with an overdose of auxin action.

116612.q: How is auxin usually transported in the plant?
a: In one direction from cell to cell, from the tip downwards
Upwards with the water in the xylem
Through the air from leaf to leaf
Not at all, it stays where it is made
116612.e: Auxin is transported in a polar way: transport proteins, the PIN proteins, sit on only one side of the cells and pass it on in one direction.
116612.m: Auxin moves in one direction, from the shoot tip downwards.

116613.q: According to the acid growth theory, how does auxin promote cell elongation?
a: Protons are pumped into the cell wall and loosen it
The cell wall is strengthened with extra cellulose
The nucleus divides several times in quick succession
The vacuole releases water into the surroundings
116613.e: Auxin activates proton pumps in the cell membrane, and the cell wall becomes acidic. This activates enzymes such as expansins, which loosen the wall, so turgor can stretch the cell.
116613.m: According to the acid growth theory, an acidified cell wall loosens its structure for elongation.

116614.q: In which crop did the fungal disease “bakanae” lead to the discovery of gibberellins?
116614.e: The fungus Gibberella fujikuroi attacked rice plants in Japan and greatly changed their growth. Japanese researchers isolated the active substance from it, gibberellin.
116614.m: Gibberellins were discovered through a fungal disease of rice.

116615.q: Which symptom do rice plants suffering from “bakanae” disease show?
116615.e: “Bakanae” means roughly “foolish seedling” in Japanese. The infected plants grow too tall, fall over and give little yield.
116615.m: Too much gibberellin makes plants grow excessively tall.

116616.q: Which enzyme does the aleurone layer of a germinating barley grain produce in response to a gibberellin signal?
116616.e: The embryo sends gibberellins to the aleurone layer. This produces alpha-amylase, which breaks down the starch in the endosperm into sugar and feeds the embryo.
116616.m: Gibberellins make the germinating grain produce a starch-digesting enzyme.

116617.q: What are the short stems of many Green Revolution wheat varieties based on?
a: Too much auxin in the stem
A lack of phytochrome in the shoot
116617.e: The so-called Rht genes change proteins in the gibberellin signalling pathway, so the stems respond less to the hormone. Short stems do not bend over under heavy ears.
116617.m: The short stems of modern wheat varieties respond more weakly to gibberellins.

116618.q: How do plants grow that can hardly make any gibberellins themselves?
116618.e: Gibberellins promote stem elongation. Without the hormone, plants stay small. Mendel's short peas also had a defect in gibberellin production.

116619.q: Which group of plant hormones mainly promotes stem elongation and germination?
116619.e: Gibberellins make shoots grow longer and break seed dormancy. Abscisic acid, by contrast, has an inhibiting effect, and ethylene promotes fruit ripening.
116619.m: Gibberellins promote stem elongation and germination.

116620.q: Which process do gibberellins trigger in rosette plants such as lettuce?
a: Bolting of a long flower stalk
Rolling up of the leaves in heat
116620.e: Rosette plants have compressed shoots. Gibberellins cause the internodes to stretch strongly, so the plant “bolts” and forms a flower stalk.
116620.m: Gibberellins make rosette plants shoot up.

116621.q: Why are seedless table grapes often sprayed with gibberellic acid during growing?
a: So that the berries become larger
So that the berries form seeds
So that the grapes fall off earlier
So that the skin becomes darker
116621.e: In seedless varieties, gibberellic acid promotes the growth of the berries and loosens the bunch. This produces larger fruit.
116621.m: Gibberellic acid makes the berries of seedless grapes bigger.

116622.q: How do stem shorteners such as chlormequat work in cereal growing?
a: They inhibit the production of gibberellins
They promote the production of gibberellins
They block the uptake of nitrogen
116622.e: Chlormequat inhibits enzymes of gibberellin synthesis. The stems stay shorter and sturdier, so the crop falls over less.
116622.m: Stem shorteners slow gibberellin production and make cereals sturdier.

116623.q: Where are cytokinins mainly produced in the plant?
116623.e: Cytokinins are produced mainly in the root tips and travel with the xylem sap into the shoot.
116623.m: Cytokinins are produced mainly in the root tips.

116624.q: Which group of substances do cytokinins such as zeatin, obtained from maize, belong to?
116624.e: Cytokinins are plant hormones that control cell division and growth. The natural cytokinin zeatin was isolated from unripe maize kernels and named after Zea mays.

116625.q: Which process do cytokinins promote, as their name also suggests?
116625.e: The name comes from cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm. Together with auxin, cytokinins stimulate cell division.

116626.q: What are cytokinins used for in the laboratory when propagating plants from tissue cultures?
a: To make new shoots grow from clumps of cells
To make the plants dry out faster
116626.e: From an undifferentiated clump of cells, the callus, shoots form with a lot of cytokinin and little auxin. A lot of auxin, on the other hand, promotes roots.
116626.m: Cytokinins make shoots form in tissue culture.

116627.q: What can be seen on a cut leaf that is treated with cytokinin?
a: It rolls up into a spiral
116627.e: Cytokinins delay the breakdown of chlorophyll and proteins. Treated areas of the leaf stay green and even attract nutrients.
116627.m: Cytokinins keep leaves green for longer.

116628.q: Which bacterium causes crown galls by transferring genes for making auxin and cytokinin into the plant?
116628.e: Agrobacterium tumefaciens inserts part of its Ti plasmid into the plant's genome. The plant cells then produce hormones uncontrollably and grow into a gall.
116628.m: Agrobacterium makes plants form galls through foreign hormone genes.

116629.q: From which nucleobase are natural cytokinins chemically derived?
116629.e: Cytokinins are adenine derivatives with a side chain on the nitrogen atom N6. Zeatin, for example, carries an isoprenoid side chain.
116629.m: Cytokinins are chemically modified adenine molecules.

116630.q: How do cytokinins affect dormant side buds of a shoot?
a: They make them dry out and fall off
116630.e: Cytokinins counteract the inhibiting effect of the shoot tip. Applied to side buds, they make them sprout.
116630.m: Cytokinins wake up dormant side buds.

116631.q: How do the stomata react when the level of abscisic acid in the leaf rises during drought?
116631.e: Abscisic acid makes the stomata close. This way the plant loses less water through transpiration when water is short.
116631.m: Abscisic acid closes the stomata in drought.

116632.q: What happens in the guard cells when abscisic acid acts?
a: Potassium ions and water flow out and turgor falls
Sugar is made and water flows in
The cell walls thicken with lignin
The chloroplasts move to the edge of the cell
116632.e: Abscisic acid opens ion channels, and potassium and chloride ions leave the guard cells. Water follows by osmosis, the turgor falls and the pore closes.
116632.m: Without turgor, the guard cells go slack and the pore closes.

116633.q: What happens to seeds that cannot make abscisic acid?
a: They germinate while still on the parent plant
116633.e: Abscisic acid keeps seeds dormant. Without it, seeds germinate too early, for example maize kernels still on the cob. This is called vivipary.
116633.m: Abscisic acid stops seeds from germinating too early.

116634.q: From which process does the name “abscisic acid” come?
a: From the shedding of plant organs
116634.e: The substance was studied in the 1960s in connection with the shedding of cotton fruits (abscission); Latin abscidere means “to cut off”. Today we know it plays only a minor role in this.
116634.m: The name abscisic acid recalls the shedding of plant parts.

116635.q: Which group of substances does abscisic acid belong to?
116635.e: Abscisic acid is a plant hormone. Even in small amounts it acts as a signal, for example for closing the stomata or for seed dormancy.
116635.m: Abscisic acid is a plant hormone.

116636.q: Why is abscisic acid often called a “stress hormone”?
a: Its level rises sharply in drought, cold or salt
It is only made when insects cause injuries
It makes the plant flower faster under stress
It is completely broken down under stress
116636.e: When water is short, in cold or in high salt levels, the plant quickly makes more abscisic acid. This switches on protective genes and reduces water loss.
116636.m: Abscisic acid helps plants survive environmental stress.

116637.q: Which plant hormone acts as the opponent of abscisic acid in seeds and promotes germination?
116637.e: Abscisic acid keeps seeds dormant, while gibberellins break dormancy and trigger germination. The balance between the two hormones decides when a seed germinates.
116637.m: Gibberellin promotes germination, abscisic acid inhibits it.

116638.q: How do the leaves find out that the soil is drying out, even before they wilt?
a: Abscisic acid from the roots reaches the leaves via the xylem
The roots send electrical signals through the phloem
The leaves measure humidity with phytochrome
The water in the xylem changes colour in drought
116638.e: Roots in dry soil make more abscisic acid. It travels with the transpiration stream into the leaves and triggers protective reactions there before water shortage becomes visible.
116638.m: Abscisic acid reports drought from the roots to the leaves.

116639.q: Which feature sets ethylene apart from almost all other plant hormones?
a: It is a gas at room temperature
It consists of a long protein chain
It is only made in flowers
116639.e: Ethylene (ethene, C2H4) is a simple gaseous hydrocarbon. It can therefore also spread through the air to other parts of the plant and to fruits.
116639.m: Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone.

116640.q: Why do hard kiwis ripen faster if you put them in a bag with a ripe apple?
a: The apple draws water out of them
116640.e: Ripe apples give off a lot of ethylene. In a closed bag the gas builds up and speeds up the ripening of the kiwis.
116640.m: A ripe apple speeds up the ripening of other fruit with ethylene.

116641.q: What are fruits such as bananas, apples or tomatoes called that keep ripening after harvest with the help of ethylene?
116641.e: Climacteric fruits show a rise in respiration and ethylene production as they ripen. That is why they can be harvested unripe and left to ripen later.
116641.m: Climacteric fruits keep ripening after harvest thanks to ethylene.

116642.q: Which of these fruits hardly ripens any further after harvest?
116642.e: Strawberries are non-climacteric. They show no rise in ethylene and do not get any sweeter after picking.
116642.m: Strawberries should only be picked when ripe, because they do not keep ripening.

116643.q: How do pea seedlings grow in the dark under ethylene (the “triple response”)?
a: Not at all, they stay in the seed
116643.e: The triple response consists of inhibited elongation, a thickened shoot and horizontal growth. This lets a seedling work its way around obstacles in the soil.
116643.m: Ethylene makes seedlings short and thick and makes them grow sideways.

116644.q: Why should you quickly separate rotten apples from the others in the fruit bowl?
a: They give off a lot of ethylene and speed up spoiling
They draw water out of the healthy apples
They produce cold that damages the apples
They bind the oxygen in the bowl
116644.e: Damaged and rotting fruits produce particularly large amounts of ethylene. The gas makes neighbouring fruits ripen and spoil faster.
116644.m: One rotten apple makes the others spoil faster with ethylene.

116645.q: How are apples kept fresh for months in large fruit stores?
a: Stored cool and with little oxygen
Stored warm and with a lot of oxygen
116645.e: In controlled atmosphere (CA) stores, temperature and oxygen levels are low. This slows respiration and the effect of ethylene, and the apples hardly ripen further.
116645.m: Cold and little oxygen slow the ripening of apples.

116646.q: What is the active substance ethephon used for in farming?
a: It releases ethylene in the plant
It binds nitrogen from the air
It kills fungal spores on leaves
116646.e: Ethephon breaks down in plant tissue and releases ethylene in the process. It is used, for example, for even ripening or to trigger flowering in pineapples.
116646.m: Ethephon is a product that releases ethylene in the plant.

116647.q: Which 19th-century observation put researchers on the trail of ethylene?
a: Plants near leaking gas pipes for street lighting grew poorly and lost leaves
Bananas on ships rotted in severe cold
Cereals grew faster next to coal power stations
116647.e: Coal gas for street lamps contained ethylene. Plants near leaks grew badly and lost their leaves early. The Russian botanist Dimitry Neljubow identified ethylene as the active component using pea seedlings and reported this in 1901.
116647.m: Leaking gas pipes revealed the effect of ethylene on plants.

116648.q: How is the behaviour of a main root that grows towards the centre of the Earth described?
116648.e: Gravitropism is a growth movement directed by gravity. If an organ grows towards gravity, it is positively gravitropic; the shoot, on the other hand, is negatively gravitropic.
116648.m: Main roots grow downwards, positively gravitropic.

116649.q: Which cell components act as gravity sensors in the root cap?
116649.e: Amyloplasts are heavy, starch-rich plastids. They sink to the bottom of the cells and so show the plant the direction of gravity. They are called statoliths.
116649.m: Starch grains in the root cap show the plant which way is down.

116650.q: What happens if the root cap of a root is removed?
a: It no longer responds to gravity
It immediately grows towards the light
It forms leaves at the tip
It grows downwards twice as fast
116650.e: The cells that sense gravity lie in the middle of the root cap. Without the root cap, the root keeps growing, but no longer bends downwards.
116650.m: The root cap is the gravity-sensing organ of the root.

116651.q: Why does a root laid horizontally bend downwards?
a: Auxin collects on the lower side and inhibits elongation there
Auxin collects on the upper side and inhibits elongation there
The root is pressed down by the weight of the soil
Water flows downwards and softens the lower side
116651.e: In the root, even small amounts of auxin inhibit growth. The lower side grows more slowly than the upper side, and the root tip bends downwards.
116651.m: In roots, auxin slows the lower side, so they grow downwards.

116652.q: Why does a cereal stem that has been bent over straighten up again after a few days?
a: Auxin promotes elongation on the lower side of the nodes
The roots pull the stem down with force
The ear becomes lighter and tips back
116652.e: In the shoot, auxin promotes elongation. It builds up on the lower side of the stem nodes, which grows more there, so the stem straightens up.
116652.m: In the shoot, auxin makes the lower side grow more and straightens it.

116653.q: Which device is used in experiments to cancel out the one-sided effect of gravity on plants?
116653.e: A clinostat slowly rotates the plant around a horizontal axis. Gravity then acts evenly from all sides, and no directed bending occurs.
116653.m: A clinostat evens out the one-sided effect of gravity.

116654.q: How do side roots grow compared with the main root?
a: At a slant, at a certain angle
116654.e: The main root grows vertically downwards. Side roots, on the other hand, grow at a slant into the soil and so reach a larger area.
116654.m: Side roots grow at a slant, the main root grows vertically.

116655.q: What did Thomas Andrew Knight show in 1806 with seedlings on a fast-spinning wheel?
a: Roots respond to centrifugal force as they do to gravity
Roots always grow towards the light
Shoots do not grow without gravity
116655.e: On the wheel, the roots grew outwards in the direction of the centrifugal force and the shoots grew towards the centre. This showed that plants respond to a mass force.
116655.m: Knight's wheel proved that roots follow a mass force.

116656.q: Which colours of light does the phytochrome system mainly sense?
116656.e: Phytochrome absorbs red light at around 660 nanometres and far-red light at around 730 nanometres. Blue light is detected by other receptors, such as cryptochromes.
116656.m: Phytochrome is the red light sensor of plants.

116657.q: Which form of phytochrome is considered biologically active?
a: Pfr, the form that absorbs far-red
Pr, the form that absorbs red
Pb, the form that absorbs blue light
Pg, the form that absorbs green light
116657.e: Red light converts Pr into Pfr, and far-red converts Pfr back into Pr. The Pfr form triggers the responses to light.
116657.m: The active form of phytochrome is called Pfr.

116658.q: Lettuce seeds are lit alternately with red and far-red light. What decides whether they germinate?
a: The colour of the last flash of light
The colour of the first flash of light
116658.e: If the sequence ends with red, there is a lot of Pfr and the seeds germinate. If it ends with far-red, germination does not happen. This shows that phytochrome can be switched back and forth.
116658.m: In lettuce seeds, the last flash of light decides germination.

116659.q: Why do plants in the shade of other plants grow noticeably taller?
a: The leaf canopy filters out red light, leaving a lot of far-red
It is cooler in the shade, which stimulates cell division
There is no carbon dioxide for photosynthesis in the shade
Shade increases moisture and softens cell walls
116659.e: Leaves absorb red light but let far-red through. Phytochrome detects the low ratio of red to far-red and triggers elongation growth to escape the shade.
116659.m: A high proportion of far-red tells the plant it is in the shade.

a: Phytochrome is a light sensor, not a photosynthetic pigment
Phytochrome is green, chlorophyll is red
116660.e: Chlorophyll captures light as a source of energy for photosynthesis. Phytochrome, by contrast, measures light and uses it to control germination, growth and flowering.
116660.m: Phytochrome measures light; chlorophyll uses it as energy.

116661.q: What does a short flash of red light in the middle of the long night do to a short-day plant?
a: It makes the leaves fall off
It has no effect at all
116661.e: Short-day plants actually measure the length of the uninterrupted night. The red flash forms Pfr and interrupts the night, so the plant does not flower. A following far-red flash cancels this effect again.
116661.m: Short-day plants need a long, uninterrupted night to flower.

116662.q: What is the growth form of seedlings that grow long and pale with small leaves in the dark called?
116662.e: In the dark, seedlings put their reserves into growing longer to reach light quickly. When light arrives, phytochrome switches to normal growth with green leaves.
116662.m: Pale seedlings grown in the dark are called etiolated.

116663.q: Why is thale cress often used as a model plant in research?
a: It grows quickly and has a small genome
It is the largest plant in Europe
It does not carry out photosynthesis
It only flowers every ten years
116663.e: Thale cress (Arabidopsis thaliana) is small, needs little space and produces seeds within a few weeks. Its genome is small and has been fully sequenced.
116663.m: Thale cress is the most important model plant in biology.

a: The promotion of flowering by a longer period of cold
The germination of seeds in spring warmth
The sprouting of buds after rain
The shedding of leaves before winter
116664.e: Many plants only flower after they have experienced several weeks of cold. This cold stimulus is called vernalisation, from the Latin ver for spring.
116664.m: Vernalisation means that cold is needed to make a plant ready to flower.

116665.q: Why is winter wheat sown in autumn?
a: It needs the winter cold to form ears later
It cannot tolerate spring sunshine on young leaves
It only germinates at temperatures below zero
It must have ripe grains before the snow
116665.e: Winter wheat needs vernalisation. If it is sown in spring, it often gets stuck in the leaf stage and forms hardly any ears.
116665.m: Winter wheat needs the winter to produce grain in summer.

116666.q: What happens to winter wheat that is not sown until spring?
a: It does not germinate at all
116666.e: Winter wheat needs a longer period of cold to become ready to flower. Without a winter it often gets stuck in the leaf stage and forms hardly any ears.
116666.m: Without cold, winter wheat forms hardly any ears.

116667.q: Which vegetable plant normally flowers only after a winter, in its second year?
116667.e: The carrot is biennial: in the first year it forms the root, and after the winter it flowers. Tomatoes, cucumbers and pumpkins flower in the year they are sown.
116667.m: Biennial plants such as the carrot only flower after a winter.

116668.q: Where does the word vernalisation come from?
a: From the Latin word for spring
From the Latin word for winter
From the Greek word for flower
From the Latin word for cold
116668.e: The Latin ver means spring. The cold makes a plant ready for spring, so to speak, and it can then flower.
116668.m: Vernalisation comes from the Latin ver for spring.

116669.q: In which temperature range is vernalisation typically most effective?
116669.e: For most plants, cool temperatures just above freezing work best, over several weeks. Hard frost is not needed.
116669.m: Vernalisation needs weeks of cool weather just above zero.

116670.q: Why does a sugar beet normally only flower in its second year?
a: It first needs the cold of a winter
It first has to shed ten leaves
It only flowers when days are very short
Its seeds need two years to germinate
116670.e: The sugar beet is biennial: in the first year it stores sugar in the root, and after the winter it bolts and flowers. The same applies, for example, to carrots or cabbage.
116670.m: Biennial plants such as sugar beet only flower after a winter.

116671.q: Is a plant's vernalised state passed on to its seeds?
a: No, it is reset in every generation
Yes, the seeds then flower without cold
Yes, but only in cereal plants
No, because the seeds do not germinate without cold
116671.e: The switching off of the flowering repressor gene lasts in the plant, but it is reversed again when seeds form. Each new generation has to experience a winter itself.
116671.m: Each plant generation has to experience the cold for vernalisation itself.

116672.q: Which plant folds up its leaflets within seconds when touched?
116672.e: The sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica) responds to touch by quickly folding up its leaflets. This is a textbook example of thigmonasty.
116672.m: The mimosa is the best-known example of thigmonasty.

116673.q: In a closed Venus flytrap, what happens when struggling prey keeps stimulating the trigger hairs?
a: After about five stimuli it produces digestive enzymes
It opens again immediately and releases the prey
It instantly forms a new second trap
It sheds the trap leaf after a short time
116673.e: The trap counts the action potentials. If the prey keeps struggling and triggers about five stimuli, the plant starts producing digestive enzymes.
116673.m: The Venus flytrap counts stimuli before it starts digesting.

a: The direction of movement does not depend on the direction of the stimulus
The movement is triggered by light instead of touch
The movement always takes several weeks
The movement only occurs in animals
116674.e: In nastic movements, the direction is fixed by the structure of the organ, wherever the stimulus comes from. In tropisms, the organ grows towards or away from the stimulus, like a tendril around a support.
116674.m: Nastic movements happen regardless of the direction of the stimulus.

116675.q: What makes the leaves of the mimosa fold up so quickly?
a: Loss of turgor in the leaf joints
Growth of the upper side of the leaf
Muscle fibres in the leaf stalk
Evaporation of water at the leaf tip
116675.e: At the base of the leaves there are joint cushions (pulvini). When stimulated, the cells on one side suddenly lose water and ions, so the joint bends.
116675.m: The mimosa moves its leaves using water pressure in the joint cushions.

116676.q: What happens when an insect touches the stamens of the barberry at their base?
a: They snap inwards towards the centre of the flower
They fall off the flower immediately
116676.e: The stamens of the barberry are sensitive to touch and quickly snap towards the centre. In doing so, they dust the insect with pollen.
116676.m: The barberry dusts insects with pollen using movable stamens.

116677.q: Which carnivorous water plant sucks prey into a bladder in a flash after its trigger hairs are touched?
116677.e: The bladderwort (Utricularia) pumps water out of its trap bladders. When a small animal touches the trigger hairs, the trapdoor opens and the animal is sucked in within a fraction of a second.
116677.m: The bladderwort catches prey with suction traps under water.

116678.q: How is the touch stimulus passed on in a Venus flytrap?
a: By nerve fibres, as in animals
By sound waves in the leaf
By ethylene gas inside the leaf
116678.e: Plants have no nerves. But the trigger hairs set off electrical action potentials that spread across the two halves of the trap.
116678.m: Plants too pass on stimuli with electrical signals.

116679.q: What did researchers observe when mimosas were repeatedly dropped a short, harmless distance?
a: Over time they stopped folding up their leaves
They folded up their leaves faster every time
They shed all their leaves after a short time
116679.e: With a repeated, harmless stimulus, the mimosas got used to it and stopped bothering to react. They still reacted to other stimuli, though.
116679.m: Mimosas can get used to harmless stimuli.

116680.q: How does leaf senescence differ from a leaf dying because of an injury?
a: It is an orderly, genetically controlled programme
It always happens suddenly within an hour
It is only triggered by pathogens
116680.e: In senescence, specific genes are switched on, and the cells break down their components in an orderly sequence. In an injury, by contrast, cells die in an uncontrolled way.
116680.m: Leaf senescence is a controlled programme, not random dying.

116681.q: Which pigments do trees such as some maple species make anew in autumn, turning the leaves red?
116681.e: Red autumn colours come from anthocyanins, which are newly made in the ageing leaves. They probably protect against too much light while the leaf is being broken down.
116681.m: The red autumn colour comes from newly made anthocyanins.

116682.q: How does a tree benefit from the orderly breakdown of its leaves before they fall?
a: It brings nutrients such as nitrogen back into the branches and trunk
It makes the leaves rot faster
It protects the soil from frost in winter
It attracts pollinators into the crown in autumn
116682.e: During senescence, proteins and chlorophyll are broken down. Nitrogen, phosphorus and other substances move into the tree and are reused in spring.
116682.m: Before the leaves fall, the tree takes valuable nutrients back from them.

116683.q: What is the layer of cells at the base of the leaf stalk called, where the leaf comes away in autumn?
116683.e: An abscission zone forms at the base of the leaf. There, enzymes dissolve the cell walls and the leaf breaks off, while a layer of cork seals the wound.
116683.m: Leaves fall off at a prepared abscission layer.

116684.q: What are plants called that flower and fruit only once and then die?
116684.e: Monocarpic plants such as agaves, many bamboo species or annual cereals put all their reserves into a single round of fruiting and then die.
116684.m: Monocarpic plants die after their one and only fruiting.

116685.q: Which plant hormone particularly speeds up leaf ageing and leaf fall?
116685.e: Ethylene promotes the breakdown in the leaf and the formation of the abscission layer. Auxin from a healthy leaf, on the other hand, works against leaf fall.
116685.m: Ethylene speeds up the ageing and falling of leaves.

116686.q: What are plant varieties called whose leaves stay green for longer thanks to delayed senescence?
116686.e: Stay-green varieties break down their chlorophyll later or more slowly. In cereals such as sorghum, this can improve resistance to drought.
116686.m: Stay-green varieties keep their green leaves for longer.

116687.q: Which of Gregor Mendel's pea traits is based on a gene for breaking down chlorophyll?
116687.e: Green peas carry a faulty version of the gene SGR, which controls chlorophyll breakdown during ripening. This was worked out in 2007.
116687.m: Mendel's green peas stay green because their chlorophyll breakdown is faulty.

116688.q: Which signal mainly triggers the start of autumn senescence in broadleaf trees in Central Europe?
116688.e: Trees measure day length with photoreceptors. Shorter days, often together with falling temperatures, start leaf breakdown in good time before the frost.
116688.m: Shorter days give many broadleaf trees the starting signal for autumn.

116689.q: What is meant by apical dominance?
a: The terminal bud inhibits the sprouting of the side buds
The root always grows faster than the shoot
The flower always forms at the lowest bud
The leaves at the top are always larger than those below
116689.e: The shoot tip suppresses the growth of the side buds below it. As a result, the plant mainly grows upwards.
116689.m: In apical dominance, the shoot tip holds back the side buds.

116690.q: Why does basil become bushier if you pinch off the shoot tips?
a: The inhibition of the side buds by the tip is removed
The plant gets more light at its roots
The cut produces a new flowering hormone
The leaves lose less water after the cut
116690.e: Without the tip, the inhibiting signal that flows from the top downwards is missing. The side buds sprout, and the plant branches out.
116690.m: Cutting off the shoot tip makes the side buds sprout.

116691.q: What happens if auxin is applied to the cut surface after the shoot tip has been removed?
a: The side buds sprout particularly quickly
The shoot dies within a few days
Flowers form on the cut surface
116691.e: In the 1930s, Thimann and Skoog showed that auxin can replace the effect of the tip. This proved that auxin is the signal for apical dominance.
116691.m: Auxin can replace the inhibiting effect of the shoot tip.

116692.q: How is apical dominance used when trimming a hedge so that it becomes dense?
a: The shoot tips are cut back regularly
116692.e: When the shoot tips are cut back, their inhibiting effect is removed. The side buds sprout and the hedge branches more densely. Auxin and other hormones such as strigolactones are involved in the inhibition.
116692.m: Cutting the tips makes hedges dense.

116693.q: Which crown shape do spruces get from a strongly dominant leading shoot?
116693.e: In spruces, the leading shoot grows more each year than the side branches, and the upper branches stay shorter. This creates the typical pointed cone shape.
116693.m: The pointed shape of a spruce shows strong dominance of the leading shoot.

116694.q: What are dense, broom-like clusters of shoots on trees called, where pathogens disrupt apical dominance?
116694.e: Fungi, bacteria or phytoplasmas change the hormone balance, often through extra cytokinin. Many side buds sprout at the same time and form a dense cluster.
116694.m: Witches' brooms form when pathogens cancel apical dominance.

116695.q: Because of apical dominance, which eyes of a potato tuber usually sprout first?
a: The eyes at the rose end
The eyes at the stem end
All the eyes at the same time
116695.e: The potato tuber is a swollen shoot, and its rose end corresponds to the tip. The eyes there sprout first and inhibit the others.
116695.m: In potatoes, the eyes at the tip of the tuber sprout first.

116696.q: In trees, the buds near the shoot tip usually sprout most strongly; in many shrubs, those at the base. What follows from this?
a: Trees grow upwards, shrubs send up many shoots from below
Trees have more roots at the top
Shrubs only flower at ground level
Trees lose all their leaves at the bottom
116696.e: In trees (acrotonic), the topmost buds sprout most strongly, creating a trunk with a crown. In basitonic shrubs, the buds at the base sprout, which is why many shoots grow from the ground.
116696.m: Trees sprout most strongly at the top, many shrubs at the bottom.

116697.q: When does a plant produce more jasmonic acid?
a: When it is eaten by insects
116697.e: Injuries caused by herbivores trigger the production of jasmonic acid. It then switches on defence reactions in the plant.
116697.m: Jasmonic acid is an alarm signal when a plant is being eaten.

116698.q: Which group of substances does jasmonic acid belong to?
116698.e: Jasmonic acid is a plant hormone. Like auxin or abscisic acid, it controls processes in the plant in small amounts, especially defence.
116698.m: Jasmonic acid is a plant hormone.

116699.q: Where does jasmonic acid get its name from?
a: Its methyl ester was found in the fragrant oil of jasmine
It was first obtained from jasmine tea
It makes jasmine flowers glow at night
A researcher named Jasmon discovered it
116699.e: Methyl jasmonate was discovered as a scent in jasmine oil. The related acid was then named jasmonic acid.
116699.m: The name jasmonic acid comes from the scent of jasmine.

116700.q: Which volatile form of jasmonic acid can also warn neighbouring plants about herbivores?
116700.e: Methyl jasmonate evaporates easily and can travel through the air to neighbouring plants. These then prepare their own defences.
116700.m: Methyl jasmonate is a scent signal that warns plants.

116701.q: What is jasmonic acid mainly responsible for in the plant?
116701.e: Jasmonic acid switches on defence genes. The plant then makes toxic or inhibiting substances against insects.
116701.m: Jasmonic acid controls defence against herbivores.

116702.q: How does an injured tomato plant hinder the caterpillars feeding on it?
a: It makes substances that inhibit the caterpillars' digestion
116702.e: Through the jasmonate signal, the tomato makes inhibitors of the caterpillars' protein-digesting enzymes. As a result, they grow less well.
116702.m: Tomatoes fight caterpillars with substances that block their digestion.

116703.q: Which well-known drug is chemically related to salicylic acid, which controls defence against pathogens in plants?
116703.e: Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid. Salicylic acid occurs in willow bark and is a hormone in plants that controls defence against pathogens.
116703.m: Salicylic acid is a plant defence hormone and related to aspirin.

116704.q: Which defensive substance does the tobacco plant produce more of after insect damage, through the jasmonate signal?
116704.e: After the leaves are damaged, jasmonic acid rises and the roots make more nicotine. This is transported into the leaves and is poisonous to many insects.
116704.m: Tobacco protects itself after insect damage with more nicotine.

116805.q: Which process does the P wave on the ECG show?
116805.e: The P wave arises when excitation spreads from the sinus node across both atria (depolarisation of the atria).
116805.m: The P wave stands for excitation of the atria.

116806.q: What does the T wave on the ECG represent?
116806.e: The T wave shows the recovery of the ventricular muscle from excitation. The spread of excitation in the ventricles, by contrast, is shown by the QRS complex.
116806.m: With the T wave the excitation of the ventricles recovers.

116807.q: What does the PQ interval on the ECG show?
a: How long the excitation takes from the atria to the ventricles
How long a whole heartbeat lasts
How much blood the heart pumps out per beat
116807.e: The PQ interval runs from the start of atrial excitation to the start of ventricular excitation. It shows how fast the excitation is passed on through the AV node.
116807.m: The PQ interval measures conduction from the atria to the ventricles.

116808.q: An ECG runs at 25 mm/s. The distance between two R waves is 20 mm. What is the heart rate?
116808.e: 20 mm divided by 25 mm/s gives 0.8 s per beat. 60 s divided by 0.8 s gives 75 beats per minute.
116808.m: You get the heart rate by dividing 60 seconds by the RR interval in seconds.

116809.q: Who received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1924 for developing the electrocardiogram?
116809.e: The Dutch physiologist Willem Einthoven developed the string galvanometer and with it the modern ECG. He received the Nobel Prize for this in 1924.
116809.m: Willem Einthoven is considered the father of the modern ECG.

116810.q: How many leads does a standard resting ECG include?
116810.e: The standard ECG consists of 6 limb leads (Einthoven and Goldberger) and 6 chest leads according to Wilson (V1 to V6).
116810.m: A standard resting ECG has twelve leads.

116811.q: Why is an ECG recorded immediately when a heart attack is suspected?
a: A heart attack changes the heart's electrical signals in a typical way
The ECG shows blocked arteries as a picture
The ECG measures the blood pressure in the coronary arteries
116811.e: When heart muscle dies from lack of oxygen, it conducts the excitation differently. This can often be seen at once on the ECG, for example as ST elevation.
116811.m: An ECG can quickly reveal a heart attack.

116812.q: Which part of the ECG curve shows the excitation of the ventricles?
116812.e: The QRS complex is the large, sharp spike on the ECG. It arises when excitation spreads through the powerful ventricular muscle.
116812.m: The large QRS spike stands for excitation of the ventricles.

116813.q: What does an ECG basically measure?
a: The blood pressure in the aorta
The blood flow in the veins
The heart sounds over the chest
116813.e: The excitation of heart muscle cells creates electric fields. Electrodes on the skin measure the resulting potential differences in the millivolt range.
116813.m: The ECG records the electrical activity of the heart.

116814.q: How fast does the AV node conduct excitation compared with the Purkinje fibres?
a: Not at all, it only conducts backwards
116814.e: In the AV node excitation is conducted at only a few centimetres per second, in the Purkinje fibres at a few metres per second.
116814.m: Conduction is slowest in the AV node and fastest in the Purkinje fibres.

116815.q: What happens to the heartbeat if the sinus node fails and the AV node takes over the rhythm?
116815.e: The AV node can step in as a backup pacemaker. However, its own rhythm of about 40 to 60 beats per minute is slower than that of the sinus node.
116815.m: The AV node is a slower backup pacemaker of the heart.

116816.q: Between which parts of the heart does the AV node pass on the excitation?
a: From the atria to the ventricles
From the ventricles to the aorta
From the lungs to the atria
From the brain to the heart
116816.e: AV stands for atrioventricular, meaning atrium and ventricle. The AV node is the only normal electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles.
116816.m: The AV node links the atria and ventricles electrically.

116817.q: Why is the excitation briefly delayed in the AV node?
a: So that the ventricles fill before they contract
So that the heart saves energy
So that the blood pressure falls
So that the lungs get more air
116817.e: First the atria contract and pump blood into the ventricles. Only then should the ventricles contract.
116817.m: The delay in the AV node gives the ventricles time to fill.

116818.q: Which examination measures the electrical excitation of the heart?
116818.e: The ECG records the excitation of the heart using electrodes on the skin. Problems with conduction in the AV node show up as longer intervals.
116818.m: The ECG shows the electrical activity of the heart.

116819.q: How does the vagus nerve (parasympathetic system) affect the AV node?
a: It has no effect at all
It makes the AV node the pacemaker
116819.e: The parasympathetic system has a negative dromotropic effect, meaning it delays conduction in the AV node. The sympathetic system, by contrast, speeds it up.
116819.m: The vagus nerve slows conduction in the AV node.

116820.q: Why does the AV node protect the ventricles during atrial fibrillation?
a: It lets only some of the impulses through
116820.e: In atrial fibrillation very many disordered impulses arrive at the AV node. Because of its slow conduction and refractory period, only some of them reach the ventricles.
116820.m: The AV node acts like a filter for atrial impulses that are too fast.

116821.q: Where is the AV node located?
a: At the floor of the right atrium near the septum
In the tip of the left ventricle
In the wall of the aorta
At the opening of the pulmonary veins
116821.e: The AV node lies in the right atrium near the atrial septum, above the transition to the ventricles (in the so-called triangle of Koch).
116821.m: The AV node sits in the right atrium at the border between the atria and ventricles.

116822.q: In which order does normal excitation pass through the heart?
a: Sinus node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres
AV node, sinus node, bundle branches, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
Sinus node, bundle of His, AV node, Purkinje fibres, bundle branches
Purkinje fibres, bundle branches, bundle of His, AV node, sinus node
116822.e: Excitation starts in the sinus node, travels across the atria to the AV node and then via the bundle of His and the bundle branches to the Purkinje fibres in the ventricular muscle.
116822.m: Excitation runs from the sinus node via the AV node to the Purkinje fibres.

116823.q: Which structure is the primary pacemaker of the healthy heart?
116823.e: The sinus node has the highest intrinsic rate of about 60 to 80 per minute and therefore sets the rhythm.
116823.m: In the healthy heart the sinus node sets the rhythm.

116824.q: What is the role of the bundle of His in the heart?
a: It carries the excitation from the AV node to the ventricles
It creates the heart's basic rhythm
It supplies the heart muscle with blood
116824.e: The bundle of His is part of the conduction system. It carries the excitation from the AV node through the septum to the bundle branches. It is named after the Basel doctor Wilhelm His Jr.
116824.m: The bundle of His carries the excitation to the ventricles.

116825.q: What does the heart's conduction system consist of?
a: Smooth muscle cells of the blood vessels
116825.e: The conduction system consists of special heart muscle cells that can excite themselves and pass on excitation quickly. That is why the heart keeps beating even without nerves.
116825.m: The heart produces its excitation with its own specialised muscle cells.

116826.q: What takes over the rhythm if the sinus node fails?
a: The AV node, with a slower rhythm
The lungs, with their breathing rhythm
116826.e: If the sinus node fails, the AV node steps in as a backup pacemaker. However, its own rhythm of about 40 to 60 beats per minute is slower.
116826.m: If the sinus node fails, the slower AV node takes over.

116827.q: Why does the AV node briefly delay passing on the excitation?
a: So that the atria can fill the ventricles first
So that the sinus node can recover
So that the heart valves can open
So that the blood in the lungs can take up oxygen
116827.e: The short delay in the AV node makes sure the atria contract first and press blood into the ventricles. Only after that do the ventricles contract.
116827.m: The AV node briefly holds back so that the ventricles fill first.

116828.q: What is the heart's ability to produce excitation itself without an outside stimulus called?
116828.e: Pacemaker cells slowly depolarise by themselves until a threshold is reached. This property is called automaticity, or the autonomy of the heart.
116828.m: Thanks to automaticity, the heart beats under its own power.

a: Stroke volume divided by heart rate
Blood volume divided by stroke volume
116829.e: Cardiac output is the amount of blood that one ventricle pumps out per minute. It is the amount per beat times the number of beats per minute.
116829.m: Cardiac output is the product of stroke volume and heart rate.

116830.q: A heart has a stroke volume of 80 ml and beats 60 times a minute. What is the cardiac output?
116830.e: 80 ml times 60 per minute makes 4,800 ml per minute, that is 4.8 litres per minute.
116830.m: For cardiac output, multiply the stroke volume by the heart rate.

116831.q: How much blood does a heart pump per day with a cardiac output of 5 l/min?
116831.e: A day has 24 times 60, that is 1,440 minutes. 1,440 times 5 litres makes 7,200 litres.
116831.m: The heart pumps several thousand litres of blood every day.

116832.q: During exercise an athlete has a stroke volume of 150 ml and a heart rate of 180 per minute. What is his cardiac output?
116832.e: 150 ml times 180 per minute makes 27,000 ml per minute, that is 27 litres per minute.
116832.m: During exercise, cardiac output can rise to several times the resting value.

116833.q: Roughly how large is the cardiac output of a healthy adult at rest?
116833.e: At rest, a healthy adult's heart pumps out about 5 litres of blood per minute. That is roughly the body's entire amount of blood.
116833.m: At rest the heart pumps about five litres of blood per minute.

116834.q: How does the heart increase its cardiac output during physical exercise?
a: Through higher stroke volume and higher heart rate
Only through a lower heart rate
116834.e: During exercise the heart beats faster and pumps out more blood per beat. Together these greatly increase the amount of blood per minute.
116834.m: More beats and more blood per beat increase cardiac output.

116835.q: Cardiac output can be calculated as oxygen uptake divided by the difference in oxygen between arterial and venous blood. What is it at 250 ml/min and 50 ml per litre of blood?
116835.e: 250 ml/min divided by 50 ml/l gives 5 l/min. This method is called the Fick principle.
116835.m: According to Fick, you divide the oxygen uptake by the arteriovenous difference.

116836.q: What does the cardiac index show?
a: Cardiac output per square metre of body surface
Heart rate per kilogram of body weight
Stroke volume per litre of blood
116836.e: The cardiac index relates cardiac output to body surface area. This makes it easier to compare large and small people.
116836.m: The cardiac index makes cardiac output comparable between people of different sizes.

116837.q: The end-diastolic volume is 130 ml and the end-systolic volume is 60 ml. What is the stroke volume?
116837.e: The stroke volume is the difference between the filling at the end of diastole and the remaining volume at the end of systole: 130 ml minus 60 ml makes 70 ml.
116837.m: Stroke volume is end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume.

116838.q: The stroke volume is 60 ml and the end-diastolic volume is 120 ml. What is the ejection fraction?
116838.e: The ejection fraction is the stroke volume divided by the end-diastolic volume: 60 divided by 120 gives 0.5, that is 50 %.
116838.m: The ejection fraction shows what share of the filling is pumped out.

116839.q: What does the Frank-Starling mechanism state?
a: Greater filling leads to a larger stroke volume
A higher heart rate always lowers stroke volume
The heart always pumps the same amount of blood
The sinus node adapts to blood pressure
116839.e: If the ventricle is filled and stretched more during diastole, it then contracts more strongly. In this way the heart automatically adapts to changing return of blood.
116839.m: According to Frank-Starling, a fuller heart pumps out more blood.

116840.q: What is meant by the afterload of the heart?
a: The resistance to pumping out blood
The filling of the ventricle before contraction
The blood left behind after the beat
116840.e: Afterload is the force the ventricle has to overcome when pumping out blood, mainly the pressure in the aorta. If it rises, stroke volume falls with the same force.
116840.m: Afterload is the resistance the heart pumps against.

116841.q: Roughly how large is the stroke volume of a healthy adult at rest?
116841.e: At rest each ventricle pumps out about 70 ml of blood per beat, and much more in trained people.
116841.m: At rest each ventricle pumps about 70 millilitres of blood per beat.

116842.q: Why do endurance athletes often have a low resting heart rate?
a: Their cardiac output is much smaller
116842.e: A trained heart is stronger and pumps out more blood per beat. So it needs fewer beats per minute for the same cardiac output.
116842.m: A larger stroke volume allows a lower resting heart rate.

116843.q: How do you calculate cardiac output, the amount of blood the heart pumps per minute?
a: Stroke volume divided by heart rate
116843.e: With 70 ml per beat and 70 beats per minute, the heart pumps about 4.9 litres of blood per minute.
116843.m: Cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate.

116844.q: What is called the preload of the heart?
a: The stretch of the ventricle at the end of filling
The number of heartbeats per minute
The resistance in the lung vessels
116844.e: Preload corresponds to the filling and stretching of the ventricle at the end of diastole. It depends mainly on the return of blood through the veins.
116844.m: Preload is the stretching of the ventricle by the incoming blood.

116845.q: Where do the coronary arteries arise?
a: From the root of the aorta
116845.e: The two coronary arteries branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve. In this way they are the first to receive oxygen-rich blood.
116845.m: The coronary arteries arise from the aorta just above the aortic valve.

116846.q: How many coronary arteries branch off directly from the aorta?
116846.e: A left and a right coronary artery arise just above the aortic valve. The left one soon divides into two large branches.
116846.m: Two coronary arteries arise from the aorta.

116847.q: In which phase of the heartbeat is the wall of the left ventricle mainly supplied with blood?
116847.e: In systole the tensed heart muscle squeezes the vessels in the wall. That is why most blood flows in the relaxation phase.
116847.m: The left heart muscle is mainly supplied with blood in diastole.

116848.q: Which disease is caused by the narrowing of the coronary arteries as a result of arteriosclerosis?
116848.e: Deposits in the vessel wall narrow the coronary arteries. The heart muscle then gets too little oxygen during exertion.
116848.m: Coronary heart disease is caused by narrowed coronary arteries.

116849.q: What is the typical feeling of tightness in the chest called when the heart muscle lacks oxygen?
116849.e: Angina pectoris literally means tightness of the chest. It typically occurs during exertion, when narrowed coronary arteries cannot deliver enough blood.
116849.m: Angina pectoris is a warning sign of poor blood supply to the heart.

116850.q: Which examination uses contrast medium to make the coronary arteries visible on an X-ray?
116850.e: Contrast medium is injected directly into the coronary arteries through a cardiac catheter. Narrowings can then be seen on the X-ray.
116850.m: Coronary angiography shows narrowed coronary arteries on an X-ray.

116851.q: Why does heart muscle usually die when a coronary artery is suddenly blocked?
a: There are hardly any adequate bypass routes
The blood flows backwards into the lungs
The heart muscle stores too much oxygen
116851.e: The connections between the coronary branches are usually not enough to replace a blocked vessel quickly. They are called functional end arteries; the area supplied dies, causing a heart attack.
116851.m: Coronary arteries have hardly any adequate bypass routes.

116852.q: Why can a heart attack trigger heart rhythm disorders?
a: The conduction system can also be left without blood
The lungs press on the heart
116852.e: The coronary arteries also supply the sinus node and the AV node. If they lack blood, conduction can be disturbed; the AV node is usually supplied by the right coronary artery.
116852.m: A heart attack can also affect the heart's conduction system.

116853.q: What is special about a bioresorbable stent?
a: It is pulled out again after a week
116853.e: Bioresorbable vessel supports are made of degradable materials such as lactic acid polymers or magnesium. After the healing phase the body breaks them down.
116853.m: A bioresorbable stent is broken down by the body.

116854.q: Who carried out the first balloon dilation of a coronary artery in a human in Zurich in 1977?
116854.e: In 1977, at University Hospital Zurich, Andreas Grüntzig widened a narrowed coronary artery with a balloon catheter for the first time. This marked the start of interventional cardiology.
116854.m: The first coronary balloon dilation was achieved in Zurich in 1977.

116855.q: What is the coating of a drug-eluting stent for?
a: It stops the vessel from growing closed again
It dissolves calcium from the aorta
It colours the stent on the X-ray
116855.e: The stent slowly releases active substances that slow cell division in the vessel wall. This lowers the risk of renewed narrowing (restenosis).
116855.m: Drug-eluting stents reduce the risk of restenosis.

116856.q: Why do patients usually receive two platelet inhibitors after a stent is implanted?
116856.e: Platelets can stick to the foreign material and form a clot. Dual antiplatelet therapy, for example with acetylsalicylic acid and clopidogrel, prevents this.
116856.m: After a stent, platelet inhibitors protect against clots.

116857.q: Through which access point is a coronary stent often inserted today?
a: Through the artery at the wrist
Through a vein in the neck
116857.e: Today the radial artery at the wrist is often punctured, or alternatively the groin artery. The stent travels to the heart through a catheter.
116857.m: A coronary stent is brought to the heart through the arteries with a catheter.

116858.q: How is a balloon-expandable stent opened up at the narrowing?
116858.e: The stent sits folded up on a balloon catheter. When the balloon is filled under pressure, the stent expands and presses against the vessel wall.
116858.m: A balloon presses the stent against the vessel wall.

116859.q: Who is the term “stent” named after?
116859.e: The name goes back to the English dentist Charles Stent, who developed an impression material in the 19th century. His name was later used for support materials.
116859.m: The stent owes its name to an English dentist.

116860.q: What is done in a heart bypass operation?
a: A narrowing is bypassed with a replacement vessel
116860.e: A vessel is connected so that the blood flows around the narrowed part of the coronary artery. Bypass means a way around.
116860.m: A bypass leads the blood past a narrowing.

116861.q: Which disease most often makes a heart bypass operation necessary?
a: Coronary arteries narrowed by hardening of the arteries
A heartbeat that is too slow
A hole in the septum of the heart
116861.e: In coronary heart disease, deposits build up in the coronary arteries. The heart muscle gets too little blood, and a bypass leads the blood past the narrowing.
116861.m: A bypass helps with narrowed coronary arteries.

116862.q: From which part of the body is a piece of vein often taken for a vein bypass on the heart?
116862.e: The superficial great saphenous vein in the leg is long, easy to reach and can be spared. A piece of it is inserted between the aorta and the coronary artery.
116862.m: Vein bypasses often use a vein from the leg.

116863.q: Which machine temporarily takes over the work of the heart and lungs in many bypass operations?
116863.e: The heart-lung machine pumps the blood and enriches it with oxygen. This allows surgeons to operate on the stopped heart.
116863.m: The heart-lung machine replaces the heart and lungs during the operation.

116864.q: How is the chest usually opened for a classic bypass operation?
116864.e: In a median sternotomy, the breastbone is cut through lengthwise. Afterwards it is closed again with wire loops.
116864.m: For a classic bypass operation, the breastbone is opened lengthwise.

a: An operation on the beating heart
An operation without a replacement vessel
116865.e: In the off-pump method no heart-lung machine is used. A stabiliser keeps the stitching site still on the beating heart.
116865.m: In an off-pump bypass the heart keeps beating during the operation.

116866.q: Which gentler treatment is often chosen instead of a bypass operation for narrowed coronary arteries?
a: A stent is inserted through a catheter
116866.e: Through a catheter in the groin or at the wrist, the narrowing is widened with a balloon and kept open with a stent. The chest does not have to be opened for this.
116866.m: A stent keeps a narrowed coronary artery open without major surgery.

116867.q: What does the German abbreviation ACVB stand for in heart surgery?
116867.e: ACVB refers to a bypass in which a vein leads from the aorta to the coronary artery beyond the narrowing. In English the operation is called CABG.
116867.m: An ACVB connects the aorta to a coronary artery via a vein.

116868.q: What is meant by heart failure?
a: The heart does not pump enough blood for the body's needs
The heart has a hole in the septum
The heart is wrapped in fat
116868.e: In heart failure the heart can no longer supply the body with enough blood, or only at raised filling pressures.
116868.m: In heart failure the heart's pumping power is not enough.

116869.q: Which symptom is typical of left-sided heart failure?
a: Breathlessness from congestion in the lungs
Strong thirst from high blood sugar
116869.e: If the left ventricle pumps too weakly, blood backs up into the lung vessels. Fluid leaks into the tissue, causing breathlessness and, in extreme cases, pulmonary oedema.
116869.m: A weak left ventricle leads to blood backing up in the lungs.

116870.q: Which sign points to right-sided heart failure?
a: Coughing up blood in the morning
116870.e: If the right ventricle pumps too weakly, blood backs up in the body's veins. This causes oedema in the legs, swollen neck veins and a congested liver.
116870.m: In right-sided heart failure, blood backs up in the body's veins.

116871.q: How can you tell severe heart failure from mild heart failure?
a: Breathlessness is present even at rest
Breathlessness only occurs during a marathon
There are no symptoms at all
116871.e: Doctors classify heart failure by its symptoms. In the most severe class, breathlessness and exhaustion are present even at rest.
116871.m: In severe heart failure, symptoms are present even at rest.

116872.q: What does the ejection fraction of the heart show?
a: The share of blood the ventricle pumps out per beat
The number of heartbeats per minute
The blood pressure in the aorta
The size of the heart in centimetres
116872.e: The ejection fraction shows what percentage of its filling the left ventricle pumps out in one beat. In healthy people it is over 50 per cent.
116872.m: The ejection fraction measures the pumping strength of the ventricle.

116873.q: Which examination assesses the heart's pumping power without an invasive procedure?
116873.e: A heart ultrasound shows the ventricles and valves moving. This makes it possible to estimate how strongly the heart pumps.
116873.m: A heart ultrasound shows how well the heart pumps.

116874.q: Why should people with heart failure weigh themselves every day?
a: A rapid gain shows fluid retention
They have to lose weight every day
116874.e: A gain of more than about 1 kg per day or 2 kg in a few days usually points to fluid in the body. The treatment must then be adjusted.
116874.m: Sudden weight gain can show that heart failure is getting worse.

116875.q: Which group of medicines flushes out water in heart failure?
116875.e: Diuretics increase the excretion of salt and water through the kidneys. This reduces oedema and breathlessness.
116875.m: Diuretics help get rid of excess water.

116876.q: From which plant does the historical heart medicine digitalis come?
116876.e: In 1785 the English doctor William Withering described the effect of foxglove leaves on dropsy. The active substances increase the strength of the heart.

a: The electrical activity of the heart
The blood pressure in the arteries
The size of the heart's ventricles
116877.e: The electrocardiogram uses electrodes on the skin to measure the electrical signals that trigger each heartbeat. This makes rhythm disorders such as atrial fibrillation visible.
116877.m: An ECG records the heart's electrical signals.

116878.q: Which serious complication is a particular risk with atrial fibrillation?
a: A stroke caused by a clot
116878.e: In the fibrillating atria, especially the left atrial appendage, blood flows slowly and can clot. A clot that breaks free can block an artery in the brain.
116878.m: Atrial fibrillation increases the risk of stroke.

116879.q: What is typically noticeable when feeling the pulse of someone with atrial fibrillation?
a: The pulse is very slow and completely regular
No pulse can be felt at all
The pulse always beats exactly 60 times a minute
116879.e: The atria twitch chaotically and the ventricles receive the signals at irregular intervals. That is why the pulse is completely irregular.
116879.m: Atrial fibrillation makes the pulse irregular.

116880.q: Which medicines do many people with atrial fibrillation take to prevent a stroke?
116880.e: Blood clots can form in the fibrillating atria. Anticoagulants make this less likely and so lower the risk of stroke.
116880.m: Blood thinners protect against stroke in atrial fibrillation.

a: A targeted electric shock that normalises the rhythm
An operation on the heart valves
116881.e: Under a short anaesthetic, an electric shock synchronised with the ECG is given. All cells are excited at the same time, and afterwards the sinus node often takes over again.
116881.m: Cardioversion uses an electric shock to put the heart back into sinus rhythm.

116882.q: Which structure sets the rhythm in the healthy heart, which is disturbed in atrial fibrillation?
116882.e: The sinus node in the right atrium is the natural pacemaker. In atrial fibrillation, chaotic excitation in the atria drowns out its rhythm.
116882.m: Normally the sinus node sets the heart's rhythm.

116883.q: Which factors particularly increase the risk of atrial fibrillation?
a: Older age and high blood pressure
Young age and a low pulse
116883.e: Atrial fibrillation becomes much more common with age. High blood pressure, being overweight, diabetes and a lot of alcohol also raise the risk.
116883.m: Age and high blood pressure are important risk factors for atrial fibrillation.

116884.q: How common is atrial fibrillation compared with other persistent heart rhythm disorders?
a: It is one of the rarest
116884.e: Atrial fibrillation is the most common persistent heart rhythm disorder. The risk rises clearly with age.
116884.m: Atrial fibrillation is the most common persistent heart rhythm disorder.

116885.q: Roughly how long does the battery of a modern pacemaker last?
116885.e: Modern pacemakers use very little power. When the battery runs out, the whole device is replaced in a small procedure.
116885.m: A pacemaker usually lasts about a decade.

116886.q: For which disorder is a pacemaker typically fitted?
a: A heartbeat that is too slow
116886.e: A pacemaker gives off electrical impulses when the heart beats too slowly, for example with AV block or sinus node disease.
116886.m: A pacemaker mainly helps when the heartbeat is too slow.

116887.q: What should people with a pacemaker watch out for in everyday life?
a: Not holding strong magnets or mobile phones directly over the device
116887.e: Strong magnetic fields can disturb how the pacemaker works. That is why mobile phones or headphones with magnets are kept a little way from the device.
116887.m: A pacemaker needs to be kept away from strong magnets.

116888.q: Which type of battery is usually used in modern pacemakers?
116888.e: Lithium batteries are small, very long-lasting and hardly discharge by themselves. With them, a pacemaker usually lasts many years.
116888.m: Pacemakers are usually powered by lithium batteries.

116889.q: By which route do the leads of a classic pacemaker reach the heart?
a: Through a vein below the collarbone
Through the aorta from the groin
Through the skin directly into the heart
116889.e: The leads are pushed through a vein below the collarbone into the right atrium or right ventricle. The device lies under the skin.
116889.m: Pacemaker leads are guided through a vein into the right side of the heart.

116890.q: What is special about a capsule pacemaker?
a: It sits directly in the right ventricle without wires
It is worn on the wrist
It is swallowed and passed out again
116890.e: The wireless capsule pacemaker is about the size of a large vitamin capsule and is placed in the right ventricle by catheter. No lead wires are then needed.
116890.m: A capsule pacemaker needs no wires.

116891.q: What is a biventricular pacemaker (CRT) for?
a: It synchronises both ventricles in heart failure
It dissolves blood clots in the atrium
It replaces a faulty heart valve
116891.e: In some forms of heart failure the ventricles contract out of step. Cardiac resynchronisation therapy stimulates both ventricles at the same time and so improves pumping.
116891.m: CRT brings both ventricles back into step.

116892.q: What can an implantable defibrillator (ICD) do in addition to a pacemaker?
a: End ventricular fibrillation with a shock
116892.e: An ICD recognises life-threatening fast rhythm disorders such as ventricular fibrillation and then gives an electric shock.
116892.m: An ICD can end ventricular fibrillation with an electric shock.

116893.q: With classic cold storage, roughly how long may a donor heart be outside the body?
116893.e: When cooled on ice, the heart should usually be supplied with blood again within about four hours. That is why removal, transport and implantation must happen very quickly.
116893.m: A donor heart must be implanted within a few hours.

116894.q: In which city did the world's first heart transplant take place in 1967?
116894.e: In December 1967 the surgeon Christiaan Barnard transplanted a human heart for the first time in Cape Town. Switzerland followed in 1969 in Zurich.
116894.m: The first heart transplant was carried out in Cape Town in 1967.

116895.q: Why do people have to take medicines for life after a heart transplant?
a: So that the immune system does not reject the donor heart
So that the heart grows faster
So that the blood becomes thicker
So that the scar heals more neatly
116895.e: The immune system recognises the donor heart as foreign. Medicines damp down the defence so that it does not attack the heart.
116895.m: After a transplant, medicines prevent rejection.

116896.q: Why does a transplanted heart react to exertion with a faster pulse only after a delay?
a: It is not connected to nerves
It is smaller than the old heart
116896.e: The nerves are cut during the transplant. So the heart only speeds up once hormones such as adrenaline rise in the blood.
116896.m: A transplanted heart is controlled mainly by hormones.

116897.q: How is rejection of a donor heart often monitored?
a: With small tissue samples from the heart muscle
116897.e: In an endomyocardial biopsy, tiny samples are taken from the inner wall of the heart through a catheter. Signs of rejection can be seen under the microscope.
116897.m: Heart muscle biopsies show the start of rejection.

116898.q: From which animal did the heart come that was transplanted into a living human for the first time in the USA in 2022?
116898.e: In January 2022, a man with severe heart disease in Maryland received a genetically modified pig heart. He lived for about two more months.
116898.m: Transplanting animal organs into humans is called xenotransplantation.

116899.q: What is a ventricular assist device (VAD) often used for before a transplant?
a: To bridge the time until a donor heart is available
116899.e: An implanted pump supports the weakened ventricle. This lets people with severe heart disease bridge the often long wait for a donor heart.
116899.m: A VAD can bridge the wait for a donor heart.

116900.q: In a usual heart transplant, what happens to the diseased heart?
a: It is removed and replaced by the donor heart
It is repaired and put back
It is moved into the abdomen
It is frozen and returned later
116900.e: The diseased heart is taken out and the donor heart is sewn in its place. Specialists call this orthotopic transplantation.
116900.m: In a usual heart transplant, the donor heart replaces the old heart.

116901.q: Apart from the coronary arteries, in which vessel are stents also often used?
a: In the portal vein of the liver
In the skin veins of the hand
116901.e: Stents are also used for narrowings of the carotid artery and the leg and kidney arteries. Everywhere the aim is to restore blood flow.
116901.m: Stents keep open not only coronary arteries but other arteries too.

116902.q: How does the sympathetic nervous system affect the sinus node?
116902.e: Through noradrenaline the sympathetic system has a positive chronotropic effect. The pacemaker cells depolarise faster and the heart beats more quickly.
116902.m: The sympathetic nervous system speeds up the heartbeat.

116903.q: Roughly what share of cardiac output flows through the coronary arteries at rest?
116903.e: The heart makes up only about half a per cent of body weight but receives about 5 % of cardiac output. Even at rest it extracts a lot of the oxygen from the blood.
116903.m: The heart receives about five per cent of cardiac output for itself.

116904.q: A 50 kg crate is lifted 10 m. How much gravitational potential energy does it gain (with g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116904.m: Gravitational potential energy is the product of mass, gravitational acceleration and height.

116905.q: An 80 kg climber climbs from 1000 m above sea level to 3000 m above sea level. By how much does her gravitational potential energy increase (with g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116905.e: What matters is the height difference of 2000 m: 80 kg · 9.81 m/s² · 2000 m = 1,569,600 J, so about 1.57 MJ.
116905.m: For the change in potential energy, only the height difference counts.

116906.q: How high do you have to lift a 2 kg body for its gravitational potential energy to rise by 100 J (with g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116906.m: You get the lifting height by dividing the energy by mass times g.

116907.q: A 100 g apple falls 1 m. Roughly how much gravitational potential energy does it lose (with g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116907.e: E = 0.1 kg · 9.81 m/s² · 1 m ≈ 0.98 J. That is about one joule.
116907.m: Lifting an apple by one metre takes about one joule.

116908.q: Apart from mass and g, what else does the numerical value of a body’s gravitational potential energy depend on?
a: On the choice of the zero level
On the colour of the body
116908.e: The height h is always measured from a freely chosen reference level. Physically, only differences in potential energy matter.
116908.m: Gravitational potential energy depends on the chosen zero level.

116909.q: How much work against gravity do you do when you carry a suitcase 20 m horizontally at the same height?
116909.e: Work against gravity is only done when the height changes. In horizontal motion the weight acts at right angles to the path, so physically the work done in lifting is zero.
116909.m: Without a change in height, no work against gravity is done.

116910.q: A 1000 kg car drives up a winding mountain pass road, climbing 100 metres in height over a distance of 2 km. By how much does its gravitational potential energy increase (with g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116910.e: For potential energy only the height difference counts, not the length of the route: 1000 kg · 9.81 m/s² · 100 m = 981,000 J.
116910.m: Gravitational potential energy does not depend on the route.

116911.q: What is the minimum work needed to pump 1 m³ of water (1000 kg) 20 m up (with g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116911.m: The minimum work for lifting equals the potential energy gained.

116912.q: A 1200 kg car is travelling at 72 km/h. What is its kinetic energy?
116912.m: For kinetic energy, the speed must be entered in m/s.

116913.q: A 40 t lorry is travelling at 25 m/s (90 km/h). What is its kinetic energy?
116913.m: Heavy vehicles have enormous kinetic energy even at moderate speed.

116914.q: A cyclist and her bicycle have a mass of 90 kg and she rides at 10 m/s. What is her kinetic energy?
116914.m: Kinetic energy is half the mass times speed squared.

116915.q: A 0.5 kg ball has 100 J of kinetic energy. How fast is it?
116915.m: From kinetic energy you get the speed via the square root of 2E divided by m.

116916.q: A 58 g tennis ball flies at 50 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
116916.m: Even small masses carry a lot of energy at high speed.

116917.q: By what percentage does kinetic energy rise if speed increases by 10 %?
116917.e: Energy is proportional to v². 1.1² = 1.21, so the energy rises by 21 %.
116917.m: Because of the square, small increases in speed have a bigger effect on energy.

116918.q: How does kinetic energy change if the mass is doubled at the same speed?
116918.e: Mass enters E = ½ · m · v² linearly. Double the mass gives double the energy.
116918.m: Kinetic energy is proportional to mass.

116919.q: Why does the braking distance become about four times as long at double the speed?
a: Because the kinetic energy is four times as large
Because the reaction time gets longer
116919.e: The brakes have to turn all the kinetic energy into heat. With the same braking force, the distance is proportional to the energy, and so to v².
116919.m: Braking distance grows with the square of the speed.

116920.q: A spring with D = 400 N/m is stretched by 5 cm and then stretched further to 10 cm. How much energy is added?
116920.e: At 10 cm: 0.5 · 400 · 0.1² J = 2 J. At 5 cm: 0.5 · 400 · 0.05² J = 0.5 J. The increase is 1.5 J.
116920.m: When stretching further, the difference in elastic energies is what counts.

116921.q: A spring with D = 500 N/m is compressed by 4 cm. How much energy is stored?
116921.m: The extension must be entered in metres.

116922.q: How does the elastic energy of a spring change if you double the extension?
116922.e: The extension enters E = ½ · D · s² squared. Double the extension gives four times the energy.
116922.m: Double the extension stores four times the energy.

116923.q: Two identical springs, each with D = 200 N/m, are hung one below the other. What is the spring constant of the whole arrangement?
116923.e: In series, each spring carries the full force, so the total extension doubles. That is why the spring constant halves: 1/D = 1/200 + 1/200, so D = 100 N/m.
116923.m: Springs in series are softer together than a single spring.

116924.q: What is the law called according to which the spring force is proportional to the extension?
116924.e: In 1678 Robert Hooke described that the force of an elastic spring is proportional to its displacement: F = D · s.
116924.m: Hooke’s law describes the linear spring force.

116925.q: A spring with D = 800 N/m is compressed by 5 cm and fires a 20 g ball. How fast does the ball become without losses?
116925.e: The elastic energy is 0.5 · 800 · 0.05² J = 1 J. From ½ · 0.02 kg · v² = 1 J it follows that v² = 100 m²/s², so v = 10 m/s.
116925.m: The spring’s elastic energy is converted into kinetic energy.

116926.q: How far must a spring with D = 400 N/m be stretched to store 2 J?
116926.m: The required extension is the square root of 2E divided by D.

116927.q: Why does the formula for elastic energy contain the factor ½?
a: The spring force grows from zero as it is stretched
The spring loses half its energy as heat
Only half the spring is stretched
The factor is purely a convention
116927.e: The force rises linearly from 0 to D · s. The work is the area under the force-distance line, a triangle with the area ½ · D · s · s.
116927.m: Elastic energy equals the area of the triangle in the force-distance graph.

116928.q: In what form is the energy mainly found at the lowest point of a trampoline jump?
116928.e: At the lowest point the jumper is still for a moment and the bed or springs are stretched as far as possible. Almost all the energy is then stored as elastic energy.
116928.m: At the lowest point on the trampoline, the elastic energy is greatest.
