a: They may be sold without any notice
They are only available in chemists
They are only allowed as animal feed
118244.e: GM ingredients must be declared. Only accidental, technically unavoidable traces below 0.9 per cent per ingredient are exempt from labelling.
118244.m: Genetically modified ingredients must be declared.

a: The genome contains genes from another species
The plant has only been crossed
The gene comes from the same plant
118245.e: In transgenic organisms, genes from another species have been inserted, for example bacterial genes into maize. In cisgenic plants the genes come from the same species or one it can be crossed with.
118245.m: Transgenic organisms carry genes from a foreign species.

118246.q: Which method shoots gold or tungsten particles coated with DNA into plant cells?
118246.e: With the gene gun, tiny metal particles are loaded with DNA and shot into cells at high speed. This gets genes into plants that are difficult to modify with bacteria.
118246.m: The gene gun shoots DNA-coated metal particles into cells.

118247.q: Which international agreement regulates the movement of genetically modified organisms across borders?
118247.e: The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety adds to the Convention on Biological Diversity. It came into force in 2003, and Switzerland is also a party to it.
118247.m: The Cartagena Protocol regulates the international trade in GMOs.

118248.q: Which characteristic did the Roundup Ready soya introduced in 1996 have?
118248.e: The soya survives being sprayed with glyphosate, while weeds do not. Herbicide tolerance is still one of the most common GM traits today.
118248.m: Roundup Ready soya tolerates the herbicide glyphosate.

118249.q: What were antibiotic resistance genes often used for in early genetically modified plants?
a: As markers to pick out modified cells
To protect the plant from insects
As a nutrient for the plant
118249.e: Only cells that had taken up the new gene together with the marker survived on a nutrient medium containing an antibiotic. Today people try to avoid such markers.
118249.m: Marker genes help to find cells that have been successfully modified.

118250.q: In which group of plants was gene transfer with Agrobacterium tumefaciens much easier at first?
118250.e: In nature, Agrobacterium mainly infects dicot plants. In cereals the method only worked later with improved procedures, which is why the gene gun was often used there.
118250.m: Agrobacterium is especially well suited to dicot plants.

118251.q: What is the plasmid called that Agrobacterium tumefaciens uses to change plant cells?
118251.e: Ti stands for “tumour-inducing”. A section of this plasmid is inserted into the genome of the plant cell.
118251.m: The Ti plasmid is the tool of Agrobacterium.

118252.q: What is the section of DNA called that Agrobacterium transfers into the plant's genome?
118252.e: The transfer DNA (T-DNA) lies on the Ti plasmid between two border sequences. Genetic engineers replace its contents with the genes they want.
118252.m: The T-DNA is inserted into the plant genome by the bacterium.

118253.q: How does the bacterium benefit from infected plant cells producing opines?
a: It can use the opines as food
The opines make the plant invisible
The opines serve as a spore coat
118253.e: The transferred genes make the plant cells produce opines, which almost only Agrobacterium can use. In this way the bacterium creates its own food source.
118253.m: Agrobacterium makes the plant produce opines as food for itself.

118254.q: Why is Agrobacterium tumefaciens often called a “natural genetic engineer”?
a: Because it naturally inserts genes into plants
118254.e: Long before humans used genetic engineering, the bacterium was transferring its own genes into plant cells. Researchers use exactly this mechanism.
118254.m: Agrobacterium naturally transfers genes into plants.

118255.q: Which disease does Agrobacterium tumefaciens cause in plants?
118255.e: The bacterium inserts genes into plant cells that make them grow out of control. This produces tumour-like swellings at the root collar, called galls.

118256.q: With which plant was one of the first genetic modifications using Agrobacterium achieved in 1983?
118256.e: Tobacco is easy to grow in the laboratory and to regenerate from single cells. That is why it was one of the first transgenic plants.
118256.m: Tobacco was one of the first plants modified with Agrobacterium.

118257.q: In nature, how does Agrobacterium tumefaciens get into a plant?
a: Through injuries at the root collar or trunk
118257.e: Injured plant tissue releases phenols such as acetosyringone. These attract the bacterium and switch on the genes for gene transfer.

118258.q: Where does the gene come from that makes Bt maize produce an insect-killing protein?
118258.e: Bt stands for Bacillus thuringiensis. This soil bacterium produces Cry proteins, which are poisonous to certain insect larvae.
118258.m: Bt maize carries a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis.

118259.q: Against which pest was Bt maize mainly developed in Europe?
118259.e: The caterpillars of the European corn borer bore into maize stalks and weaken the plant. The Cry protein in Bt maize kills these caterpillars.
118259.m: Bt maize protects against the European corn borer.

118260.q: Why is the Bt protein harmless to humans but deadly to certain insect larvae?
a: It is only activated in the alkaline gut of the larvae and needs matching receptors
It only works in the cold
118260.e: The protein is split in the alkaline insect gut and binds to special receptors in the gut wall. Mammals have neither these conditions nor these receptors.
118260.m: Bt protein only works in the alkaline gut of certain insects.

118261.q: How is the growing of genetically modified plants such as Bt maize regulated in Switzerland?
a: It is only allowed in Ticino
It is only allowed for organic farms
118261.e: After a popular vote in 2005, Switzerland has had a GM moratorium for agriculture. Parliament has extended it several times since then.
118261.m: Switzerland has a GM moratorium on growing such crops.

118262.q: In what form is the Bt protein also used in organic farming?
a: As a spray containing the bacteria or their proteins
As a seed treatment against fungi
118262.e: Products made from Bacillus thuringiensis are allowed as insecticides in organic farming. They are sprayed onto the outside of the plants.
118262.m: Bt products are also sprayed in organic farming.

118263.q: What are the so-called refuges next to Bt maize fields meant to prevent?
a: Pests developing resistance to the Bt protein
118263.e: Maize without the Bt gene grows in the refuges. Sensitive insects survive there and mate with resistant ones, which slows the spread of resistance.
118263.m: Refuges slow down the development of resistance to Bt plants.

118264.q: Which group of insects does the European corn borer, which Bt maize works against, belong to?
118264.e: The European corn borer is a small moth. Its caterpillars eat their way into maize stalks and are killed by the Bt protein.
118264.m: The European corn borer is a moth.

118265.q: What advantage is Bt maize meant to bring for crop protection?
a: Fewer insecticide sprayings against boring caterpillars
118265.e: Caterpillars inside the stalk are hard to reach with sprays. Because the plant produces the toxin itself, insecticides can often be avoided.
118265.m: Bt maize can save insecticide sprayings.

118266.q: Where is the International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV) based?
118266.e: UPOV was founded in 1961 by a convention signed in Paris. It is based in Geneva and is closely linked with WIPO.
118266.m: The plant variety union UPOV is based in Geneva.

118267.q: Which three technical criteria must a variety meet to receive plant variety protection?
118267.e: The DUS test (distinctness, uniformity, stability) checks whether the variety clearly stands out, is uniform and stays the same over generations. Novelty and a variety name are also required.
118267.m: A protected variety must be distinct, uniform and stable.

118268.q: What does the so-called breeders' exemption in plant variety protection allow?
a: Using protected varieties freely to breed new varieties
Selling other people's varieties under your own name
118268.e: Other breeders may use a protected variety for crosses without permission. This clearly distinguishes plant variety protection from a patent.
118268.m: Thanks to the breeders' exemption, protected varieties may be used for further breeding.

118269.q: What applies to a plant variety once its protection has expired?
a: Anyone may freely propagate and sell it
It may no longer be grown
It becomes the property of the state
118269.e: Plant variety protection is limited in time, in Switzerland usually to 25 years, and to 30 years for vines and trees. After that the variety can be used freely.
118269.m: Once protection expires, a variety can be used freely.

118270.q: What does the farmers' privilege allow?
a: Sowing harvested seed of a protected variety again on your own farm
Registering any variety as your own
118270.e: With the farmers' privilege, farmers may sow seed they have harvested themselves on their own farm for certain species. Selling it remains forbidden.
118270.m: The farmers' privilege allows saved seed to be sown again on your own farm.

118271.q: Which federal office is responsible for granting plant variety protection in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)
The Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)
118271.e: The Plant Variety Protection Office is part of the Federal Office for Agriculture. It checks applications and grants the protection titles.
118271.m: In Switzerland the FOAG grants plant variety protection.

118272.q: Can plant varieties as such be patented in Europe?
a: No, they are excluded from patent protection
Yes, every variety is automatically patented
118272.e: The European Patent Convention excludes plant varieties from being patented. Plant variety protection exists for them instead.
118272.m: In Europe plant varieties are protected by plant variety protection instead of patents.

118273.q: What is the international organisation UPOV, based in Geneva, responsible for?
a: The protection of newly bred plant varieties
The protection of endangered wild plants
118273.e: UPOV is based on a convention from 1961. It makes sure that breeders can have their new varieties protected in many countries under the same rules. Switzerland is a member.
118273.m: UPOV regulates international plant variety protection.

118274.q: What is the aim of the Swiss foundation ProSpecieRara?
a: Preserving rare livestock breeds and crop varieties
118274.e: ProSpecieRara saves breeds and varieties of cultural, historical and genetic value from dying out. To do this it works with farmers, gardeners and variety keepers.
118274.m: ProSpecieRara saves old livestock breeds and crop plants.

118275.q: What did ProSpecieRara focus on first when it was founded?
118275.e: The foundation was set up in 1982 and first looked after endangered livestock breeds. Crop varieties were added later.
118275.m: ProSpecieRara began by saving old livestock breeds.

118276.q: Which breed of goat is looked after by ProSpecieRara?
118276.e: The booted goat from the St Gallen Oberland had almost died out in the 1980s. ProSpecieRara helped to build up its numbers again.
118276.m: The booted goat is a goat breed saved by ProSpecieRara.

118277.q: Which breed of cattle from the Grisons was rebuilt thanks to ProSpecieRara?
118277.e: The Rhaetian Grey was thought to be extinct in Switzerland. From the 1980s it was reintroduced using animals from Tyrol.
118277.m: The Rhaetian Grey returned to Switzerland thanks to ProSpecieRara.

118278.q: Which old Swiss chicken breed with a forward-pointing crest of feathers is preserved by ProSpecieRara?
118278.e: The Appenzeller Spitzhauben had almost died out by around 1950. ProSpecieRara started a conservation project for the breed in 1983.
118278.m: The Appenzeller Spitzhauben is an old Swiss chicken breed.

118279.q: How does ProSpecieRara keep old vegetable varieties alive?
a: By having many gardeners grow them and save their seed
Only by freezing them in the laboratory
118279.e: The varieties are grown in gardens and on farms, and their seed is collected anew every year. This way they stay adapted to their environment and alive.
118279.m: ProSpecieRara preserves varieties by having them grown regularly in many gardens.

118280.q: Why are most ProSpecieRara varieties suitable for saving your own seed, but modern F1 hybrids hardly at all?
a: Because they are open-pollinated and breed true
118280.e: Open-pollinated varieties pass their characteristics on to their offspring. In F1 hybrids the traits split up in the next generation.
118280.m: Open-pollinated varieties can be grown again from your own seed.

118281.q: In which city does the ProSpecieRara foundation have its head office?
118281.e: The head office is in Basel on the Brüglingen site. There are also offices in French-speaking Switzerland and in Ticino.
118281.m: ProSpecieRara has its head office in Basel.

118282.q: In mutation breeding, how are changes in the genes triggered?
118282.e: Seeds or plant parts are treated with gamma rays, X-rays or chemicals, for example. The random mutations that result are then selected.
118282.m: Mutation breeding uses radiation or chemicals to create random mutations.

a: A substance or radiation that causes mutations
118283.e: Mutagens such as UV radiation, X-rays or certain chemicals change the genes. In mutation breeding they are used deliberately.
118283.m: Mutagens cause changes in the genes.

118284.q: Do plants from classic mutation breeding legally count as GMOs that must be labelled in the EU and Switzerland?
a: No, they are exempt from genetic engineering regulation
Only if they come from Japan
118284.e: Conventional mutagenesis is exempt because it has been used safely for a long time. Such varieties are also widespread in organic farming.
118284.m: Classic mutation breeding is exempt from GMO regulation.

118285.q: Which international organisations jointly run a database of over 3,000 mutant varieties?
118285.e: The joint division of the Food and Agriculture Organization FAO and the International Atomic Energy Agency IAEA promotes mutation breeding. Its database lists over 3,000 varieties worldwide.
118285.m: FAO and IAEA jointly promote mutation breeding.

118286.q: Why do a great many plants have to be checked after seeds have been irradiated?
a: Most mutations are useless or harmful
Every plant has the same mutation
118286.e: The mutations arise randomly. Only very rarely does one of them improve a desired characteristic, which is why a large selection is needed.

118287.q: Are foods from plants produced by mutation breeding radioactive themselves?
a: No, only the genes were changed
Yes, they give off radiation for life
118287.e: The radiation changes the DNA of the treated seeds but does not make them radioactive. The offspring are normal plants with changed characteristics.
118287.m: Mutation breeding does not make plants radioactive.

118288.q: Which kind of radiation can damage the genes of skin cells in humans, just as in mutation breeding?
118288.e: UV radiation can change the DNA in skin cells. Such mutations can cause skin cancer, which is why sun protection is important.
118288.m: UV radiation can damage the genes.

118289.q: What is the biggest disadvantage of mutation breeding compared with genome editing?
a: The mutations are undirected, so many plants have to be searched
It is banned in every country
It does not change the genes at all
118289.e: Radiation or chemicals hit the genome randomly in many places. That is why thousands of plants have to be checked to find a useful mutant.
118289.m: Mutation breeding is undirected and needs a large selection.

118290.q: What is a “gamma garden” in plant breeding?
a: A trial field around a radiation source to cause mutations
A garden with only plants of the genus Gamma
A school garden with three beds
118290.e: In gamma gardens, plants grow in circles around a radioactive source, usually cobalt-60. The closer they are, the stronger the radiation and the more mutations there are.
118290.m: In gamma gardens, plants are irradiated for mutation breeding.

118387.q: Which enzyme already starts splitting starch in the mouth?
118387.e: The salivary glands release alpha-amylase into saliva. It already splits starch into shorter pieces while you chew.
118387.m: Starch digestion already starts in the mouth.

118388.q: Which bonds in starch does alpha-amylase split?
118388.e: Alpha-amylase hydrolyses the alpha-1,4 links between glucose units inside the starch chains. Humans cannot split beta-1,4 bonds such as those in cellulose.
118388.m: Alpha-amylase breaks the alpha-1,4 bonds of starch.

118389.q: Which disaccharide is mainly produced when amylase splits starch?
118389.e: Amylase breaks starch down mainly into maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins. Maltose consists of two glucose units.
118389.m: Amylase turns starch mainly into maltose.

118390.q: Why does bread taste slightly sweet when you chew it for a long time?
a: Amylase in saliva splits starch into sugar
Saliva itself contains a lot of sugar
The tongue makes sweeteners while chewing
The bread releases fat while being chewed
118390.e: Salivary amylase breaks the long starch chains in bread down into smaller sugars such as maltose. These taste sweet.
118390.m: Salivary amylase turns starch into sweet sugar.

118391.q: Besides the salivary glands, which organ also produces alpha-amylase for digestion?
118391.e: The pancreas releases pancreatic amylase into the duodenum. There it continues the digestion of starch.

118392.q: Why does salivary amylase soon stop working in the stomach?
118392.e: Salivary amylase works best at a neutral pH. As soon as stomach acid soaks through the food mass, the enzyme is inactivated.

118393.q: A greatly raised amylase level in the blood is a typical sign of which disease?
118393.e: When the pancreas is inflamed, more of its enzymes get into the blood. That is why amylase is measured in diagnosis.
118393.m: High amylase in the blood can point to pancreatitis.

118394.q: Why does amylase no longer split starch after being heated to 100 °C?
a: The enzyme is denatured by the heat
The amylase is broken down into sugar
118394.e: Enzymes are proteins with a precise three-dimensional shape. Great heat destroys this shape, and the active site no longer fits the starch.
118394.m: Too much heat destroys enzymes such as amylase.

118395.q: You mix starch solution with saliva and test it repeatedly with iodine solution. What does it show when the blue colour disappears?
a: The starch has been broken down
118395.e: Iodine only turns long starch chains blue. If amylase splits the starch, the blue colour no longer appears.
118395.m: The iodine test shows whether starch is still present.

118396.q: In which inactive precursor form is pepsin produced?
118396.e: The stomach lining releases pepsin as pepsinogen. Only in the inside of the stomach is the active enzyme formed from it.

118397.q: Which substance in the stomach creates the acidic environment in which pepsin works?
118397.e: The stomach lining releases hydrochloric acid. It activates pepsinogen to pepsin and kills many germs in food.
118397.m: Hydrochloric acid makes the stomach acidic.

118398.q: What activates pepsinogen in the stomach?
a: Hydrochloric acid and pepsin that is already active
118398.e: In the acidic environment, a piece breaks off pepsinogen. Pepsin that has already formed speeds up this activation autocatalytically.
118398.m: Acid and pepsin itself activate pepsinogen.

118399.q: In which pH range does pepsin work best?
118399.e: Pepsin is adapted to the strongly acidic environment of the stomach. Its optimum is at a pH of about 1.5 to 2.

118400.q: In what form do the chief cells of the stomach first release pepsin?
a: As part of the hydrochloric acid
118400.e: Pepsin is released as the inactive precursor pepsinogen. Only stomach acid turns it into active pepsin, so the cells do not digest themselves.
118400.m: Pepsin forms in the stomach from the precursor pepsinogen.

118401.e: Pepsin splits proteins in the stomach into shorter polypeptides. Enzymes in the small intestine take over the further breakdown.

118402.q: What protects the stomach wall from being digested by pepsin itself?
118402.e: Mucous neck cells and the surface lining form a thick layer of mucus. It keeps acid and pepsin away from the lining cells.
118402.m: Mucus protects the stomach from digesting itself.

118403.q: What happens to pepsin when the food mass reaches the small intestine?
a: It stops working in the less acidic environment
It is absorbed into the blood and keeps working
118403.e: In the small intestine, the food mass is neutralised with bicarbonate. Pepsin needs a strongly acidic environment and loses its effect there; other enzymes take over.
118403.m: Pepsin only works in the acidic stomach.

118404.q: Where is the inactive precursor trypsinogen converted into active trypsin?
118404.e: An enzyme of the small intestine lining, enteropeptidase, cuts a short piece off trypsinogen in the duodenum. Only then is trypsin active.
118404.m: Trypsin is only activated in the small intestine.

118405.q: Which nutrients does the digestive enzyme trypsin split?
118405.e: Trypsin is a protease from the pancreas. It breaks down proteins in the small intestine into shorter peptides.
118405.m: Trypsin is a protein-splitting digestive enzyme.

118406.q: Why is trypsin also used in the lab to study proteins?
a: It cuts proteins only at very specific points
It stains proteins so they are visible
It builds proteins from amino acids
118406.e: Trypsin cuts after the amino acids lysine and arginine. Because the pieces are therefore predictable, it is often used in research.
118406.m: Trypsin cuts proteins at precisely defined points.

118407.q: Which enzyme precursor is activated directly by trypsin in the small intestine?
118407.e: Trypsin activates other pancreatic proenzymes such as chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidases. In this way it triggers an activation cascade.

118408.q: Why does the pancreas produce trypsin as an inactive precursor?
a: To protect itself from digesting itself
Because otherwise it would get into the blood
So that it can split fat
118408.e: Active trypsin would attack the tissue of the pancreas. It is only activated in the gut.
118408.m: Proenzymes protect the pancreas from digesting itself.

118409.q: At roughly what pH does trypsin work best?
118409.e: Trypsin works in the slightly alkaline environment of the small intestine. Its optimum is roughly at pH 8.
118409.m: Trypsin works in the slightly alkaline range.

118410.q: What can happen if trypsin already becomes active in the pancreas?
118410.e: Active trypsin attacks the body's own tissue and activates other enzymes. Normally the inhibitor SPINK1 blocks small amounts; if this protection fails, pancreatitis can develop.
118410.m: Trypsin that is active too early can attack the pancreas itself.

118411.q: In which inherited disease do too few digestive enzymes such as trypsin often get from the pancreas into the gut?
118411.e: In cystic fibrosis, thick mucus blocks the ducts of the pancreas. The enzymes do not reach the gut, so patients take enzyme capsules with their meals.
118411.m: In cystic fibrosis, digestive enzymes are often missing in the gut.

118412.q: Into which building blocks do lipases split dietary fats (triglycerides)?
a: Into fatty acids and glycerol parts
118412.e: A triglyceride consists of glycerol and three fatty acids. Pancreatic lipase usually splits off the two outer fatty acids, producing monoacylglycerol and free fatty acids.
118412.m: Lipases split fats into fatty acids and glycerol parts.

118413.q: Why do lipases in the gut need the help of bile salts?
a: Bile salts break the fat up into small droplets
Bile salts split the fat completely themselves
Bile salts make the fat acidic
Bile salts protect the fat from digestion
118413.e: Bile salts emulsify fat into fine droplets and so enlarge the surface on which lipase works. A helper protein, colipase, anchors the lipase to the droplet.
118413.m: Bile salts enlarge the fat surface for lipase.

118414.q: What kind of chemical bond do lipases split in a fat molecule?
118414.e: In fats, fatty acids are attached to glycerol by ester bonds. Lipases split these by adding water, preferably at the two outer positions.
118414.m: Lipases split the ester bonds of fats.

118415.q: Which lipase starts splitting fat even before the small intestine?
118415.e: The chief cells of the stomach make an acid-stable gastric lipase. It already splits a small part of the dietary fats.
118415.m: The stomach already splits some fat too.

118416.q: Which enzyme does the weight-loss medicine orlistat block in the gut?
118416.e: Orlistat blocks gastric and pancreatic lipases. Part of the dietary fat is then passed out undigested.
118416.m: Orlistat blocks fat splitting in the gut.

118417.q: Which class of enzymes do lipases belong to?
118417.e: Lipases split bonds by adding water. Like all digestive enzymes, they therefore belong to the hydrolases.

118418.q: What is a typical sign that too little pancreatic lipase is reaching the gut?
118418.e: Without enough lipase, fat is not split and not absorbed. The stools then become bulky, shiny and fatty (steatorrhoea).
118418.m: If lipase is missing, fatty stools result.

118419.q: Where does a lipase attack fats in the gut?
a: At the boundary between fat and water
118419.e: Lipases are water-soluble, their substrates are not. That is why they work on the surface of the fat droplets (interfacial activation).
118419.m: Lipase works on the surface of the fat droplets.

118420.q: From which starting material does the liver make bile acids?
118420.e: The liver converts cholesterol into bile acids in several enzyme steps. This is an important way of getting rid of cholesterol.
118420.m: Bile acids are made from cholesterol.

118421.e: The liver makes bile all the time. The gall bladder does not make it itself, it only stores and concentrates it.
118421.m: Bile is made in the liver, not in the gall bladder.

118422.q: How are secondary bile acids formed?
a: By being changed by gut bacteria
By being changed in the kidney
118422.e: Bacteria in the gut remove conjugates and hydroxyl groups from the primary bile acids. This produces, for example, deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid.
118422.m: Gut bacteria turn primary bile acids into secondary ones.

118423.q: Bile acids in the gut help with the digestion of which nutrients?
118423.e: Bile acids break large drops of fat into fine droplets. This lets the fat-splitting enzymes work better.
118423.m: Bile acids help with fat digestion.

118424.q: What percentage of bile acids return to the liver through the enterohepatic circulation?
118424.e: Most bile acids are taken up again in the lower small intestine and carried back to the liver in the blood. Only a small remainder is lost in the stools.
118424.m: Almost all bile acids are reused.

118425.e: If bile contains too much cholesterol compared with bile acids, it comes out of solution and forms stones in the gall bladder.
118425.m: Most gallstones are made of cholesterol.

118426.q: Where does bile from the gall bladder go during a meal?
118426.e: After a fatty meal, the gall bladder contracts. Bile flows through the bile duct into the duodenum, the start of the small intestine.

118427.q: Where is bile stored and thickened between meals?
118427.e: The liver makes bile all the time. The gall bladder stores it and removes water from it, so it becomes more concentrated.
118427.m: The gall bladder stores and concentrates bile.

118428.q: What does the emulsification of dietary fats in the small intestine do?
a: Large fat drops break up into many small ones
118428.e: Bile salts and the mixing of the food mass break large fat drops into many fine droplets. No chemical bonds are split in the process.
118428.m: Emulsification enlarges the surface of fats.

118429.q: What does it mean that bile salts are amphiphilic?
a: They have water-loving and fat-loving parts
They are strongly acidic and alkaline
118429.e: Bile salts have a water-loving and a fat-loving side. This lets them sit at the boundary between fat and water.
118429.m: Amphiphilic substances link fat and water.

118430.q: What are the tiny clusters of bile salts and fat breakdown products that travel to the gut wall called?
118430.e: Bile salts form tiny micelles with monoacylglycerols and fatty acids. These carry the fat building blocks through the watery layer to the gut cell.
118430.m: Micelles carry fat building blocks to the gut wall.

118431.q: Which food is an emulsion of oil droplets in water?
118431.e: In mayonnaise, fine oil droplets are spread through the watery egg yolk and vinegar. Butter, the other way round, is an emulsion of water droplets in fat.

a: A fine mixture of two liquids that do not mix
A mixture of gas and liquid
118432.e: In an emulsion, droplets of one liquid are spread through another, for example oil in water. Milk is an example.
118432.m: An emulsion spreads one liquid finely through another.

118433.q: Besides bile salts, what helps emulsify fats mechanically?
a: The muscle movements of the stomach and gut
The breathing movements of the lungs
118433.e: The stomach and small intestine mix and knead the food mass hard. These shearing forces break up fat drops even further.
118433.m: Mixing the food mass helps with emulsifying.

118434.q: Which phospholipid in bile helps emulsify fats?
118434.e: Lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) is also amphiphilic. Together with the bile salts it forms mixed micelles.

118435.q: Why does emulsification speed up fat digestion even though it does not split any bonds?
a: The surface for enzymes to work on gets bigger
The fats are heated in the process
The enzymes are made in the process
118435.e: Fat-splitting enzymes can only work on the surface of the droplets. Many small droplets offer a much larger surface than one big drop.

118436.q: In which section of the digestive tract are most nutrients absorbed?
118436.e: The small intestine is long and, thanks to folds, villi and microvilli, has a huge surface. Most nutrients get into the blood there.
118436.m: The small intestine absorbs most nutrients.

118437.q: What are the tiny projections of the gut cell membrane that form the brush border called?
118437.e: Every gut lining cell carries thousands of microvilli on its surface. They greatly enlarge the absorbing surface once again.
118437.m: Microvilli form the brush border of gut cells.

118438.q: How does glucose get from the inside of the gut into the gut lining cell?
a: By secondary active transport together with sodium
118438.e: The transporter SGLT1 takes up glucose together with sodium ions. The energy comes from the sodium gradient maintained by the sodium-potassium pump.
118438.m: Glucose travels into the gut cell with sodium.

118439.q: Why do some people have trouble digesting milk sugar?
a: Their small intestine makes too little lactase
Their stomach makes too much acid
Their pancreas makes too little insulin
Their liver breaks down fat too slowly
118439.e: The enzyme lactase splits milk sugar into glucose and galactose, which are absorbed. If it is missing, the milk sugar reaches the large intestine and causes wind and stomach ache.
118439.m: Without lactase, milk sugar is not absorbed.

118440.q: Which factor from the parietal cells of the stomach is needed to absorb vitamin B12?
118440.e: Vitamin B12 binds to intrinsic factor and is only absorbed as a complex. If the factor is missing, pernicious anaemia can develop.
118440.m: Without intrinsic factor, no vitamin B12 is absorbed.

118441.q: After absorption in the small intestine, where do dietary fats go first before they reach the blood?
118441.e: In the gut cell, fats are packed into large fat droplets. These are too big for the blood vessels of the villi and take a detour through the lymph vessels before reaching the blood.
118441.m: Fats take a detour through the lymph.

118442.q: Which vitamins depend on micelles and fat digestion to be absorbed in the gut?
a: Vitamins A, D, E and K
Vitamins B1, B2, B6 and B12
118442.e: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble. They are absorbed together with the products of fat breakdown, which is why poor fat digestion leads to a lack of them.
118442.m: Fat-soluble vitamins need fat to be absorbed.

118443.q: Which vessel first carries absorbed sugars and amino acids from the gut to the liver?
118443.e: The blood from the gut collects in the portal vein. This lets the liver process the absorbed substances first.
118443.m: The portal vein carries nutrients to the liver.

118444.q: In what form does the small intestine mainly absorb proteins from food?
a: As amino acids and short peptides
118444.e: Digestive enzymes break proteins down into amino acids and very short chains of two or three amino acids. Only these small building blocks can be taken up by the gut cells.
118444.m: Proteins are absorbed as small building blocks.

118445.q: In which section of the digestive tract do most bacteria live?
118445.e: Conditions in the large intestine are favourable and the food mass stays there a long time. Trillions of microorganisms live there.
118445.m: Most gut bacteria live in the large intestine.

118446.q: Which substances do gut bacteria mainly produce when breaking down dietary fibre?
118446.e: Bacteria ferment dietary fibre into acetate, propionate and butyrate. The body uses these short-chain fatty acids as energy and as signals.
118446.m: Bacteria turn dietary fibre into short-chain fatty acids.

118447.q: What effect can antibiotic treatment have on the gut flora?
a: Useful gut bacteria are killed as well
The gut flora is permanently strengthened
The gut bacteria become immune to viruses
It has no effect on the gut
118447.e: Antibiotics do not distinguish between harmful and useful bacteria. After treatment, the gut flora can therefore be changed for weeks, often with diarrhoea.
118447.m: Antibiotics also harm the useful gut flora.

118448.q: What is a disturbed balance in the make-up of the gut flora called?
118448.e: In dysbiosis, the variety of gut bacteria is reduced or shifted. It can occur, for example, after antibiotics.
118448.m: A disturbed gut flora is called dysbiosis.

118449.q: What do gut bacteria do for humans?
a: They make vitamin K, for example
They digest protein already in the mouth
118449.e: Gut bacteria make vitamins such as vitamin K and some B vitamins. They also break down dietary fibre and keep harmful germs in check.
118449.m: Gut bacteria supply us with vitamins such as vitamin K.

118450.q: What is transferred in a faecal transplant?
a: Gut bacteria from a healthy person
Stem cells from the bone marrow
A piece of healthy large intestine
118450.e: Prepared stool from a healthy donor brings a varied gut flora into the gut. It can push out harmful germs, for example after repeated infections caused by antibiotics.
118450.m: In a faecal transplant you receive healthy gut flora.

118451.q: What are indigestible food components called that specifically support useful gut bacteria?
118451.e: Prebiotics such as inulin serve as food for useful bacteria. Probiotics, on the other hand, are the living microorganisms themselves.
118451.m: Prebiotics feed the good gut bacteria.

118452.q: According to newer estimates, what is the ratio of bacterial cells to body cells in humans?
118452.e: The often quoted figure of 10 to 1 is considered outdated. An estimate from 2016 finds about as many bacteria as body cells.
118452.m: We carry about as many bacteria as our own cells.

118453.q: Which cells make the hormone gastrin?
118453.e: Gastrin comes mainly from the G cells in the antrum of the stomach. It is released into the blood.

118454.q: What is the most important effect of gastrin?
a: It increases hydrochloric acid production in the stomach
118454.e: Gastrin stimulates the parietal cells to produce acid. It also promotes the growth of the stomach lining.

118455.q: Which stimulus triggers the release of gastrin especially strongly?
a: Protein building blocks in the stomach
118455.e: Peptides and amino acids in the stomach and stretching of the stomach wall stimulate the G cells. The vagus nerve also promotes the release.
118455.m: Protein in the stomach triggers gastrin.

118456.q: Where in the body is the hormone gastrin mainly made?
118456.e: Gastrin is made in cells of the stomach lining in the lower part of the stomach. The name comes from the Greek word gaster, meaning stomach.

118457.q: How does gastrin get from the cells that make it to its target cells?
a: Through the lymph into the gut
118457.e: Gastrin is a hormone. Like all hormones, it is released into the blood and reaches the acid-producing cells in the stomach that way.
118457.m: Gastrin is spread through the blood like other hormones.

118458.q: What can be the result of producing too much stomach acid over a long time?
118458.e: Too much acid attacks the protective mucus layer of the stomach and the duodenum. Painful ulcers can develop.
118458.m: Too much stomach acid can cause ulcers.

118459.q: Which component of gastric juice is produced in greater amounts because of gastrin?
118459.e: Gastrin stimulates the parietal cells to produce hydrochloric acid. The acid kills germs and helps with protein digestion.
118459.m: Gastrin promotes the production of hydrochloric acid in the stomach.

118460.q: Where does the hormone gastrin get its name from?
a: From the Greek word for stomach
From the Latin word for gas
From the name of its discoverer
From the English word for hunger
118460.e: Gaster is Greek for stomach. The same word is found in gastritis, inflammation of the stomach lining.
118460.m: Gastrin is named after the stomach.

118461.q: Why does acidic gastric juice slow down the further release of gastrin?
a: It is negative feedback against too much acid
Acid destroys the cells that make it immediately
Acid dissolves the gastrin in the blood
118461.e: When there is enough acid in the stomach, less gastrin is released. That way the body regulates acid production itself, much like a thermostat controls the heating.
118461.m: A lot of stomach acid slows down gastrin release.

118462.q: Which hormone is considered the very first hormone ever discovered?
118462.e: William Bayliss and Ernest Starling detected it in 1902. They showed that a substance from the gut stimulates the pancreas through the blood.
118462.m: Secretin was the first hormone discovered.

118463.q: In which section of the digestive tract is secretin made?
118463.e: Secretin is made in the lining of the duodenum, just after the stomach. From there it enters the blood.
118463.m: Secretin is made in the duodenum.

118464.q: Which stimulus triggers the release of secretin?
a: Acidic food mass in the duodenum
118464.e: When acidic food mass reaches the duodenum and the pH there drops below about 4.5, secretin is released. That is how the gut reacts to stomach acid.
118464.m: Acid in the duodenum triggers secretin.

118465.q: What effect does secretin have on the pancreas?
118465.e: Secretin stimulates the duct cells of the pancreas to release fluid rich in bicarbonate. This neutralises stomach acid in the gut.
118465.m: Secretin brings bicarbonate from the pancreas.

118466.q: What effect does secretin have on the production of stomach acid?
118466.e: Secretin is released when too much acid arrives in the gut. It therefore slows acid production in the stomach and so protects the gut.

118467.q: What is the job of the bicarbonate that reaches the gut after a secretin signal?
118467.e: Bicarbonate is alkaline and raises the pH in the duodenum. This protects the gut lining and lets the digestive enzymes work.
118467.m: Bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralises stomach acid.

118468.q: Which group of hormones does secretin belong to?
118468.e: Secretin is a short chain of amino acids and therefore a peptide hormone. Steroid hormones such as cortisol, on the other hand, are built from cholesterol.

118469.q: How does secretin get from the gut to the pancreas?
118469.e: Like all hormones, secretin is released into the blood. Bayliss and Starling showed exactly that: the effect occurred even without a nerve connection.
118469.m: Hormones such as secretin travel in the blood.

118470.q: Which parts of the digestive tract can Crohn's disease affect?
a: The whole tract from mouth to anus
118470.e: Crohn's disease can affect any section of the digestive tract. Ulcerative colitis, on the other hand, is limited to the large intestine.
118470.m: Crohn's disease can occur anywhere in the digestive tract.

118471.q: How is the disease typically distributed in Crohn's disease?
a: In patches with healthy sections in between
Always in the whole gut at the same time
118471.e: Inflamed segments alternate with healthy sections (skip lesions). This distinguishes Crohn's from ulcerative colitis, which is continuous.
118471.m: Crohn's disease affects the gut in patches.

118472.q: How deep into the gut wall does the inflammation reach in Crohn's disease?
a: Through all layers of the wall
Only into the top layer of the lining
118472.e: The inflammation is transmural and affects all layers of the gut wall. As a result, fistulas and abscesses can form.
118472.m: Crohn's disease inflames the whole gut wall.

118473.q: Together with ulcerative colitis, which group of diseases does Crohn's disease belong to?
118473.e: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are the two most important chronic inflammatory bowel diseases. They usually come in flare-ups and are not contagious.
118473.m: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease.

118474.q: Which complaints are typical of Crohn's disease?
118474.e: The inflammation in the gut causes cramping stomach pain and diarrhoea. Tiredness and weight loss are often added.
118474.m: Crohn's disease often shows as stomach pain and diarrhoea.

118475.q: Which lifestyle factor clearly increases the risk and severity of Crohn's disease?
118475.e: Smokers get the disease more often and have more severe courses. Stopping smoking is therefore part of the treatment.

118476.q: According to current knowledge, what works together in causing Crohn's disease?
a: Genes, the immune system and gut bacteria
118476.e: Certain gene variants, for example in the NOD2 gene, make people more susceptible. Together with environmental factors such as smoking, the immune system then overreacts to the gut bacteria.
118476.m: In Crohn's disease, genes, the immune system and the environment work together.

118477.q: Which typical complication arises in Crohn's disease because of the deep inflammation?
118477.e: The inflammation can bore through the wall and form channels to other organs or to the skin. Such fistulas often occur around the anus.
118477.m: Fistulas are a typical complication of Crohn's.

118478.q: Who is Crohn's disease named after?
118478.e: The American gastroenterologist Burrill B. Crohn described the disease with colleagues in 1932. Since then it has carried his name.
118478.m: Crohn's disease is named after Burrill B. Crohn.

118479.q: Which discovery earned Barry Marshall and Robin Warren the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2005?
a: A bacterium causes many stomach ulcers
Stomach ulcers are caused only by stress
Stomach acid reliably kills all bacteria
118479.e: The two Australians showed that Helicobacter pylori causes inflammation of the stomach lining and ulcers. Before that, stress and acid were mainly thought to be the cause.
118479.m: Helicobacter pylori is a main cause of stomach ulcers.

118480.q: How does Helicobacter pylori survive in the very acidic environment of the stomach?
a: It neutralises the acid in its immediate surroundings
It lives only outside the stomach
It forms a shell of lime
118480.e: The bacterium makes an enzyme that produces ammonia from urea. Ammonia neutralises the acid around the bacterium.
118480.m: Helicobacter pylori protects itself by neutralising the acid around it.

118481.q: How can an infection with Helicobacter pylori be detected without a gastroscopy?
118481.e: You drink a solution containing labelled urea. If the bacterium is in the stomach, it splits the urea, and labelled carbon dioxide appears in your breath.
118481.m: A breath test reveals Helicobacter pylori.

118482.q: Which serious later disease can a years-long infection with Helicobacter pylori make more likely?
118482.e: The chronic inflammation damages the stomach lining over years. This clearly increases the risk of stomach cancer.
118482.m: A long-term infection with Helicobacter pylori increases the risk of stomach cancer.

118483.q: What shape is the bacterium Helicobacter pylori?
118483.e: The name “Helico” suggests a screw or spiral. With its shape and its flagella, the bacterium bores its way through the stomach mucus.
118483.m: Helicobacter pylori is a spiral-shaped bacterium.

118484.q: When do most people become infected with Helicobacter pylori?
a: Often in childhood, usually within the family
Only in old age in hospital
Only through mosquito bites in the tropics
118484.e: The bacterium is passed from person to person, often in childhood. Many infected people notice nothing for years.
118484.m: Helicobacter pylori is often passed on in childhood.

118485.q: What does the classic eradication therapy against Helicobacter pylori consist of?
a: An acid blocker plus two antibiotics
118485.e: A proton pump inhibitor is combined with two antibiotics, usually for 7 to 14 days. Because of resistance, four-drug therapies are often used today.
118485.m: Helicobacter pylori needs a combination therapy.

118486.q: How did Barry Marshall prove in 1984 that Helicobacter pylori causes stomach inflammation?
a: He drank a bacterial culture himself
118486.e: Marshall swallowed a culture of the bacterium and developed gastritis. The experiment on himself helped convince other experts.
118486.m: Barry Marshall proved his idea by experimenting on himself.

118487.q: What is the branch of fluid mechanics that mainly studies how air flows around bodies called?
118487.e: Aerodynamics deals with flows of gases, especially air, for example around aircraft and vehicles. Hydrodynamics deals with flowing liquids.
118487.m: Aerodynamics is the study of flowing air.

118488.q: Which equations describe the motion of viscous fluids with friction?
118488.e: The Navier-Stokes equations are the momentum balance of a viscous fluid. Whether they always have smooth solutions is one of the Millennium Prize Problems of mathematics.
118488.m: Viscous flows are described by the Navier-Stokes equations.

118489.q: What properties does an ideal fluid have in fluid mechanics?
118489.e: An ideal fluid has no internal friction and does not change its density. This simplification makes many calculations possible in the first place.
118489.m: An ideal fluid is frictionless and incompressible.

118490.q: Which force mainly determines a ship's bow waves and must therefore be modelled correctly in towing tank tests?
118490.e: Water waves form because gravity pulls raised water back down. That is why model and ship are compared using a number based on inertia and gravity, the Froude number.
118490.m: Bow waves are determined by gravity.

118491.q: Which mathematician from Basel set up the equations of motion of frictionless fluids around 1755?
118491.e: Leonhard Euler formulated the Euler equations named after him. Daniel Bernoulli had earlier described the link between pressure and velocity.
118491.m: Frictionless flows are described with the Euler equations.

a: A line that points in the direction of the velocity everywhere
The path of the fastest particle
118492.e: The tangent to a streamline gives the direction of the flow velocity at every point. In a steady flow, streamlines and particle paths are the same.
118492.m: Streamlines show the direction of the flow.

118493.q: What is typical of a steady flow?
a: At each point, the velocity stays constant over time
The pressure is the same everywhere
118493.e: In a steady flow, velocity and pressure at a fixed point do not change over time. They may, however, differ from place to place.
118493.m: In a steady flow, the picture stays the same at every point.

118494.q: What does the Mach number tell you?
a: Speed divided by the speed of sound
Speed divided by the speed of light
118494.e: Mach 1 means the speed of sound. From about Mach 0.3 the density of air changes noticeably and it has to be treated as compressible.
118494.m: Mach 1 is the speed of sound.

118495.q: Which scientist founded boundary layer theory in 1904?
118495.e: Ludwig Prandtl showed that friction is only important in a thin layer at the surface of a body. With this he linked frictionless theory with practice.
118495.m: Ludwig Prandtl is seen as the father of boundary layer theory.

118496.q: What does the continuity equation state for an incompressible flow in a pipe?
a: The product of cross-section and velocity stays the same
The pressure stays the same everywhere
The velocity stays the same everywhere
118496.e: A₁ · v₁ = A₂ · v₂. Whatever flows into the pipe each second must also flow out again.
118496.m: The volume flow rate in a pipe stays constant.

118497.q: Why does the stream of water under a tap get thinner and thinner further down?
a: The water gets faster as it falls
The water evaporates on the way
The air squeezes the stream together
118497.e: Gravity accelerates the water. Because the same amount of water passes every point each second, the cross-section must get smaller as the speed increases.
118497.m: A falling stream of water gets faster and therefore thinner.

118498.q: The diameter of a pipe is halved. How does the flow velocity change?
118498.e: The cross-sectional area depends on the square of the diameter, so it becomes a quarter as large. That is why the velocity rises to four times as much.
118498.m: The area grows with the square of the diameter.

118499.q: Water flows at 1 m/s through a garden hose with a cross-section of 2 cm². How fast does it come out of a nozzle of 0.5 cm²?
118499.e: v₂ = v₁ · A₁ / A₂ = 1 m/s · 2 cm² / 0.5 cm² = 4 m/s. That is why the jet from the nozzle squirts further.
118499.m: A narrower nozzle makes the jet faster.

118500.q: Water flows at 3 m/s through a pipe with a cross-section of 0.02 m². What is the volume flow rate?
118500.e: Volume flow rate = A · v = 0.02 m² · 3 m/s = 0.06 m³/s. That is 60 litres per second.
118500.m: Volume flow rate is area times velocity.

118501.q: Which physical conservation law is behind the continuity equation?
118501.e: The continuity equation says that no mass is created or lost in a flow. Whatever flows into a volume must leave it again or collect there.
118501.m: The continuity equation expresses conservation of mass.

118502.q: Which quantity stays constant along a stream tube in a steady, compressible flow?
a: The mass flow rate ρ · A · v
The volume flow rate A · v
118502.e: With gases the density can change, so the volume flow rate is not conserved. What stays constant is the product of density, cross-section and velocity.
118502.m: In gas flows the mass flow rate is conserved.

118503.q: A river is 40 m wide, 2 m deep and flows at 0.5 m/s. How fast does it flow at a point 25 m wide and 2 m deep?
118503.m: A river flows faster at narrow points.

118504.q: Why does blood flow much more slowly in the capillaries than in the aorta?
a: The total cross-section of all the capillaries is much larger
The blood gets thicker in the capillaries
The heart beats more weakly there
118504.e: Individual capillaries are tiny, but together they have a cross-section several hundred times larger than the aorta. According to the continuity equation, the velocity therefore drops.
118504.m: Many small vessels together slow the blood down.

118505.q: According to Bernoulli, what happens to the static pressure in a horizontal flow when the velocity increases?
118505.e: Along a streamline, p + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant. If v increases at the same height, the static pressure p must decrease.
118505.m: Where the flow is faster, the pressure is lower.

118506.q: What is the dynamic pressure ½ρv² of air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³) at 20 m/s?
118506.m: Dynamic pressure grows with the square of the velocity.

118507.q: At what speed does water flow out of a hole 5 m below the water surface (g = 9.81 m/s², without friction)?
118507.e: According to Torricelli, v = √(2gh) = √(2 · 9.81 · 5) m/s ≈ 9.9 m/s. That is the same speed as in a free fall from a height of 5 m.
118507.m: The outflow speed equals the speed of free fall.

118508.q: In 1738 the Basel scholar Daniel Bernoulli published a fundamental work on flowing fluids. What is it called?
118508.e: In “Hydrodynamica”, Daniel Bernoulli described the link between pressure and velocity. The present form of the equation comes mostly from Leonhard Euler.

118509.q: Which instrument works out the airspeed from the difference between total pressure and static pressure?
118509.e: The Prandtl tube measures the total pressure at the front and the static pressure at the side. According to Bernoulli, the speed follows from the difference.
118509.m: The Prandtl tube measures speed using pressures.

118510.q: Which conservation law is the Bernoulli equation based on?
118510.e: The Bernoulli equation balances pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per volume. Without friction their sum stays constant.
118510.m: The Bernoulli equation is conservation of energy for fluids.

118511.q: Water flows horizontally at 2 m/s at 150 kPa. At a narrow point it flows at 4 m/s. What is the pressure there (ρ = 1000 kg/m³)?

118512.q: A probe in air (ρ = 1.25 kg/m³) measures a dynamic pressure of 500 Pa. How fast is the air flowing?
118512.m: You can calculate the speed from the dynamic pressure.

118513.q: What does the Venturi effect describe?
a: In a narrowing of a pipe the static pressure falls
In a narrowing the pressure rises
A fluid gets warmer as it flows
118513.e: In the narrowing the velocity increases, so the static pressure falls. This can be measured directly with standpipes.
118513.m: The pressure is lowest at the narrowest point.

118514.q: What happens when you blow hard between two freely hanging sheets of paper?
118514.e: Between the sheets the air flows fast through a narrow gap, and the static pressure falls there. The higher pressure of the still air outside pushes the sheets together.
118514.m: Fast air in the gap pulls the sheets together.

118515.q: In which part of older petrol engines was the Venturi effect used to draw in fuel?
118515.e: In the carburettor the intake air flows through a narrowing. The low pressure this creates draws petrol out of a jet and turns it into a fine spray.
118515.m: The carburettor uses the Venturi effect.

118516.q: Which piece of laboratory equipment creates low pressure using running tap water?
118516.e: A fast jet of water flows through a nozzle and creates low pressure there. This sucks air out of a connected container, for example when filtering.
118516.m: The water jet pump sucks using the Venturi effect.

118517.q: What is a Venturi tube mainly used for in engineering?
118517.e: From the pressure difference between the wide and the narrow part you can calculate the velocity and so the flow rate. The device is also called a Venturi meter.
118517.m: A Venturi tube measures flow rate.

118518.q: In a Venturi tube, the narrow part is four times smaller than the inlet. Water flows at 2 m/s in the inlet. What is the pressure difference (ρ = 1000 kg/m³)?
118518.e: In the narrow part, v₂ = 4 · 2 m/s = 8 m/s. Δp = ½ · 1000 · (64 − 4) Pa = 30,000 Pa.
118518.m: Continuity and Bernoulli together give the pressure difference.

118519.q: How does a simple perfume atomiser work?
a: Fast air over a small tube draws the liquid up
The liquid is heated and evaporates
A piston presses drops through a sieve
118519.e: The airflow over the opening of the riser tube creates low pressure. The liquid rises and is broken into a fine spray by the airflow.
118519.m: Atomisers draw up liquid with fast air.

118520.q: Why does a Venturi tube widen only gradually after the narrow part?
a: So that the flow does not separate and the pressure is recovered
So that the tube is cheaper
So that the water gets faster
So that the water warms up
118520.e: A slender diffuser slows the flow down without separation. This lets the pressure rise almost back to its starting value, and the losses stay small.
118520.m: A gentle diffuser saves pressure losses.

118521.q: How does air reach the gas in a Bunsen burner?
a: The gas jet creates low pressure and draws air in
The air is supplied with a pump
The flame only draws air from above
118521.e: The gas flows quickly out of a small nozzle and drags air along through the side opening. This creates a gas-air mixture before the flame.
118521.m: In a Bunsen burner, the gas jet draws in air.

118522.q: A wing with an area of 20 m² and a lift coefficient of 0.5 meets air flowing at 50 m/s (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³). How large is the lift?
118522.m: Lift depends on density, speed, area and coefficient.

118523.q: How does the lift of a wing change if the speed is doubled (everything else the same)?
118523.e: Lift is proportional to v². So twice the speed gives 2² = 4 times the lift.
118523.m: Lift grows with the square of the speed.

118524.q: What is meant by the angle of attack of a wing?
a: The angle between the chord line and the direction of the oncoming air
The angle between wing and fuselage seen from the front
The climbing angle of the flight path
118524.e: The angle of attack tells you how steeply the air meets the aerofoil. Within a certain range, the lift increases almost linearly with it.
118524.m: The angle of attack strongly determines the lift.

118525.q: What happens if the angle of attack of a wing becomes too large?
a: The airflow separates and the lift collapses
118525.e: Above a critical angle, the flow over the upper surface can no longer follow it and separates. This is called a stall.
118525.m: Too large an angle of attack leads to a stall.

118526.q: In level, unaccelerated flight, which force balances the lift?
118526.e: In level flight at constant speed, the lift is exactly as large as the weight. Thrust and drag balance each other in the direction of flight.
118526.m: In cruising flight, the lift carries exactly the weight.

118527.q: What is the effect called that makes a spinning ball curve sideways through the air?
118527.e: The spinning ball drags air with it and deflects the flow to one side. This creates a sideways force, as with a curling cross in football.
118527.m: The Magnus effect makes spinning balls curve.

118528.q: According to Newton's third law, which movement of air behind a wing is linked to lift?
a: The air is only deflected sideways
118528.e: The wing deflects air downwards and exerts a force on it. The opposite force of the air on the wing acts upwards.
118528.m: A wing pushes air down and is pushed up in return.

118529.q: Why do aircraft need longer take-off distances at high airfields such as Samedan in the Engadine?
a: Because of the lower air density
118529.e: With lower air density, the wing produces less lift at the same speed. So the aircraft has to go faster and roll further.
118529.m: Thin air makes the take-off distance longer.

118530.q: What is the straight line between the leading edge and the trailing edge of an aerofoil called?
118530.e: The chord line is the reference line of the aerofoil. Its length is called the chord.
118530.m: The chord line joins the nose and the trailing edge.

118531.q: What is it called when the centre line of an aerofoil is curved upwards?
118531.e: A cambered aerofoil produces lift even at an angle of attack of zero degrees. Symmetrical aerofoils have no camber.
118531.m: Cambered aerofoils lift even without an angle of attack.

118532.q: Why do airliners extend flaps for take-off and landing?
a: To produce enough lift at low speed
118532.e: Flaps increase the camber and often also the area of the wing. This raises the lift coefficient so the aircraft can fly more slowly.

118533.q: What are winglets at the wing tips for?
a: They steer the aircraft about its vertical axis
118533.e: Winglets weaken the vortices at the wing tips. This lowers the induced drag and the aircraft saves fuel.

118534.q: Why do wingtip vortices form at the tips of a wing?
a: Air flows from the higher pressure underneath to the upper side
118534.e: The pressure under the wing is higher than above it. At the tip, air flows round the edge and rolls up into vortices.
118534.m: Pressure evening out at the wing tip creates vortices.

118535.q: A glider has a wingspan of 20 m and a wing area of 16 m². What is its aspect ratio (span² divided by area)?
118535.e: Aspect ratio = b² / A = (20 m)² / 16 m² = 400 / 16 = 25. Gliders have slender wings with a high aspect ratio.
118535.m: Slender wings have a high aspect ratio.

118536.q: What is true for a symmetrical aerofoil without camber?
a: At 0° angle of attack it produces no lift
It produces a lot of lift even at 0°
It only works in supersonic flight
118536.e: The upper and lower sides have the same shape, so lift only arises with an angle of attack. Such aerofoils are used, for example, on aerobatic aircraft that also fly upside down.
118536.m: Symmetrical aerofoils need an angle of attack to lift.

118537.q: Which aviation pioneer studied cambered wings systematically and made gliding flights from 1891?
118537.e: Otto Lilienthal recognised that cambered wings give more lift than flat ones. He made thousands of flights with his gliders.
118537.m: Otto Lilienthal flew with cambered wings.

118538.q: What is typical of laminar flow?
a: The layers of fluid slide past each other in order without mixing
The flow is full of eddies
118538.e: In laminar flow the layers move side by side in parallel. There is hardly any exchange across the flow.

118539.q: The flow through a narrow pipe grows with the fourth power of the radius. How does the flow change at the same pressure if you double the radius?
118539.e: According to the Hagen-Poiseuille law, the volume flow rate is proportional to r⁴. 2⁴ = 16. That is why even slightly narrowed blood vessels have a much smaller flow.
118539.m: The radius enters the flow rate to the fourth power.

118540.q: What shape is the velocity profile of laminar flow in a round pipe?
118540.e: The flow is fastest in the middle and decreases quadratically towards the wall. This creates a paraboloid.
118540.m: Laminar pipe flow has a parabolic profile.

118541.q: Where does water flow fastest in laminar flow in a round pipe?
a: In the middle of the pipe
Halfway between the middle and the wall
118541.e: At the wall the water sticks and stands still. The velocity increases towards the middle, creating a parabolic profile with its maximum in the middle of the pipe.
118541.m: The flow is fastest in the middle of the pipe.

118542.q: According to Stokes' law, how does the friction force on a small sphere in slow flow depend on the velocity?
a: Proportional to the square of the velocity
118542.e: According to Stokes, F = 6πηrv. In creeping, laminar flow around the sphere, the force grows linearly with v.
118542.m: In creeping flow, friction is proportional to velocity.

118543.q: What is the velocity of a viscous fluid right at a wall at rest?
a: Half as great as in the middle
The same as in the middle
118543.e: According to the no-slip condition, the fluid particles stick to the wall. From there the velocity increases towards the middle.
118543.m: The fluid sticks to the wall.

118544.q: What mainly determines whether a flow is laminar or turbulent?
118544.e: The Reynolds number compares the inertia and viscosity of a flow. If it is small, the flow stays laminar; if it is large, it becomes turbulent.
118544.m: A small Reynolds number means laminar flow.

118545.q: Why do designers try to keep the boundary layer on glider wings laminar for as long as possible?
a: Because it produces less frictional drag
118545.e: A laminar boundary layer produces much less skin friction than a turbulent one. So-called laminar aerofoils improve gliding performance in this way.

118546.q: What is typical of turbulent flow?
118546.e: In turbulent flow, velocity and pressure vary randomly. Eddies of different sizes mix the fluid thoroughly.

118547.q: The smoke from a candle that has been blown out first rises as a smooth thread and then becomes tangled. What does this show?
a: The change from laminar to turbulent flow
The change from gas to liquid
A chemical reaction of the smoke
The influence of the magnetic field
118547.e: The warm smoke speeds up as it rises. Above a certain speed, the smooth flow becomes unstable and turns into turbulence.
118547.m: A thread of smoke shows the change to turbulence.

118548.q: What is the idea called that in turbulent flows energy is passed on from large eddies to smaller and smaller ones?
118548.e: Large eddies break up into smaller ones until the motion in the smallest eddies is turned into heat by friction. This picture goes back to Richardson and Kolmogorov.
118548.m: In turbulence, energy moves from large to small eddies.

118549.q: In fully turbulent flow, roughly how does the pressure loss in a rough pipe depend on the velocity?
118549.e: In fully developed turbulence, the pipe friction factor is almost constant. The pressure loss then grows roughly with the square of the velocity.
118549.m: Turbulent pressure losses grow with the square of the velocity.

118550.q: Why does a golf ball with dimples fly further than a smooth ball?
a: The turbulent boundary layer separates later and makes the wake smaller
The dimples make the ball lighter
The dimples store air as propulsion
118550.e: The dimples make the boundary layer turbulent. It clings to the ball for longer, the region of eddies behind it becomes smaller and the drag drops sharply.
118550.m: Dimples reduce the air resistance of a golf ball.

118551.q: What is the pattern of eddies breaking away alternately left and right behind a cylinder in a flow called?
118551.e: Within a certain range of flow, opposite eddies regularly break away behind cylinders. They can make masts or bridges vibrate.
118551.m: A Kármán vortex street forms behind cylinders.

118552.q: What do you call turbulence in a cloudless sky that often occurs near jet streams?
118552.e: Strong wind shear at high altitude can cause turbulence without any visible clouds. Pilots cannot see it and can hardly detect it with weather radar.

118553.q: Which number decides whether a pipe flow is laminar or turbulent?
118553.e: The Reynolds number compares the inertia and viscosity of the flow. If it is above about 2300 in a pipe, the flow usually becomes turbulent.
118553.m: A large Reynolds number means turbulence.

118554.q: Which ratio of forces does the Reynolds number describe?
118554.e: The Reynolds number Re = v · L / ν compares inertial forces with frictional forces. Large values mean that inertia dominates.
118554.m: The Reynolds number compares inertia and viscosity.

118555.q: Below which critical Reynolds number does a pipe flow usually stay laminar?
118555.e: For pipe flows, the critical value is usually Re ≈ 2300. Above it, the flow can become turbulent.
118555.m: Below about 2300 a pipe flow stays laminar.

118556.q: Water (ν = 1 · 10⁻⁶ m²/s) flows at 0.5 m/s through a pipe 2 cm in diameter. What is the Reynolds number?
118556.e: Re = v · d / ν = 0.5 m/s · 0.02 m / 10⁻⁶ m²/s = 10,000. So the flow is turbulent.
118556.m: Everyday pipe flows are usually turbulent.

118557.q: Air (ν = 1.5 · 10⁻⁵ m²/s) flows at 30 m/s around a model car 1 m long. What is the Reynolds number?
118557.m: Air flowing around vehicles has very large Reynolds numbers.

118558.q: What unit does the Reynolds number have?
118558.e: All the units in v · L / ν cancel out. That is why flows of different sizes can be compared directly.
118558.m: The Reynolds number has no unit.

118559.q: How did Osborne Reynolds make the change from laminar to turbulent flow visible in 1883?
a: With a thread of dye in water in a glass tube
With smoke in a wind tunnel
118559.e: Reynolds fed dye into flowing water. At low speed the thread stayed smooth; at higher speed it frayed.
118559.m: Reynolds showed the change with dyed water.

118560.q: A 1:10 scale model is tested in the same fluid. How fast must the flow be for the Reynolds number to stay the same?
a: 10 times faster than for the original
As fast as for the original
10 times slower than for the original
100 times faster than for the original
118560.e: Re = v · L / ν stays the same if, with L ten times smaller, the speed is ten times greater. This is often hard to achieve.
118560.m: Small models need high flow speeds.

118561.q: Why can a bacterium hardly glide on at all after a swimming stroke?
a: At a very small Reynolds number, viscosity dominates
Because water is too thin for bacteria
Because their flagella are too short
118561.e: For bacteria the Reynolds number is far below 1. Inertia hardly matters, so they stop immediately when they stop swimming.
118561.m: For microbes, water feels as thick as honey.

118562.q: What is the SI unit of dynamic viscosity?
118562.e: Dynamic viscosity is given in Pa · s. The smaller unit millipascal second is often used.
118562.m: Dynamic viscosity is measured in pascal seconds.

118563.q: Roughly what is the dynamic viscosity of water at 20 °C?
118563.e: At 20 °C water has a viscosity of about 1.0 mPa · s. Honey is several thousand times thicker.
118563.m: Water has a viscosity of about one millipascal second.

118564.q: How does the viscosity of a gas change when you heat it?
118564.e: In gases, internal friction comes from the exchange of momentum between flying molecules. Warmer molecules are faster, so the viscosity rises, unlike in liquids.
118564.m: Gases become more viscous when heated.

118565.e: Kinematic viscosity ν = η / ρ has the unit m²/s. It appears directly in the Reynolds number.
118565.m: Kinematic viscosity is viscosity divided by density.

118566.q: What do you call fluids whose viscosity increases sharply under sudden stress, such as a paste of cornflour and water?
118566.e: Dilatant or shear-thickening fluids become almost solid under a quick impact. That is why you can briefly run across a pool of cornflour paste.
118566.m: Dilatant fluids turn solid under impact.

118567.q: Ketchup flows much more easily after being shaken hard. What is this property called?
118567.e: In shear-thinning fluids the viscosity falls when they are moved strongly. Ketchup is an everyday example.
118567.m: Ketchup gets runnier when you shake it.

118568.q: Water (η = 0.001 Pa · s) has a velocity gradient of 100 per second. What is the shear stress according to Newton?
118568.e: According to Newton's law of viscosity, τ = η · dv/dy = 0.001 Pa · s · 100 s⁻¹ = 0.1 Pa.
118568.m: Shear stress is viscosity times velocity gradient.

118569.q: Which device measures viscosity from the sinking speed of a ball?
118569.e: A ball sinks through the liquid at a constant speed. The viscosity can be calculated from this sinking speed.
118569.m: A falling-ball viscometer measures viscosity with a sinking ball.

118570.q: What is the air resistance of a car with a drag coefficient of 0.3 and a frontal area of 2.2 m² at 30 m/s (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³)?
118570.m: Air resistance depends on the drag coefficient, area and speed.

118571.q: How does the power needed to overcome air resistance change at twice the speed?
118571.e: The drag force grows with v², and power is force times velocity. So it grows with v³, and 2³ = 8.
118571.m: The power against air resistance grows with the cube of the speed.

118572.q: Which body has the smallest drag coefficient for the same frontal area?
a: A flat plate facing the flow
A hemisphere open at the front
118572.e: The teardrop shape hardly lets the flow separate. Its drag coefficient is many times smaller than that of a plate standing across the flow.

118573.q: Which area is usually used as the reference area for a car's drag coefficient?
118573.e: For vehicles, the drag coefficient refers to the outline of the car seen from the front. This frontal area is also the shadow area when lit from the front.
118573.m: For cars, the drag coefficient refers to the frontal area.

118574.q: Why do cyclists save energy when they ride close behind others?
a: In the slipstream the speed of the oncoming air is lower
The rider in front pulls them with a rope
118574.e: Behind a rider, the air partly moves along too. The relative airflow, and with it the air resistance, falls noticeably.
118574.m: Riding in the slipstream is easier.

118575.q: What is the product of drag coefficient and frontal area called?
118575.e: The product cw · A combines shape and size. In cycling or skiing it directly determines the air resistance.
118575.m: Drag area is the drag coefficient times the frontal area.

118576.q: A car speeds up from 72 km/h to 108 km/h. By what factor does the air resistance increase?
118576.e: The speed rises by a factor of 108 / 72 = 1.5. The drag grows with v², so 1.5² = 2.25.
118576.m: Air resistance grows with the square of the speed.

118577.q: Which part of the drag dominates for a blunt body such as a lorry?
118577.e: Behind blunt bodies the flow separates and forms a large area of low pressure. This pressure drag is much greater than the friction on the surface.
118577.m: Blunt bodies suffer mainly from pressure drag.

118578.q: What is mainly measured on a model car in a wind tunnel in order to reduce fuel consumption?
118578.e: The smaller the air resistance, the less energy a car needs at high speed. The wind tunnel shows which shape creates the least drag.
118578.m: Air resistance is measured in the wind tunnel.

118579.q: Which aviation pioneers tested aerofoils in a wind tunnel they built themselves in 1901?
118579.e: Wilbur and Orville Wright measured hundreds of small model wings in their wind tunnel. The data helped them build the first powered aeroplane in 1903.
118579.m: The Wright brothers used a wind tunnel early on.

118580.q: What is often used to make streamlines visible in a wind tunnel?
118580.e: Fine threads of smoke follow the airflow and show streamlines and eddies. Tufts of thread on the surface or coats of oil are also used.

118581.q: What is used to measure the forces on a model in a wind tunnel?
118581.e: The model is mounted on a multi-component balance. It measures lift, drag and moments at the same time.
118581.m: A wind tunnel balance measures forces on the model.

118582.q: What is a moving belt under a model car in a wind tunnel for?
a: It drives the wheels like a motor
118582.e: On the road, the ground moves relative to the car. A moving belt makes sure the flow under the vehicle is realistic.
118582.m: A moving belt simulates the road in a wind tunnel.

118583.q: Why must a model not be too large compared with the test section?
a: Otherwise the tunnel walls distort the flow
Otherwise the air would get too cold
Otherwise the fan would run backwards
118583.e: A large model blocks the cross-section and artificially speeds up the air beside it. This blockage must stay small or be corrected for.
118583.m: Models that are too large distort the measurement.

118584.q: What is the strong narrowing (nozzle) before the test section of a wind tunnel for?
a: It speeds up the air and makes the flow even
118584.e: In the nozzle the air is strongly accelerated. This makes unevenness and fluctuations in the flow relatively smaller.
118584.m: The nozzle ensures an even airflow.

118585.q: In which municipality in the canton of Lucerne does RUAG run one of Europe's largest wind tunnels, where aircraft and car models are tested?
118585.e: The large wind tunnel in Emmen has a test section about 7 m wide and 5 m high. As well as aircraft, cars are also studied aerodynamically in Emmen.
118585.m: There is a large Swiss wind tunnel in Emmen.

118586.q: Why is a wind tunnel used to test a model at rest in moving air, rather than a moving model in still air?
a: Only the relative motion matters for the flow
118586.e: According to the principle of relativity, it makes no difference whether the body or the air moves. A model at rest is much easier to measure.
118586.m: In a wind tunnel only the relative motion counts.

a: Plant communities and where they grow
The inheritance of individual flower colours
118587.e: Phytosociology studies which plants grow together and under what conditions. One well-known founder was Josias Braun-Blanquet from the Grisons.

118588.q: Why do certain plant species keep growing together in the same community?
a: They have similar needs for soil, light and climate
They are all descended from the same parent plant
They can only form seeds together
118588.e: Plants with similar needs keep meeting in suitable places. This produces typical communities such as beech forest or nutrient-poor meadow.
118588.m: Similar needs lead to typical plant communities.

118589.q: What does a dense patch of stinging nettles reveal about the soil?
a: It is especially acidic and poor in nutrients
It is frozen all year round
118589.e: Stinging nettles are indicator plants for nitrogen-rich soils, for example near cowsheds or compost heaps.

118590.q: Which plant community would grow on most land in the Swiss Plateau without human use?
118590.e: In the damp, temperate climate of the Plateau, beech competes very strongly. Without clearing and farming, large beech forests would be widespread there.
118590.m: The Swiss Plateau would naturally be mostly beech forest.

118591.q: In a vegetation survey, what is estimated for each plant species in the sample area?
a: How much of the area it covers
How much nitrogen its leaves contain
118591.e: You estimate what share of the area a species covers and how common it is. This means plant communities can be compared.
118591.m: In a vegetation survey you estimate the cover of each species.

118592.q: Why must the sample area in a vegetation survey not be too small?
a: Otherwise many species of the plant community are missing
Otherwise the area is too heavily shaded
118592.e: On a small area you only find some of the species present. Only from a certain size is the community mostly fully recorded.
118592.m: A sample area must be big enough to record all typical species.

118593.q: What do you call a species that occurs almost only in one particular plant community and therefore marks it out?
118593.e: Character species are tied to one community and are used to define it. Companion species, on the other hand, occur in many communities.
118593.m: A character species marks out a particular plant community.

118594.q: How does the number of species found change if a sample area is enlarged step by step?
a: It rises quickly at first, then only slowly
It always stays exactly the same
It keeps rising at the same speed
118594.e: At first, many new species are added with each enlargement. Later you hardly find any new ones, and the species-area curve flattens out.
118594.m: As the area grows, fewer and fewer new species are added.

118595.q: What is meant by a forest community?
a: A typical combination of plant species at a forest site
