118595.e: A forest community is a plant community that keeps forming in a similar way under certain soil and climate conditions, such as a beech forest or a larch and stone pine forest.
118595.m: A forest community is a typical plant community of a forest site.

118596.q: Which tree species would naturally dominate in the submontane and lower montane zones of the Swiss Plateau?
118596.e: Under today's climate conditions, beech competes very strongly in the Plateau. Many spruce stands there were planted.
118596.m: Beech usually dominates naturally in the Swiss Plateau.

118597.q: Which tree species forms typical forests of the upper subalpine zone in the Engadine and Valais together with the larch?
118597.e: Larch and stone pine forests can stand the cold winters and short growing seasons of the inner Alpine valleys. The stone pine reaches the tree line there.
118597.m: Larch and stone pine form the forests at the tree line in the Central Alps.

118598.q: What do so-called indicator plants show in a forest?
a: Features of the site such as soil or moisture
The number of animals in the forest
118598.e: Indicator plants only grow under certain conditions. Stinging nettles, for example, show nitrogen-rich soil, bilberries rather acidic soil.
118598.m: Indicator plants reveal what the soil is like.

118599.q: Which forest is typical of dry, warm rocky slopes on limestone, for example in Valais or at the southern foot of the Jura?
118599.e: The downy oak copes well with drought and heat. Its forests are open and rich in warmth-loving plants.
118599.m: Downy oak forests grow on dry, warm slopes.

118600.q: Which tree characterises the natural floodplain forest along mountain rivers, which floods regularly?
118600.e: The grey alder copes well with flooding and gravel and grows fast. Grey alder floodplain forests line many Alpine rivers.
118600.m: Along mountain rivers the grey alder forms typical floodplain forests.

118601.q: Which forest community is typical of shady, damp ravines with boulder scree and nutrient-rich soil?
118601.e: In ravines the air is cool and damp, and the ground is constantly moving. Sycamore, ash and elm compete better than beech there.
118601.m: Maple and ash forests grow in damp ravines.

118602.q: In Swiss forestry, what are the altitude zones of vegetation called from bottom to top?
118602.e: From the lowlands (colline), it goes through submontane and montane to the subalpine zone with the tree line. Above that come the alpine and nival zones.
118602.m: The altitude zones are called colline, submontane, montane and subalpine.

118603.q: Which property of plants do Ellenberg indicator values describe?
a: Their ecological behaviour in relation to site factors
Their flowering time in the year
How poisonous they are to grazing animals
118603.e: Indicator values show under which conditions a species is mainly found in the wild. They describe ecological behaviour under competition, not the physiological optimum.
118603.m: Ellenberg indicator values describe the ecological behaviour of plants.

118604.q: Which site factor is given by the Ellenberg indicator value N?
118604.e: The N value shows whether a species tends to occur in places poor or rich in nitrogen. High values point to over-fertilisation.
118604.m: The indicator value N stands for nitrogen supply.

118605.q: Which plant is a typical indicator of very nitrogen-rich places with an N value of 9?
118605.e: The stinging nettle grows abundantly near dung heaps, places where livestock rest and on over-fertilised forest edges. It is one of the strongest nitrogen indicators.
118605.m: The stinging nettle indicates nitrogen-rich soils.

118606.q: Which plant tends to indicate acidic soils in a forest and has a low reaction value R?
118606.e: The bilberry grows on acidic, base-poor soils, for example under spruce. Wild garlic and liverleaf prefer base-rich places.
118606.m: The bilberry is an indicator of acidic soil.

118607.q: Which plants have an especially high Ellenberg moisture value F?
118607.e: The moisture value shows how wet the soil is where a species grows. Plants in marshes and in water have the highest values.
118607.m: A high moisture value indicates wet places.

118608.q: What does an “x” instead of a number mean in an Ellenberg indicator value?
118608.e: An x means that the species has a wide range for this factor. It therefore does not indicate the factor.
118608.m: An x marks indifferent behaviour of a species.

118609.q: What do you call plants whose presence tells you something about the soil, such as its acidity or nitrogen?
118609.e: Indicator plants grow mainly where certain conditions exist. The stinging nettle, for example, indicates nitrogen-rich soils, the bilberry acidic ones.
118609.m: Indicator plants reveal features of the soil.

118610.q: How can Ellenberg indicator values be used to assess the site of a meadow?
a: You evaluate the indicator values of all the species growing there together
You measure the height of the tallest plant
You count only the flowering plants
You weigh the amount of plants harvested
118610.e: A single species may grow somewhere by chance. If you evaluate the indicator values of many species together, you get a more reliable picture of the site.
118610.m: Many indicator plants together give a reliable picture of the site.

118611.q: Which factor does the Ellenberg value L give?
118611.e: The light value ranges from 1 for plants of deep shade to 9 for plants of full light. Many forest floor plants have low light values.
118611.m: The indicator value L stands for light.

118612.q: What is meant by a climax community?
a: A relatively stable final stage of a succession
The first pioneer community on bare ground
A plant community after a forest fire
118612.e: The climax community is the final stage that develops under the given climate and soil conditions without disturbance. After that it only changes slowly.
118612.m: The climax community is the final stage of a succession.

118613.q: According to monoclimax theory, which single factor determines which final community develops in an area?
118613.e: The American ecologist Frederic Clements saw succession as development towards a single climax determined by climate. Later researchers also stressed soil and landscape.
118613.m: According to monoclimax theory, climate determines the final community.

118614.q: Why do different types of forest grow side by side permanently in the same climate area, for example on limestone rock and in damp hollows?
a: Soil and water supply also shape the forest
The trees change their location every year
The differences arise purely by chance
Animals plant different trees in every place
118614.e: According to Arthur Tansley's polyclimax theory, soil type, water supply and slope lead to several stable final communities in the same climate area.
118614.m: Soil and water also decide which forest develops in the end.

118615.q: Why does a pine forest on dry rock not develop into a beech forest even after centuries?
a: The site is too dry and shallow for beeches
Pines poison the soil for ever
The pine forest is mown regularly
118615.e: On special sites such as rocks, bogs or steep slopes, succession comes to a halt. Experts call such stable plant communities permanent communities.
118615.m: On extreme sites a plant community stays stable for good.

118616.q: What does a large, untouched natural forest typically look like from above?
a: Like a patchwork of young, old and decaying parts
The same age and height everywhere
Like a meadow with single trees
Closed, with no gaps and no dead wood
118616.e: According to Hermann Remmert's mosaic cycle concept, a natural forest consists of small patches in phases of regeneration, maturity and decay. Overall the system still stays stable.
118616.m: A natural forest is a mosaic of different stages of development.

118617.q: What would happen to a hay meadow in the Swiss Plateau if it were never mown or grazed again?
a: It would slowly turn into forest
It would stay a meadow for ever
It would become a raised bog
118617.e: The meadow is a replacement community that only survives through use. Without mowing, shrubs come up first, then trees, until beech forest grows again.
118617.m: Meadows in the Plateau only stay open through mowing or grazing.

118618.q: What is the imagined vegetation called that would develop under today's site conditions without human influence?
118618.e: The concept was introduced by Reinhold Tüxen. It is used as a basis for forestry suited to the site.
118618.m: Potential natural vegetation shows what would grow without humans.

118619.q: In which phase of a natural forest do old trees die and lots of dead wood form?
118619.e: In the decay phase, old trees collapse and open up the canopy. Light and dead wood make new regeneration possible.
118619.m: In the decay phase a natural forest produces lots of dead wood.

118620.q: How does primary succession differ from secondary succession?
a: It begins on bare ground with no soil formed
It begins after a forest fire
It only takes place in water
118620.e: In primary succession there is no soil at all at first, for example on moraines or lava. Secondary succession begins on existing soil after a disturbance.
118620.m: Primary succession begins on bare ground without humus.

118621.q: Which habitat in the Alps is a classic example of primary succession?
118621.e: When glaciers retreat, bare moraine material is left behind. Plants gradually settle on it.
118621.m: Glacier forefields show primary succession especially well.

118622.q: How does the pH of the topsoil on lime-rich moraine typically change as the area gets older?
a: It falls because lime is washed out
It always stays exactly the same
118622.e: Rainwater dissolves the lime and washes it out of the topsoil, and acids also form during decomposition. Older areas in the forefield are therefore often more acidic than young ones.
118622.m: As a moraine gets older, its topsoil usually becomes more acidic.

118623.q: Why is the green alder especially competitive on young bare soils?
a: It fixes nitrogen from the air with bacteria in root nodules
118623.e: The green alder lives in symbiosis with Frankia bacteria in root nodules. This gives it nitrogen, which is scarce in bare soils.
118623.m: The green alder gets nitrogen from the air with the help of bacteria.

118624.q: Why is a glacier forefield a good place to study succession?
a: The further the areas are from the ice, the older they are
The soil is the same age everywhere
It is warm there all year round
118624.e: The ice has gradually uncovered the forefield. If you walk away from the glacier, you see older and older stages of colonisation. In this way space replaces a long period of observation.
118624.m: In a glacier forefield, areas of different ages lie side by side.

118625.q: Which tree is a typical pioneer on moraines and scree in the Alps?
118625.e: The larch needs a lot of light and germinates well on bare ground. Shade-tolerant species such as fir or beech only follow later.
118625.m: The larch is a pioneer tree on bare Alpine ground.

118626.q: Which volcanic island off Iceland became a famous research site for primary succession from 1963?
118626.e: Surtsey was formed in 1963 by an eruption in the sea. Since then its colonisation by plants and animals has been documented closely, and people are hardly allowed on it.
118626.m: Surtsey is an open-air laboratory for primary succession.

118627.q: Which dwarf shrub with white flowers is a typical pioneer plant on limestone scree in the glacier forefield?
118627.e: Mountain avens (Dryas octopetala) forms carpets on lime-rich scree. It gave the Younger Dryas period its name.
118627.m: Mountain avens colonises lime-rich scree as a pioneer.

118628.q: What do you call disturbances that arise from within the ecosystem itself, such as large trees collapsing with age?
118628.e: Endogenous disturbances come from internal processes such as ageing. Exogenous disturbances such as storms, fire or avalanches act from outside.
118628.m: Endogenous disturbances arise within the ecosystem itself.

118629.q: Which beetle often multiplies in huge numbers in weakened spruces after storms and in dry years?
118629.e: The European spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus) breeds under the bark of spruces. Lots of fresh, fallen spruce wood encourages mass outbreaks.
118629.m: The spruce bark beetle mainly attacks weakened spruces.

118630.q: What does Joseph Connell's intermediate disturbance hypothesis say?
a: Species diversity is greatest with a medium level of disturbance
Species diversity is greatest without disturbance
Strong disturbances always increase species diversity
Disturbances have no effect on species diversity
118630.e: With rare disturbance, a few strongly competitive species push out the others, and with very frequent disturbance only pioneers survive. In between, both groups can exist side by side.
118630.m: A medium level of disturbance can do most to promote species diversity.

118631.q: Near which municipality in Valais did a large forest fire burn in August 2003, whose area has been scientifically observed ever since?
118631.e: The forest fire above Leuk destroyed around 300 hectares of forest. The WSL studies there how plants and animals develop after the fire.
118631.m: After the 2003 forest fire at Leuk, recolonisation is being researched.

118632.q: Which three features describe a disturbance regime?
118632.e: A disturbance regime sums up how often, how strongly and over how large an area disturbances occur. These features shape the structure of an ecosystem.
118632.m: A disturbance regime is described by frequency, severity and extent.

118633.q: What did WSL research plots after storm Lothar show about cleared and uncleared areas of windthrow?
a: Wood left lying often protected natural regeneration
Cleared areas never became forest again
118633.e: On areas left as they were, the wood protected young trees from being browsed by deer and created small sheltered spots. Reforestation there often went as well or better.
118633.m: Storm wood left lying can help natural regeneration.

118634.q: Which disturbance is a natural factor in steep mountain forests and creates permanent treeless corridors?
118634.e: In avalanche tracks the forest is destroyed again and again. Flexible shrubs such as green alders grow there, as they can survive the pressure of the snow.
118634.m: Avalanches keep corridors open in mountain forests.

118635.q: What do you call tree species that are the first to come up after a large-scale disturbance, such as birch, aspen and goat willow?
118635.e: Pioneer tree species have light seeds that fly far and grow fast in full light. Later they are replaced by shade-tolerant tree species.
118635.m: Birch, aspen and goat willow are typical pioneer tree species.

118636.q: What is an old-growth island in a Swiss forest?
a: A small stand left standing until it decays naturally
An island in a forest lake
118636.e: In old-growth islands no timber is taken, so that the trees can grow old and decay. This creates habitat for species that live in dead wood.
118636.m: An old-growth island is a small patch of forest that is allowed to grow old.

118637.q: What do you call a single tree with holes, cracks or fungi that is left standing because of its value for animals and plants?
118637.e: Habitat trees offer micro-habitats such as woodpecker holes or hollows filled with rotting wood. They add to old-growth islands and reserves.
118637.m: A habitat tree gives shelter to many species.

118638.q: What role do old-growth islands play in the network of forest reserves?
a: They act as stepping stones between reserves
They supply building timber for municipalities
118638.e: Many dead-wood species only spread over short distances. Old-growth islands link larger reserves and make exchange possible.
118638.m: Old-growth islands link forest reserves as stepping stones.

118639.q: What do you call organisms that depend on wood, especially dead wood, as their habitat?
118639.e: Xylobiont species include, for example, many beetles, fungi and lichens. They break down wood or live in wooden structures.
118639.m: Xylobiont species live in and on wood.

118640.q: Which rare Swiss woodpecker especially depends on broadleaf forests rich in dead wood with many old trees?
118640.e: The white-backed woodpecker looks for insect larvae mainly in rotting broadleaf wood. It only lives where there is plenty of dead wood.
118640.m: The white-backed woodpecker needs lots of dead wood in broadleaf forest.

118641.q: Roughly how much dead wood per hectare of forest do many demanding dead-wood species in Central Europe need?
a: None at all, a tree stump is enough
118641.e: Studies show that many dead-wood species can only survive from about 20 to 50 cubic metres of dead wood per hectare. In many managed forests there is much less dead wood.
118641.m: Many dead-wood species need a few dozen cubic metres of dead wood per hectare.

118642.q: How do old-growth islands in Switzerland usually differ from natural forest reserves?
a: They are smaller and often only protected for a limited time
They are larger and permanently protected
They are only above the tree line
118642.e: Natural forest reserves are larger and secured for the long term. Old-growth islands are small areas that are often protected by contracts for a certain time.
118642.m: Old-growth islands are smaller than natural forest reserves.

118643.q: Which fungus, as a cause of white rot, often breaks down standing dead beech wood and forms large, bracket-shaped fruiting bodies?
118643.e: The tinder fungus (Fomes fomentarius) grows on weakened and dead beeches. In the past it was used for lighting fires.
118643.m: The tinder fungus breaks down dead beech wood.

118644.q: What applies in a Swiss natural forest reserve?
118644.e: In natural forest reserves the forest is left to develop naturally. Over time this produces forest similar to primeval forest.
118644.m: In a natural forest reserve the forest may develop freely.

118645.q: What is the second type of forest reserve in Switzerland called, in which deliberate action is taken to support certain species?
118645.e: In special forest reserves, open forest is managed for orchids or capercaillies, for example. Natural forest reserves, by contrast, are left without intervention.
118645.m: In special forest reserves, management targets particular species.

118646.q: What share of the forest area does the federal government want to secure as forest reserves in Switzerland by 2030?
118646.e: According to the targets of the federal government and the cantons, around 10 per cent of the forest area should be reserves by 2030. According to the FOEN, it was around 7.8 per cent at the end of 2024.
118646.m: By 2030, 10 per cent of Swiss forest is meant to be reserves.

118647.q: What is typical of a forest which, like the Scatlè reserve in the Grisons, has not been used for over 100 years?
a: Lots of dead wood and trees of all ages
Only young trees of the same height
Straight rows of trees like in a plantation
118647.e: Without timber harvesting, old and dead trees stay standing or lying. The dead wood provides a habitat for many fungi, insects and birds.
118647.m: Unused forests have lots of dead wood and trees of every age.

118648.q: Which Swiss national park from 1914 also protects large forests completely from use?
a: Swiss National Park in the Engadine
118648.e: The Swiss National Park is a strict reserve where nature is left to itself. It is the oldest national park in the Alps.
118648.m: The Swiss National Park in the Engadine is a strict reserve.

118649.q: Why are natural forest reserves also valuable for forestry research?
a: They show how forests develop without intervention
They are free of all insects
118649.e: In reserves you can observe how structure, dead wood and regeneration develop naturally. They serve as a comparison with managed forests.
118649.m: Natural forest reserves serve as comparison areas for managed forest.

118650.q: For how long are natural forest reserves in Switzerland usually secured by contract?
118650.e: Natural forest reserves are usually secured for 50 years by contracts with the forest owners, sometimes even for 99 years. The owners receive payments for this.
118650.m: Natural forest reserves are usually secured for 50 years.

118651.q: Which organisation owns or looks after many forest reserves in Switzerland, including Derborence?
118651.e: Pro Natura, formerly the Swiss League for Nature Protection, is the oldest nature conservation organisation in Switzerland. In 1959 it bought the primeval forest of Derborence.
118651.m: Pro Natura protects many forest reserves in Switzerland.

118652.q: In which canton is the primeval forest of Derborence?
118652.e: Derborence is in the municipality of Conthey in Valais, below the Diablerets. The forest is one of the last primeval forests in Switzerland.
118652.m: The primeval forest of Derborence is in Valais.

118653.q: Which events in 1714 and 1749 shaped the valley of Derborence and protected the forest from use for a long time?
118653.e: The rockslides buried Alpine pastures and made it hard to get into the valley. The remote forest therefore stayed untouched.
118653.m: Rockslides made Derborence hard to reach and saved the primeval forest.

118654.q: What formed when the rockslides of Derborence buried the Derbonne stream?
a: A bog with no open water
118654.e: The rockslide material dammed the Derbonne. This formed the Lac de Derborence, which is slowly silting up.
118654.m: Rockslides can dam streams into lakes.

118655.q: Which tree species, together with the spruce, dominates the primeval forest of Derborence and grows very large there?
118655.e: Mighty silver firs grow in Derborence, some of them several centuries old. The forest is a primeval fir and spruce forest.
118655.m: Giant silver firs stand in Derborence.

118656.q: Which writer from French-speaking Switzerland made Derborence famous with a novel from 1934?
118656.e: In the novel “Derborence”, Ramuz tells the story of a shepherd who survives the rockslide. The book was made into a film in 1985.
118656.m: Charles Ferdinand Ramuz wrote the novel “Derborence”.

118657.q: Why is a primeval forest like Derborence so valuable for research?
a: It shows a forest that has never been managed
It consists only of exotic trees
118657.e: True primeval forests have never been used for forestry. They show natural structures with old trees and lots of dead wood.
118657.m: Primeval forests show what forest looks like without management.

118658.q: Which rare woodpecker, an indicator of natural conifer forests rich in dead wood, lives in the primeval forest of Derborence?
118658.e: The three-toed woodpecker looks for bark beetle larvae in dying spruces and firs. It needs mountain conifer forests with lots of standing dead wood.
118658.m: The three-toed woodpecker lives in mountain conifer forests rich in dead wood.

118659.q: What status does the landscape of Derborence have at federal level?
a: It is listed in the BLN inventory
It is a military training ground
118659.e: The Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments (BLN) lists landscapes of national importance. Derborence has been one of the sites in this inventory since 1977.
118659.m: Derborence is a landscape of national importance.

118660.q: In which valley in the canton of Schwyz is the Bödmeren forest?
118660.e: The Bödmeren forest lies high above the Muotatal below the Pragel Pass, mostly at over 1,500 metres. It is considered one of the largest primeval spruce forests in the Alps.
118660.m: The Bödmeren forest lies above the Muotatal.

118661.q: Which tree species mainly characterises the Bödmeren forest?
118661.e: The Bödmeren forest is a subalpine spruce forest with very old trees. It was never used intensively because of the difficult terrain.
118661.m: The Bödmeren forest is a primeval spruce forest.

118662.q: On what kind of ground does the Bödmeren forest grow?
118662.e: The forest grows on fissured limestone with karren and sinkholes. Water quickly seeps away underground.
118662.m: The Bödmeren forest grows on karst limestone.

118663.q: Which large cave system lies beneath the Bödmeren forest?
118663.e: The Hölloch is one of the longest known cave systems in the world, with over 200 kilometres of surveyed passages. It lies in the karst beneath the Bödmeren.
118663.m: The Hölloch lies beneath the Bödmeren forest.

118664.q: What are the channels and furrows dissolved in limestone by water, which are common in the Bödmeren forest, called?
118664.e: Karren form when rainwater containing carbonic acid dissolves the limestone. Humus and moss collect between them, and trees germinate on these.
118664.m: Karren are channels dissolved in limestone.

118665.q: Why was the Bödmeren forest hardly ever used commercially?
a: The fissured karst terrain made transporting timber difficult
The forest always belonged to a city abroad
The forest lay under a glacier
118665.e: Crevices, sinkholes and rock steps made it almost impossible to take timber away. So original structures were preserved.
118665.m: The difficult karst terrain saved the Bödmeren forest from being used.

118666.q: Where do spruces in the Bödmeren forest especially often germinate, because the soil is otherwise too thin or too wet?
118666.e: Fallen, rotting trunks store moisture and nutrients and lie above the snow. This regeneration on rotten wood is typical of mountain spruce forests.
118666.m: Young spruces often grow on rotting tree trunks.

118667.q: What do lots of long beard lichens on the old spruces of the Bödmeren forest indicate?
a: A fungal disease of the trees
118667.e: Beard lichens take up water and substances directly from the air and are sensitive to pollutants. Long beard lichens only grow slowly on old, undisturbed trees.
118667.m: Beard lichens indicate clean air and old forests.

118668.q: At which glacier in the Upper Engadine do markers along a nature trail show earlier positions of the glacier and the colonisation of the forefield?
118668.e: On the Morteratsch glacier trail, signs mark where the ice lay in earlier years. The older the area, the further the vegetation has developed.
118668.m: At the Morteratsch Glacier you can see the colonisation of the glacier forefield.

118669.q: Which storm caused great damage, mainly in Swiss mountain forests, in February 1990?
118669.e: Storm Vivian blew down many trees in the Alps in 1990, including in protection forests. Since then researchers have studied natural reforestation on such areas.
118669.m: Storm Vivian hit mountain forests especially hard in 1990.

118670.q: Which tree species copes especially well with dry, shallow limestone slopes and forms open forests there?
118670.e: The Scots pine manages with little water and nutrient-poor soil. On dry limestone slopes it forms open pine forests, where more demanding trees such as beech fall behind.
118670.m: The Scots pine colonises dry, poor slopes.

118671.q: In which canton is the Sihlwald?
118671.e: The Sihlwald lies south of the city of Zurich in the Sihl valley. It is part of the Wilderness Park Zurich.
118671.m: The Sihlwald is in the canton of Zurich.

118672.q: Which tree species mainly characterises the Sihlwald?
118672.e: The Sihlwald is considered the largest continuous mixed beech forest in the Swiss Plateau. Silver fir, ash and maple are found there too.
118672.m: The Sihlwald is a large mixed beech forest.

118673.q: Since when has the city of Zurich stopped taking timber from the Sihlwald?
118673.e: Timber harvesting was stopped around 2000 so that a natural forest could develop again. Before that, the Sihlwald had been a managed forest for centuries.
118673.m: No timber has been cut in the Sihlwald since around 2000.

118674.q: Which chain of hills borders the Sihlwald on its western side?
118674.e: The Sihlwald stretches from the bank of the Sihl up the slopes of the Albis chain. The Albis separates the Sihl valley from the Knonauer Amt.
118674.m: The Sihlwald lies on the eastern slope of the Albis.

118675.q: How did timber from the Sihlwald get to the city of Zurich in the past?
a: It was floated down the Sihl
It was carried over the Gotthard
It was pulled upstream on the Rhine
118675.e: The Sihl flows from the Sihlwald straight to Zurich. That is why for centuries the logs were floated down the river, until a road took over the transport in 1864.
118675.m: Timber from the Sihlwald used to be floated down the Sihl.

118676.q: What is the wildlife park near Langnau am Albis called, which together with the Sihlwald makes up the Wilderness Park Zurich?
118676.e: Langenberg Wildlife Park shows native and formerly native animals such as European bison, elk and lynx. Together with the Sihlwald it forms the Wilderness Park Zurich.
118676.m: Langenberg Wildlife Park is part of the Wilderness Park Zurich.

118677.q: Which railway line runs through the Sihl valley with a station right by the Sihlwald?
118677.e: The Sihltal railway links Zurich with Sihlwald. This makes the forest area easy to reach by public transport.
118677.m: The Sihltal railway serves the Sihlwald.

118678.q: Which long-term development is expected in the Sihlwald now that it is no longer used?
a: More old trees and more dead wood
All beeches being replaced by palms
118678.e: Without felling, the trees grow older and die where they stand. This increases the dead wood and the species that depend on it.
118678.m: Without timber use, the Sihlwald gains more dead wood.

118679.q: Where does the research institute WSL have its headquarters?
118679.e: The WSL headquarters are in Birmensdorf in the canton of Zurich. There are other sites in places including Davos, Lausanne and Cadenazzo.
118679.m: The WSL has its headquarters in Birmensdorf.

118680.q: Which institute in Davos belongs to the WSL and publishes the avalanche bulletin?
a: Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF
118680.e: The SLF researches snow, avalanches and permafrost. With the avalanche bulletin it warns of the current avalanche danger.
118680.m: The SLF in Davos belongs to the WSL.

118681.q: Which group of universities and research institutes does the WSL belong to?
a: University of Applied Sciences Northwestern Switzerland
118681.e: The ETH Domain includes ETH Zurich, EPFL and the research institutes PSI, WSL, Empa and Eawag. It is funded by the federal government.
118681.m: The WSL belongs to the ETH Domain.

118682.q: Which regular survey of the Swiss forest does the WSL carry out together with the FOEN?
118682.e: The National Forest Inventory (NFI) records the condition and development of the forest on sample plots. The first survey took place in the 1980s.
118682.m: The National Forest Inventory records the condition of the Swiss forest.

118684.q: Why does the WSL measure soil, climate and tree growth on the same forest plots for decades?
a: To detect long-term changes in the forest
To fell the trees every year
118684.e: Many changes, for example due to climate change or air pollutants, only show up over a long time. Long-term monitoring plots make such trends visible.
118684.m: Long-term monitoring makes gradual changes in the forest visible.

118685.q: With which method does the WSL, among other things, study past climate conditions using trees?
118685.e: The width and density of tree rings depend on the weather of each year. Long tree-ring records allow conclusions about the climate of past centuries.
118685.m: Tree rings reveal the climate of the past.

118786.q: Which enzyme links glucose units with α-1,4-glycosidic bonds during glycogenesis?
118786.e: Glycogen synthase attaches glucose units to the non-reducing end of a glycogen chain. It is the key enzyme of glycogen building.
118786.m: Glycogen synthase is the key enzyme of glycogenesis.

118788.q: Which hormone most strongly promotes glycogenesis in the liver and muscle?
118788.e: Insulin is released after a meal and activates glycogen synthase. That way extra glucose is stored.
118788.m: Insulin promotes the storage of glucose as glycogen.

118789.q: Which plant storage substance is similar to glycogen?
118789.e: Starch and glycogen both consist of glucose units and serve as stores. Cellulose is also made of glucose, but it is a structural material.
118789.m: Plants store sugar as starch, animals as glycogen.

118790.q: Why is the highly branched structure of glycogen useful?
a: Glucose can be broken off at many ends at the same time
It lets the cell save water
118790.e: Every branch creates an extra chain end. Enzymes can split off glucose at many ends at once, so the energy is available quickly.
118790.m: Many branches make glycogen quick to break down.

118791.q: Roughly how much glycogen does an adult's liver store?
118791.e: The liver stores about 100 grams of glycogen. Without food, this supply lasts only about a day.
118791.m: The liver stores only about 100 grams of glycogen.

118792.q: Which hormone makes glycogen break down quickly in stressful situations?
118792.e: Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight. It makes glycogen in the liver and muscles break down so that glucose is quickly available.
118792.m: Adrenaline releases glucose from glycogen during stress.

118793.q: In which two tissues do humans store the largest amounts of glycogen?
118793.e: The liver stores glycogen for the blood sugar of the whole body. Because of its large mass, skeletal muscle has the largest total glycogen store.
118793.m: Liver and muscles are the big glycogen stores.

118794.q: When does the body build up especially large amounts of glycogen?
a: After a meal rich in carbohydrates
118794.e: After a meal with lots of carbohydrates, blood sugar rises. Insulin then makes sure the liver and muscles store extra glucose as glycogen.
118794.m: After eating, the glycogen stores fill up.

118795.q: From which starting materials can the liver make glucose during gluconeogenesis?
a: Lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids
Acetyl-CoA, ketone bodies and fatty acids
118795.e: Lactate, glycerol from fat breakdown and glucogenic amino acids can be converted into pyruvate or intermediates of the citric acid cycle. From these, the liver builds new glucose.
118795.m: Lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids are building blocks of gluconeogenesis.

a: Making new glucose from other substances
Taking up glucose in the gut
118796.e: In gluconeogenesis, the body builds new glucose from substances such as lactate, glycerol or amino acids. The name literally means making new sugar.

118797.q: In which organ does gluconeogenesis mainly take place?
118797.e: It is mainly the liver that makes new glucose and releases it into the blood. During long fasting, the kidney also contributes a share.
118797.m: The liver is the main site of gluconeogenesis.

a: During sugar digestion in the gut
118798.e: When nothing has been eaten for a long time and the glycogen stores run empty, the liver makes new glucose. That keeps blood sugar stable.
118798.m: During fasting the liver makes new glucose.

118799.q: Why is gluconeogenesis during fasting especially important for the brain?
a: The brain constantly needs glucose as a source of energy
The brain stores a lot of glycogen
The brain only breaks down protein
The brain does not need oxygen
118799.e: The brain can hardly store energy and depends on a continuous supply of glucose. Gluconeogenesis in the liver secures this supply.

118800.q: Which substance from hard-working muscles is built back into glucose in the liver?
118800.e: During intense exercise, muscles produce lactate. It travels in the blood to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose.
118800.m: The liver turns lactate back into glucose.

118801.q: Which hormone stimulates gluconeogenesis in the liver especially strongly?
118801.e: Glucagon is released from the alpha cells of the pancreas when blood sugar is low. In the liver it increases glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis.

118802.q: Is gluconeogenesis simply glycolysis in reverse?
a: No, some steps use different enzymes
Yes, all steps are exactly the same
No, it only takes place in plants
118802.e: Most steps are reversible, but three steps of glycolysis are not. Gluconeogenesis bypasses these with its own enzymes.
118802.m: Gluconeogenesis is not simply glycolysis in reverse.

a: It uses energy in the form of ATP
It produces a lot of ATP
It runs without any energy change
118803.e: Building glucose costs a lot of energy. The liver uses ATP and GTP for it, which it gets partly from breaking down fat.

118804.q: In which organ does the urea cycle mainly take place in humans?
118804.e: Only liver cells have all the enzymes of the urea cycle. The kidney then excretes the urea that has been made.
118804.m: Urea is made in the liver.

118805.q: Why does the body turn ammonia into urea?
a: Urea provides a lot of energy
Ammonia is too heavy for the blood
Urea is needed to build muscle
118805.e: Breaking down proteins produces poisonous ammonia. The liver turns it into harmless urea, which the kidneys excrete.
118805.m: Urea is the harmless form of ammonia.

118806.q: From which nutrients does the nitrogen excreted in urea come?
118806.e: Only proteins and their amino acids contain significant amounts of nitrogen. When the amino acids are broken down, it is excreted as urea.
118806.m: The nitrogen in urea comes from proteins.

118807.q: How does urea production change with a very high-protein diet?
118807.e: More protein means more broken-down amino acids and therefore more ammonia. The liver makes correspondingly more urea.
118807.m: A lot of protein leads to a lot of urea.

118808.q: What can happen when a badly damaged liver hardly makes any urea?
a: Ammonia builds up and damages the brain
118808.e: Without the urea cycle, poisonous ammonia stays in the blood. It mainly damages the brain, which can lead to confusion and even coma.
118808.m: Without urea production, ammonia poisons the brain.

118809.q: What about energy in the urea cycle?
a: It uses energy in the form of ATP
It produces a lot of ATP
It runs without any energy change
118809.e: Detoxifying ammonia costs the liver energy. Several high-energy bonds from ATP are used for every urea molecule.

118810.q: How many nitrogen atoms does a urea molecule contain?
118810.e: Urea has the formula CO(NH2)2. So it contains one carbon, one oxygen and two nitrogen atoms.
118810.m: A urea molecule contains two nitrogen atoms.

118811.q: Which chemist first made urea artificially in 1828?
118811.e: Friedrich Wöhler obtained urea from an inorganic salt. He showed that substances from living things can also be made in the lab.

118812.q: Which scientist, after whom the citric acid cycle is also named, described the urea cycle in 1932?
118812.e: In 1932 Hans Krebs discovered the urea cycle with his student Kurt Henseleit. Later he described the citric acid cycle, which is also called the Krebs cycle.
118812.m: Hans Krebs discovered the urea cycle and the citric acid cycle.

118813.q: From which molecule is bilirubin formed in the body?
118813.e: When old red blood cells are broken down, the haem from haemoglobin is released. Bilirubin is formed from it in several steps.
118813.m: Bilirubin is a breakdown product of haem.

118814.q: Why does a bruise turn greenish and then yellow over time?
a: The blood pigment is broken down step by step
The blood freezes under the skin
118814.e: In the bruise, the haem from haemoglobin is broken down. First green biliverdin forms, and from it yellow bilirubin.
118814.m: The colours of a bruise show the breakdown of the blood pigment.

118815.q: Which organ is often diseased when the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow because of bilirubin?
118815.e: The liver takes up bilirubin and releases it with the bile. If the liver is ill or the flow of bile is disturbed, bilirubin builds up and jaundice (icterus) develops.
118815.m: Jaundice often points to a liver problem.

118816.q: What does the liver do with bilirubin so that it can be excreted?
a: It makes it water-soluble and releases it into the bile
It turns it back into haemoglobin
It stores it permanently in fat cells
It releases it through the lungs
118816.e: In the liver, bilirubin is linked to glucuronic acid and so becomes water-soluble. That way it can reach the gut with the bile.

118817.q: How is water-insoluble, unconjugated bilirubin carried in the blood to the liver?
118817.e: Unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble. Albumin binds it and carries it to the liver, where it is taken up.

118818.q: What gives stools their typical brown colour?
a: Breakdown products of the bile pigment bilirubin
118818.e: Gut bacteria break down bilirubin from the bile into brown pigments such as stercobilin. If bile is missing, for example when it is blocked, the stools turn pale.
118818.m: Broken-down bilirubin colours the stools brown.

118819.q: Why do many newborn babies get mild jaundice in their first days of life?
a: Their liver still breaks down bilirubin slowly
They have too few red blood cells
118819.e: After birth, many red blood cells are broken down and a lot of bilirubin forms. The newborn's liver cannot process it fast enough yet.
118819.m: The young liver of newborns cannot keep up with the bilirubin yet.

118820.q: How is marked jaundice in newborn babies often treated?
118820.e: Blue light turns bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble forms. These can be excreted without conjugation.
118820.m: Blue light helps newborns break down bilirubin.

118821.q: What is the main job of the cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver?
a: They break down medicines and foreign substances
118821.e: P450 enzymes change medicines and other foreign substances chemically. This makes them easier to excrete.
118821.m: P450 enzymes help the liver break down medicines.

118822.q: Why can two medicines affect each other if they are broken down by the same liver enzyme?
a: They compete for the enzyme and are broken down more slowly
They combine into sugar in the stomach
They always cancel each other out
They are then not absorbed at all
118822.e: If two drugs share the same breakdown enzyme, one can slow the breakdown of the other. Its level in the blood then rises, and side effects can occur.
118822.m: Shared breakdown enzymes can lead to interactions.

118823.q: In which organ are most medicines broken down?
118823.e: The liver contains many enzymes that change medicines. The breakdown products are then excreted through the kidneys or the bile.
118823.m: The liver breaks down most medicines.

118824.q: What happens if a liver enzyme that breaks down a medicine is blocked?
a: The medicine works more strongly and for longer
The medicine no longer works at all
The medicine turns into a vitamin
118824.e: If the breakdown enzyme is slowed, more of the drug stays in the blood for longer. This can increase the effect and the side effects.
118824.m: Blocked breakdown raises the drug level in the blood.

118825.q: Which food blocks CYP3A4 in the gut wall and can increase the effect of some medicines?
118825.e: Furanocoumarins from grapefruit block CYP3A4 permanently. As a result, more of the drug gets into the blood.
118825.m: Grapefruit juice can increase the effect of medicines.

118826.q: Why does the liver chemically change fat-soluble foreign substances?
a: So that they become water-soluble and can be excreted
So that they are stored in fatty tissue
So that they work more strongly
So that they are turned into muscle
118826.e: Fat-soluble substances are hard to excrete in urine. The liver, for example, attaches oxygen to them and makes them more water-soluble.
118826.m: The liver makes foreign substances water-soluble for excretion.

118827.q: What is it called when a substance such as St John's wort increases the production of P450 enzymes?
118827.e: In induction, more enzyme is made. As a result, other medicines are broken down faster and may work less well.
118827.m: Enzyme induction speeds up the breakdown of medicines.

118828.q: Which organ breaks down most of the alcohol in the body?
118828.e: Over 90 per cent of alcohol is broken down in the liver. Only a small part leaves the body through breath, sweat and urine.
118828.m: Alcohol is mainly broken down in the liver.

118829.q: Which vessel lies at the centre of a classic liver lobule?
118829.e: Blood flows from the corners of the lobule to the middle and collects in the central vein. From there it reaches the inferior vena cava through the hepatic veins.
118829.m: The central vein lies in the middle of the liver lobule.

118830.q: Through which vessels does blood enter the liver?
a: Through the portal vein and the hepatic artery
Through the pulmonary artery and the aorta
118830.e: The liver receives nutrient-rich blood from the gut through the portal vein and oxygen-rich blood through the hepatic artery. Their branches run with a bile duct in the corners of the liver lobules (portal triad).
118830.m: The liver gets blood from the portal vein and the hepatic artery.

118831.q: What are the widened capillaries between the rows of liver cells called?
118831.e: In the sinusoids, blood from the portal vein and hepatic artery mixes. Their leaky walls make the exchange of substances easier.
118831.m: Liver sinusoids are the capillaries of the liver.

118832.q: What are the resident macrophages in the liver sinusoids called?
118832.e: Kupffer cells eat bacteria, cell debris and old red blood cells from the portal vein blood. They are considered the largest group of resident macrophages in the body.
118832.m: Kupffer cells are the scavenger cells of the liver.

118833.q: Why does the wall of the liver capillaries have gaps?
a: So that substances pass easily between blood and liver cells
So that blood cells get into the bile
So that the liver grows faster
118833.e: Through the gaps, blood plasma reaches a narrow gap called the space of Disse. There the liver cells take up some substances and release others.
118833.m: Capillaries with gaps make exchange of substances in the liver easier.

118834.q: Roughly what shape does a classic liver lobule have in cross-section?
118834.e: The classic liver lobule is a roughly six-sided prism. The portal areas lie at its corners.
118834.m: A liver lobule is roughly hexagonal.

118835.q: Which vitamin does the liver store in especially large amounts?
118835.e: Most of the body's vitamin A is stored in the liver, mainly in the Ito cells. With chronic damage, these cells can also form scar tissue.
118835.m: The liver is the body's big vitamin A store.

118836.q: In which direction does bile flow in the liver lobule compared with the blood?
a: The opposite way, from the middle outwards
At right angles to it, into the central vein
Not at all, it stays in the cells
118836.e: Blood flows from the portal areas to the central vein. Bile flows the other way in the bile canaliculi, to the bile ducts at the edge.
118836.m: Bile and blood flow in opposite directions in the liver lobule.

118837.q: Why does a fatty liver often go unnoticed for a long time?
a: It usually causes no complaints for a long time
118837.e: The liver has no pain fibres inside it. A fatty liver is therefore often discovered by chance in an ultrasound or because of raised liver values.
118837.m: A fatty liver causes no complaints for a long time.

118838.q: Apart from being overweight, which habit is a common cause of fatty liver?
118838.e: The liver breaks down alcohol. This produces substances that promote fat storage in the liver cells. Even regular moderate amounts can make the liver fatty.
118838.m: Alcohol is an important trigger of fatty liver.

118839.q: Which drink, in large amounts, especially promotes non-alcoholic fatty liver?
118839.e: Soft drinks contain a lot of sugar, especially fructose. The liver easily turns extra fructose into fat and stores it.
118839.m: A lot of sugar in drinks can make the liver fatty.

118840.q: In what form is the fat in a fatty liver mainly stored?
118840.e: In fatty liver, mainly triglycerides collect in fat droplets of the liver cells. They form when more fatty acids arrive than are broken down or exported.
118840.m: A fatty liver mainly stores triglycerides.

118841.q: What is a fatty liver called when inflammation with cell damage is added?
118841.e: In steatohepatitis, liver cells die and inflammatory cells move in. It can progress to scarring of the liver.
118841.m: An inflamed fatty liver is called steatohepatitis.

118842.q: Which serious long-term consequence can a progressing fatty liver disease have?
118842.e: Over years, inflammation can turn into fibrosis and finally cirrhosis. This also increases the risk of liver cancer.
118842.m: An untreated fatty liver can turn into cirrhosis.

118843.q: What are the most important risk factors for non-alcoholic fatty liver?
a: Lack of vitamin C and sunburn
118843.e: Metabolic fatty liver is closely linked to being overweight, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. High blood pressure and raised blood fats also play a part.
118843.m: Being overweight and diabetes favour fatty liver.

118844.q: What is the most important treatment for metabolic fatty liver?
a: Losing weight through diet and exercise
118844.e: Even losing a few per cent of body weight can clearly lower liver fat. Exercise also improves sensitivity to insulin.
118844.m: Losing weight and exercise are the best therapy for fatty liver.

118845.q: Which organ does the hepatitis B virus mainly attack?
118845.e: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. The hepatitis B virus multiplies in the liver cells and can damage the liver permanently.
118845.m: The hepatitis B virus attacks the liver.

118846.q: What is the most effective protection against hepatitis B in Switzerland?
a: A vaccination, ideally as a baby or teenager
None, because there is no vaccine
118846.e: The FOPH recommends the hepatitis B vaccination for all babies and for teenagers who have not yet been vaccinated. It protects very reliably.
118846.m: A vaccination protects against hepatitis B.

118847.q: How do you check whether a hepatitis B vaccination has worked?
a: You measure the antibodies in the blood
You take an X-ray of the liver
118847.e: After the vaccination, the body makes antibodies against the virus. If their level in the blood is high enough, you are considered protected.
118847.m: Antibodies in the blood show vaccine protection.

118848.q: Why can you not get hepatitis B from the hepatitis B vaccination?
a: It contains only one part of the virus coat, not a whole virus
It only works after ten years
118848.e: The vaccine contains only one protein from the virus coat. The immune system learns from it to recognise the virus, but an infection is impossible.
118848.m: The hepatitis B vaccine contains no virus that can multiply.

118849.q: In whom does a hepatitis B infection especially often become chronic?
118849.e: The immune system of babies usually cannot get rid of the virus. In adults, on the other hand, the infection usually heals.
118849.m: In babies, hepatitis B especially often becomes chronic.

118850.q: Which serious long-term consequences can chronic hepatitis B have?
a: Cirrhosis of the liver and liver cell cancer
118850.e: The constant inflammation leads to scarring of the liver. In addition, the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma rises sharply.
118850.m: Chronic hepatitis B can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

118851.q: Through which route, among others, is the hepatitis B virus passed on?
a: Through blood, for example via shared syringes
118851.e: The virus is present in the blood in high concentration and is very contagious. Even tiny amounts of blood on needles can cause an infection.
118851.m: Hepatitis B is passed on mainly through blood and body fluids.

118852.q: Why do antibiotics not help against hepatitis B?
a: Because hepatitis B is caused by a virus
Because the liver breaks down antibiotics immediately
Because hepatitis B is an allergy
Because antibiotics only work in children
118852.e: Antibiotics only work against bacteria. Against viruses such as the hepatitis B virus, antiviral medicines are needed.
118852.m: Antibiotics do not work against viruses.

118853.q: Which organ can become scarred over years in chronic hepatitis C?
118853.e: The hepatitis C virus often inflames the liver unnoticed for years. This can lead to cirrhosis of the liver.
118853.m: Hepatitis C can scar the liver.

118854.q: Which statement about vaccination against hepatitis C is true (as of 2025)?
a: It is part of the measles vaccination
A single dose protects for life
118854.e: Because the virus changes so much, no vaccine has been approved so far. Protection comes mainly from avoiding contact with blood and treating infected people.
118854.m: There is no vaccine against hepatitis C yet.

118855.q: Which medicines are mostly used to cure hepatitis C today?
118855.e: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) specifically block virus proteins. Treatment usually lasts 8 to 12 weeks.

118856.q: What is the cure rate for hepatitis C with modern direct-acting antivirals?
118856.e: With today's combination therapies, the virus is permanently removed in well over 90 per cent of patients. Earlier interferon therapies were much less effective.
118856.m: Hepatitis C can almost always be cured today.

118857.q: What did the discovery of the hepatitis C virus, honoured with the Nobel Prize in 2020, make possible?
a: Blood tests for blood donations and targeted medicines
118857.e: Since the virus has been known, blood donations can be tested for it. Medicines have also been developed that now almost always cure hepatitis C.
118857.m: The discovery of the hepatitis C virus made blood tests and cures possible.

118858.q: How does a hepatitis C infection often progress without treatment?
a: It becomes chronic in a large share of infected people
It always heals within a week
It always causes a high fever
118858.e: In most infected people, the virus stays in the body permanently. The infection often goes on for years with almost no complaints.
118858.m: Hepatitis C often becomes chronic without being noticed.

118859.q: What is the most important way the hepatitis C virus is passed on in Switzerland?
a: Blood contact, for example when sharing syringes
118859.e: Hepatitis C is passed on almost only through blood. Today this mainly concerns sharing injecting equipment when using drugs.
118859.m: Hepatitis C is passed on mainly through blood.

118860.q: How long does a modern treatment for hepatitis C usually last?
118860.e: Modern antiviral tablets are usually taken for 8 to 12 weeks. Afterwards the virus is gone in the vast majority of patients.
118860.m: Hepatitis C can be cured in a few weeks today.

118861.q: Which enzyme in the blood is most specific for damage to liver cells?
118861.e: Alanine aminotransferase is found mainly in the cytoplasm of liver cells. When the cells are damaged, it passes into the blood.
118861.m: ALT is the most typical liver cell value.

118862.q: For which causes is gamma-GT in the blood typically raised?
a: Drinking alcohol and blocked bile flow
118862.e: Gamma-glutamyl transferase reacts sensitively to alcohol and cholestasis. It is therefore a common screening value.
118862.m: A raised gamma-GT often points to alcohol or blocked bile flow.

118863.q: Which lab value typically rises together with gamma-GT when bile flow is blocked?
118863.e: In cholestasis, more alkaline phosphatase is made in the bile ducts. However, it can also come from bone.
118863.m: Alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT show blocked bile flow.

118864.q: Why should you not do hard sport before a blood test for liver values?
118864.e: Intense exercise releases enzymes from the muscles, including AST. A raised value could then wrongly be read as liver damage; the De Ritis ratio of AST to ALT helps to interpret it.
118864.m: Hard sport can distort liver values such as AST.

118865.q: Which clotting value quickly shows that the liver is producing less?
118865.e: Many clotting factors are made in the liver and have a short half-life. If the liver produces less, the Quick value falls and the INR rises.
118865.m: The prothrombin time shows how well the liver is producing.

118866.q: Which blood protein is made in the liver and falls in chronic liver failure?
118866.e: Albumin is the most common plasma protein and is made by the hepatocytes. Because of its long half-life, it only falls when the liver has been weak for a longer time.
118866.m: Low albumin can show chronic liver weakness.

118867.q: Why is AST less specific to the liver than ALT?
a: Because it is also plentiful in heart and skeletal muscle
Because it is made only in the brain
Because it never gets into the blood
118867.e: Aspartate aminotransferase is found in many tissues, especially in muscle cells. A raised AST can therefore also come from muscle damage.
118867.m: AST can also come from muscles.

118868.q: Why do low levels of albumin and clotting factors show a weakened liver?
a: The liver breaks these proteins down
These proteins are made in the kidney
118868.e: The liver makes many blood proteins, such as albumin, clotting factors and cholinesterase. If their levels fall, the liver's production is limited.
118868.m: Low liver-made blood proteins show weak liver production.

118869.q: What made liver transplantation a successful treatment from the 1980s onwards?
118869.e: Thomas Starzl attempted the first liver transplant in 1963, but many recipients rejected the organ. Only with ciclosporin from the early 1980s did many survive long-term.
118869.m: Medicines against rejection made transplants successful.

118870.q: Why can a living person also donate for a liver transplant?
a: Because part of the liver can be removed and grows back
Because the liver is not needed for life
Because only the gall bladder is transplanted
118870.e: The liver has a great ability to regenerate. After part of it is removed, the liver parts grow back considerably in both donor and recipient.
118870.m: The liver can grow back after part of it is removed.

118871.q: Which foundation runs the national allocation of donor organs in Switzerland?
118871.e: Swisstransplant runs the national allocation office on behalf of the Confederation. For the liver, urgency counts most, measured with the MELD score.
118871.m: Swisstransplant allocates donor organs in Switzerland.

118872.q: Which visible sign of liver disease goes with a high bilirubin level?
118872.e: Bilirubin is a yellow breakdown product of the red blood pigment, which the liver excretes. It is also one of the values in the MELD score, together with INR and creatinine.
118872.m: A high bilirubin level turns skin and eyes yellow.

118873.q: Where is a donor liver usually placed during a transplant?
a: In the place of the removed diseased liver
In the pelvis next to the bladder
Under the skin of the thigh
In the chest, next to the old liver
118873.e: The diseased liver is removed and the donor liver is put in its place. Experts call this orthotopic, meaning “in the right place”. Kidneys, on the other hand, are usually placed in the pelvis.
118873.m: The donor liver usually goes in the place of the old liver.

118874.q: Why is a liver transplant for liver cancer only an option in early stages?
a: Because otherwise the cancer keeps growing despite the new liver
Because otherwise the donor liver is too small
Because large tumours do not allow anaesthesia
118874.e: If the cancer has already spread, it keeps growing despite the new liver, especially as the medicines against rejection weaken the immune defences. The Milan criteria set how large and how many the tumours may be.
118874.m: For liver cancer, a transplant only helps early on.

118875.q: Which medicines do recipients of a donor liver usually have to take for life?
a: Blood pressure lowerers such as ramipril
118875.e: The immune system recognises the foreign organ and would reject it. Immunosuppressants damp down this reaction.
118875.m: After a transplant, immunosuppressants prevent rejection.

118876.q: What happens in newborn babies with blocked bile ducts (biliary atresia)?
a: Bile builds up and the liver scars
The stomach no longer makes acid
118876.e: In biliary atresia, bile cannot drain away. The children turn yellow and the liver scars quickly; this is the most common reason for liver transplants in children.
118876.m: Blocked bile ducts damage the liver of newborns.

118877.q: What is a transplant called in which a donor liver is divided and supplies two recipients?
118877.e: In a split liver, the organ is usually divided into a smaller left part for a child and a larger right part for an adult. That way one donor organ helps two people.
118877.m: A split liver supplies two recipients.

118878.q: What does ammonia in the human body mainly come from?
a: From the breakdown of amino acids
From the breakdown of fatty acids
118878.e: When amino acids are broken down, the amino group is released as ammonia. Gut bacteria also make ammonia from protein.
118878.m: Ammonia is produced when amino acids are broken down.

118879.q: Which condition arises when a lot of ammonia reaches the brain in liver failure?
118879.e: Ammonia is toxic to nerve cells and astrocytes. It causes confusion, drowsiness and, in the worst case, coma.
118879.m: Too much ammonia damages the brain.

118880.q: In which organ is poisonous ammonia turned into urea?
118880.e: The liver converts ammonia into harmless urea in the urea cycle. This is then excreted through the kidneys.
118880.m: The liver turns ammonia into urea.

118881.q: How does the urea made from ammonia mainly leave the body?
118881.e: Urea dissolves well in water and is filtered from the blood by the kidneys. It is the most important nitrogen-containing component of urine.

118882.q: Which amino acid is the most important harmless way to transport ammonia in the blood?
118882.e: Many tissues attach ammonia to glutamate and release glutamine into the blood. In the liver and kidney, the nitrogen is released again.
118882.m: Glutamine carries ammonia safely through the blood.

118883.q: Which enzyme attaches ammonia to glutamate?
118883.e: Glutamine synthetase uses ATP and makes glutamine from glutamate and ammonia.
118883.m: Glutamine synthetase detoxifies ammonia into glutamine.

118884.q: In what form is ammonia mainly found in the blood at normal pH?
118884.e: The pKa of ammonium is about 9.2. At a blood pH of 7.4, by far the largest part is therefore protonated.
118884.m: In the blood, ammonia is mostly present as ammonium.

118885.q: Which organ excretes ammonium and so helps remove acid from the body?
118885.e: The kidney tubules make ammonia from glutamine, which binds protons in the urine. In this way acids are excreted as ammonium.
118885.m: The kidney also excretes acid as ammonium.

118886.q: What does the zeroth law of thermodynamics state?
a: Two systems in thermal equilibrium with a third are also in equilibrium with each other
Energy can be neither created nor destroyed
The entropy of an isolated system never decreases
118886.e: The zeroth law makes temperature a measurable quantity. A thermometer is exactly such a third system.
118886.m: The zeroth law is the basis of temperature measurement.

118887.q: What do you call the state in which the macroscopic quantities of a system no longer change over time?
118887.e: In equilibrium, temperature, pressure and composition are constant everywhere and no longer change. State variables are only clearly defined for such states.
118887.m: In thermodynamic equilibrium nothing changes macroscopically any more.

118888.q: What is typical of an isolated system?
a: It exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings
It exchanges only matter, but no energy
It exchanges energy and matter freely
It exchanges only heat, but no work
118888.e: An isolated system is completely separated from its surroundings. So its total energy stays constant.
118888.m: An isolated system exchanges nothing with its surroundings.

118889.q: What is typical of a closed system in thermodynamics?
a: Energy can be exchanged, but matter cannot
Matter can be exchanged, but energy cannot
Neither energy nor matter is exchanged
It always has a constant volume
118889.e: A closed saucepan on the hob is an example. Heat gets in, but no water escapes.
118889.m: A closed system exchanges energy, but not matter.

118890.q: Which of the following is not a state variable but a process quantity?
118890.e: State variables depend only on the current state. How much heat is transferred, by contrast, depends on the path between two states.
118890.m: Heat is a process quantity, not a state variable.

118891.q: What is a change of state in which the volume stays constant called?
118891.e: The prefix “iso” means equal, and “choric” comes from the Greek for space. In isobaric processes, by contrast, the pressure stays the same.
118891.m: In an isochoric change of state the volume stays the same.

118892.q: What do you call a change of state without heat exchange with the surroundings?
118892.e: In an adiabatic process the gas is thermally insulated or the process happens very quickly. Changes in temperature then come only from work.
118892.m: An adiabatic process happens without heat exchange.

118893.q: Roughly what volume does 1 mol of an ideal gas take up at 0 °C and 1013.25 hPa?
118893.e: From p·V = n·R·T it follows that V = 1 mol · 8.314 J/(mol·K) · 273.15 K / 101,325 Pa, so about 0.0224 m³. That is about 22.4 litres.
118893.m: One mole of ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres under standard conditions.

118894.q: What is the first law if W is the work done on the system?
a: ΔU equals W divided by Q
118894.e: The internal energy changes by the heat supplied and the work done on the system. This is the law of conservation of energy for thermodynamic systems.
118894.m: Internal energy changes by the heat and work supplied.

118895.q: Which machine does the first law of thermodynamics rule out?
a: A perpetual motion machine of the first kind
A perpetual motion machine of the second kind
118895.e: A perpetual motion machine of the first kind would deliver work without any energy being supplied. That contradicts the conservation of energy.
118895.m: No machine can keep doing work without an energy supply.

118896.q: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. By how much does its internal energy change?
118896.e: ΔU is 500 J minus 200 J. The work given off is subtracted from the heat absorbed, so U increases by 300 J.
118896.m: Work given off reduces the gain in internal energy.

118897.q: An ideal gas absorbs 800 J of heat during an isothermal expansion. How much work does it give off to its surroundings?
118897.e: In an isothermal change of state, the temperature, and so the internal energy of an ideal gas, stays the same. So all the heat is given off as work.
118897.m: In isothermal expansion, all the heat supplied becomes work.

118898.q: 150 J of work is done on a thermally insulated gas during compression. What happens?
a: The internal energy rises by 150 J and the gas gets warmer
The internal energy falls by 150 J and the gas cools down
The internal energy stays the same
The gas gives off 150 J of heat
118898.e: Without heat exchange, Q is zero. All the work increases the internal energy, which makes the temperature rise.

118899.q: 1200 J of heat is supplied to a gas in a rigid container. What is the change in internal energy?
118899.e: At constant volume, the gas does no expansion work. All the heat supplied increases the internal energy.
118899.m: At constant volume, all the heat goes into internal energy.

118900.q: A gas expands by 3 litres at a constant pressure of 2·10⁵ Pa. How much expansion work does it do?
118900.e: The expansion work is p times ΔV, so 2·10⁵ Pa times 3·10⁻³ m³. That gives 600 J.
118900.m: Expansion work is pressure times change in volume.

118901.q: Why is the molar heat capacity of an ideal gas greater at constant pressure than at constant volume?
a: Because at constant pressure part of the heat is given off as expansion work
Because the gas does not warm up at constant pressure
Because heat is lost at constant volume
Because the particles get heavier at constant pressure
118901.e: If the gas expands, it does work on its surroundings. So it needs more heat for the same rise in temperature; the difference is exactly R per mole.
118901.m: At constant pressure a gas needs more heat to warm up.

118902.q: 1 mol of a monatomic ideal gas is heated by 20 K at constant pressure. Roughly how much heat must be supplied?
118902.e: At constant pressure Q = 5/2 · n·R·ΔT, because the expansion work n·R·ΔT is added to the internal energy (3/2 n·R·ΔT). So 2.5 · 1 · 8.314 · 20, which gives about 416 J.
118902.m: At constant pressure a gas needs extra heat for the expansion work.

118903.q: What is Clausius's statement of the second law?
a: Heat never flows by itself from a colder to a warmer body
Energy is conserved in an isolated system
The entropy of a crystal is zero at 0 K
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional at constant temperature
118903.e: Transferring heat from cold to warm is only possible with extra effort. By themselves, temperatures always even out.
118903.m: Heat flows by itself only from warm to cold.

118904.q: What is a perpetual motion machine of the second kind?
a: A machine that turns heat from a single reservoir completely into work
A machine that creates energy out of nothing
A machine that runs without friction
A machine that conducts heat from warm to cold
118904.e: Such a machine could, for example, drive a ship just by cooling the seawater. The second law rules this out.
118904.m: Heat from only one reservoir cannot be turned completely into work.

118905.q: What does Carnot's theorem say about engines working between the same two heat reservoirs?
a: None has a higher efficiency than a reversible engine
All have exactly the same efficiency
The efficiency depends only on the working gas
118905.e: If there were a better engine, you could couple it with a reversible engine running backwards. The result would break the second law.
118905.m: A reversible engine is unbeatable between two reservoirs.

118906.q: Which physicist stated in 1851 that no cyclically working machine can turn heat from just one reservoir into work?
118906.e: William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, set out this statement in 1851. Max Planck later gave it a similar form.
118906.m: Lord Kelvin formulated a version of the second law in 1851.

118907.q: Which quantity decreases in a spontaneous process at constant pressure and constant temperature?
118907.e: At constant pressure and constant temperature, the second law can be expressed through the Gibbs energy G. A process happens spontaneously if ΔG is negative.
118907.m: Spontaneous processes lower the Gibbs energy at constant pressure and temperature.

118908.q: Why does a fridge not break the second law, even though it moves heat from the cold inside to the outside?
a: Because work is supplied to it for this
Because the inside contains no heat at all
Because it only runs at night
118908.e: The second law only forbids heat flowing from cold to warm without any further effort. The compressor supplies the work needed.
118908.m: With work, heat can be pumped from cold to warm.

118909.q: What follows from the second law for every cyclically working heat engine?
a: Its efficiency is always less than 100 per cent
Its efficiency is always exactly 50 per cent
It gives off no waste heat
118909.e: Part of the heat taken in must always be given off to a colder reservoir. So never can all the heat be turned into work.
118909.m: Every heat engine must give off waste heat.

118910.q: What is the direction of time set by the second law called?
118910.e: Irreversible processes such as milk mixing into coffee only run in one direction. This tells you what came earlier and what came later.
118910.m: The increase in entropy gives time a direction.

118911.q: What is the hypothetical final state of the universe called, in which there are no longer any differences in temperature?
118911.e: If the temperature is the same everywhere, no more work can be obtained. The idea goes back to thoughts of Lord Kelvin around 1852.
118911.m: In heat death there would be no usable temperature differences left.

118912.q: Which quantity always increases in an isolated system during irreversible processes?
118912.e: According to the second law, the entropy of an isolated system can never decrease. In irreversible processes such as mixing or friction it increases, while the energy is conserved.
118912.m: In isolated systems entropy never decreases.

118913.q: Which physical chemist formulated the third law of thermodynamics around 1906?
118913.e: The third law is also called the Nernst theorem or Nernst heat theorem. Nernst received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1920.
118913.m: Walther Nernst formulated the third law.

118914.q: What does the unattainability statement of the third law say?
a: Absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps
Heat never flows from cold to warm
118914.e: Each cooling step brings the system only a fraction closer to 0 K. You can approach absolute zero, but never quite reach it.
118914.m: You can never quite reach absolute zero.

118915.q: According to the third law, what is the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero?
118915.e: At 0 K a perfect crystal has only one possible microstate. So its entropy becomes zero.
118915.m: A perfect crystal has no entropy at zero kelvin.

118916.q: Which Celsius temperature is absolute zero?
118916.e: 0 K is minus 273.15 °C. Minus 459.67 is the same point in degrees Fahrenheit.

118917.q: How does the heat capacity of a solid behave as the temperature approaches absolute zero?
118917.e: Close to 0 K hardly any vibrations can be excited. According to the Debye model, the heat capacity of insulators falls in proportion to T³.
118917.m: At the lowest temperatures the heat capacity disappears.

118918.q: Why does water ice still have some entropy even at absolute zero?
a: The hydrogen atoms can be arranged in many equivalent ways
The atoms vibrate especially strongly at 0 K
118918.e: In the ice lattice there are many equivalent ways of arranging the hydrogen atoms. This disorder stays frozen in as it cools. It is called residual entropy.
118918.m: Even at 0 K, ice is not a perfect crystal.

118919.q: Which element stays liquid at normal pressure even very close to absolute zero?
118919.e: Helium only becomes solid under high pressure. Its atoms are very light and attract each other only weakly, so their zero-point motion prevents freezing.
118919.m: At normal pressure helium stays liquid almost down to 0 K.

118920.q: In which SI unit is entropy given?
118920.e: Entropy links an energy with an absolute temperature. This gives the unit J/K.
118920.m: Entropy is measured in joules per kelvin.

118921.e: Clausius formed the word from the Greek “tropē” for transformation. It was deliberately meant to sound similar to “energy”.
118921.m: Rudolf Clausius coined the term entropy in 1865.

118922.q: Which formula is on Ludwig Boltzmann's gravestone in Vienna?
a: S equals k times log W
p times V equals n times R times T
118922.e: The formula links the entropy S with the number W of possible microstates. The constant k is called the Boltzmann constant.
118922.m: Boltzmann linked entropy with the number of microstates.

118923.q: 600 J of heat is supplied reversibly to a system at 300 K. What is its change in entropy?
118923.e: At constant temperature, ΔS = Q / T. So 600 J divided by 300 K gives 2 J/K.
118923.m: Change in entropy is heat divided by temperature.

118924.q: 1 kg of ice melts at 0 °C; the specific latent heat of fusion is 334 kJ/kg. Roughly how large is the increase in entropy?
118924.e: ΔS = Q / T, so 334,000 J divided by 273.15 K. That gives about 1223 J/K, or 1.22 kJ/K.

118925.q: From the point of view of statistical physics, what does entropy describe?
a: The number of microstates that match a macrostate
The average speed of the particles
The total mass of a system
118925.e: The more microscopic arrangements give the same macroscopic state, the greater the entropy. In simple terms it is often called disorder.
118925.m: Many possible microstates mean high entropy.

118926.q: 1000 J of heat flows from a body at 400 K to a body at 200 K. How does the total entropy change?
118926.e: The hot body loses 1000/400 = 2.5 J/K, the cold body gains 1000/200 = 5 J/K. Overall the entropy rises by 2.5 J/K.
118926.m: Heat conduction from warm to cold increases the total entropy.

118927.q: What happens to the entropy when two different ideal gases mix?
118927.e: Each gas spreads out over a larger volume, which allows more microstates. This increase is called the entropy of mixing.
118927.m: Entropy rises when different gases mix.

118928.q: A gas flows from one container into a second, empty container and spreads out over both. What happens to its entropy?
118928.e: In the larger volume there are many more possible arrangements of the particles. So the entropy rises, and the gas never returns into one container by itself.
118928.m: More volume means more entropy for a gas.

118929.q: What is meant by the internal energy of a system?
a: The sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its particles
The kinetic energy of the whole body
The potential energy of the body in the gravitational field
The energy it radiates as light
118929.e: Internal energy includes the random motion of the particles and the interactions between them. The motion of the body as a whole is not part of it.
118929.m: Internal energy is stored in the particles of a body.

118930.q: For a fixed amount of substance, what does the internal energy of an ideal gas depend on?
a: On the shape of the container
118930.e: In an ideal gas there are no interactions between the particles. So the internal energy consists only of kinetic energy and depends on T alone.
118930.m: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on the temperature.

118931.q: Roughly what is the internal energy of 1 mol of a monatomic ideal gas at 300 K?
118931.e: For a monatomic ideal gas, U = 3/2 · n·R·T. With 1.5 · 8.314 · 300 you get about 3741 J.
118931.m: A monatomic gas has one and a half times R of internal energy per mole and kelvin.

118932.q: Why does nitrogen (N₂) need more heat per mole than helium for the same rise in temperature?
118932.e: Helium atoms store energy only in their movement from place to place. Diatomic molecules can also rotate and so take in more energy for the same rise in temperature.
118932.m: Diatomic gases also store heat in the rotation of their molecules.

118933.q: How does the average kinetic energy of the particles of an ideal gas depend on the temperature?
a: It is proportional to the absolute temperature
It is proportional to the Celsius temperature
It does not depend on the temperature
It is proportional to the square of the temperature
118933.e: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. If the temperature in kelvin doubles, this energy doubles too.
118933.m: Twice the kelvin temperature means twice the average kinetic energy.

118934.q: By how much does the internal energy of 2 mol of a monatomic ideal gas rise when it is heated by 10 K?
118934.e: ΔU = 3/2 · n·R·ΔT, so 1.5 · 2 · 8.314 · 10. That gives about 249 J.
118934.m: The change in internal energy is proportional to the change in temperature.

118935.q: What is the change in the internal energy of a working gas after a complete cycle?
