119268.e: Calcium is found almost entirely as hydroxyapatite in bones and teeth. The small remainder in the blood is essential for clotting, muscles and nerves.
119268.m: Almost all the body's calcium is in the bones.

119269.q: Which diseases are the most common causes of chronic kidney failure?
119269.e: High blood sugar and high blood pressure damage the small kidney vessels and the glomeruli over years. In many countries they are the main reasons people need dialysis.
119269.m: Diabetes and high blood pressure harm the kidneys most.

119270.q: What does the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) tell you?
a: How much blood the kidneys filter per minute
How much urine you drink per day
How much sugar is in the blood
119270.e: The GFR measures the kidneys' filtering in millilitres per minute. If it falls sharply, this is called kidney failure.
119270.m: The GFR shows how well the kidneys filter.

119271.q: What does the term uraemia mean?
a: Waste substances that should be passed in urine build up in the blood
There is blood in the urine
There is sugar in the urine
119271.e: In uraemia, waste substances such as urea stay in the body. The results include nausea, itching and confusion.
119271.m: Uraemia is poisoning by the body's own waste substances.

119272.q: Why can heavy fluid loss, for example from severe diarrhoea, lead to acute kidney failure?
a: The kidneys get too little blood
The kidneys are attacked by bacteria
119272.e: When fluid is lacking, blood pressure falls and the kidneys get too little blood to filter. Doctors call this prerenal kidney failure.
119272.m: Too little blood for the kidneys can make them fail.

119273.q: Which mineral rises in the blood in advanced kidney failure and can trigger dangerous heart rhythm disorders?
119273.e: The diseased kidney no longer excretes enough potassium. A potassium level that is too high disturbs the electrical excitation of the heart.
119273.m: In kidney failure, potassium in the blood rises.

119274.q: What does permanently raised albumin in the urine show?
a: A harmless, meaningless effect of sport
119274.e: Healthy glomeruli let hardly any albumin through. If it can be detected in the urine permanently, this is considered an early sign of kidney damage.
119274.m: Albumin in the urine is a warning sign for the kidney.

119275.q: Which treatments replace the function of the kidneys in the final stage?
a: A blood transfusion or a plaster cast
119275.e: In end-stage kidney failure, kidney replacement therapy is needed. The best long-term solution is usually a transplant.
119275.m: Without kidney function, only dialysis or a new kidney can help.

119276.q: Why does chronic kidney disease often damage the bones too?
a: The kidney activates too little vitamin D
The kidney makes too much bone marrow
The kidney burns the calcium in the bones
119276.e: The diseased kidney activates too little vitamin D and excretes too little phosphate. The calcium-phosphate balance is thrown off, and the bone is damaged.
119276.m: Diseased kidneys also weaken the bones.

119277.q: Which physical principle does haemodialysis mainly use to remove toxins?
119277.e: Blood and dialysis fluid are separated by a semi-permeable membrane. Small substances such as urea move along their concentration gradient into the dialysate.
119277.m: In dialysis, toxins pass through a membrane.

119278.q: How often is haemodialysis typically carried out for kidney failure?
119278.e: Three sessions a week of about four to five hours each are usual. In between, patients have to be careful with drinking and with foods rich in potassium.
119278.m: Haemodialysis usually takes place three times a week.

119279.q: Which vascular access is often created by surgery on the arm for haemodialysis?
a: An access into the spinal cord
119279.e: In an arteriovenous fistula, often called a Cimino shunt, an artery is joined to a vein. This makes the vein strong and easy to puncture.
119279.m: The shunt vein in the arm is the lifeline of dialysis patients.

119280.q: How is excess water removed during haemodialysis?
a: By ultrafiltration with a pressure gradient
119280.e: A pressure difference across the membrane presses water out of the blood into the dialysate. This ultrafiltration replaces the missing urine production.
119280.m: Ultrafiltration removes excess water from the blood.

119281.q: Which substance usually stops the blood from clotting in the dialysis machine?
119281.e: Heparin blocks clotting while the blood flows outside the body through tubes and filters. Vitamin K, fibrinogen and thrombin, on the other hand, promote clotting.
119281.m: Heparin keeps the blood liquid in the dialysis circuit.

119282.q: Which dialysis method uses the patient's own peritoneum as the membrane?
119282.e: In peritoneal dialysis, dialysis solution is filled into the abdominal cavity and changed after a few hours. It can be done at home.
119282.m: In peritoneal dialysis, your own peritoneum does the filtering.

119283.q: How do blood and dialysis fluid usually flow relative to each other in the dialyser?
a: Not at all, they stand still
119283.e: With countercurrent flow, the concentration gradient is kept along the whole length of the filter. That way more waste substances are removed.
119283.m: In the dialyser, blood and dialysate flow against each other.

119284.q: Which waste product of protein breakdown is removed from the blood in large amounts during dialysis?
119284.e: Urea is produced when proteins are broken down and is normally excreted through the kidneys. How much it decreases is also used to measure how effective a dialysis is.
119284.m: The dialysis dose is measured by urea.

119285.q: Which assumption is part of the ideal gas model?
a: The particles have no volume of their own and do not attract each other
The particles strongly attract each other
The particles rest at fixed places
The particles are bigger than the distances between them
119285.e: In an ideal gas the particles are point-like and interact only through elastic collisions. Forces of attraction and the particles' own volume are ignored.
119285.m: Ideal gas particles are tiny spheres that do not attract each other.

119286.q: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?
a: High temperature and very high pressure
119286.e: At low pressure the particles are far apart, so their own volume hardly matters. At high temperature the forces of attraction hardly count compared with the kinetic energy.
119286.m: Hot and thin, gases behave almost ideally.

119287.q: Which equation describes real gases with corrections for the particles' own volume and attraction?
119287.e: Johannes Diderik van der Waals added an internal pressure for attraction and a co-volume for the particles' own volume to the gas equation. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 1910.
119287.m: The van der Waals equation describes real gases.

119288.q: Which gas behaves especially close to an ideal gas at room temperature?
119288.e: Helium atoms are small and hardly attract each other. Gases such as water vapour or ammonia, by contrast, have strong forces of attraction between their molecules.
119288.m: Helium is almost an ideal gas.

119289.q: What is the value of the universal gas constant R?
119289.e: The gas constant is about 8.314 joules per mole and kelvin. It links pressure, volume, amount of substance and temperature.
119289.m: The gas constant R is about 8.3 joules per mole and kelvin.

119290.q: What is the value of the compressibility factor p·V/(n·R·T) for an ideal gas?
119290.e: For an ideal gas the equation of state applies exactly, so the ratio is 1. For real gases, the difference from 1 shows how far they depart from the ideal.
119290.m: For an ideal gas the compressibility factor is exactly one.

119291.q: What can happen to a real gas, but never to an ideal gas, if you cool it strongly and compress it?
119291.e: Liquefying needs forces of attraction between the particles. These are missing in the ideal gas model, so it can never condense.

119292.q: Air at 100 kPa contains about 21 per cent oxygen. What is the partial pressure of the oxygen?
119292.e: In a mixture of ideal gases, each gas contributes to the total pressure according to its mole fraction. 0.21 times 100 kPa gives 21 kPa.
119292.m: Each gas in a mixture has its own partial pressure.

119293.q: What is the ideal gas equation with the amount of substance n?
119293.e: Pressure times volume is proportional to amount of substance and temperature. The constant of proportionality is the gas constant R.
119293.m: Pressure times volume grows with amount of substance and temperature.

119294.q: What is the pressure of 2 mol of ideal gas at 300 K in a volume of 0.05 m³?
119294.e: p is nRT divided by V: 2 times 8.314 times 300 divided by 0.05 gives 99,768 Pa. That is about 100 kPa.
119294.m: For the pressure, divide nRT by the volume.

119295.q: How many moles of air does 1 m³ contain at 20 °C and 100 kPa?
119295.e: n is pV divided by RT: 100,000 times 1 divided by 8.314 times 293.15. That gives about 41 mol.
119295.m: One cubic metre of air contains about 41 moles of particles.

119296.q: A gas is at 2 bar, 10 litres and 300 K. What is its volume at 1 bar and 450 K?
119296.e: From p1V1/T1 = p2V2/T2 it follows that V2 = 2 times 10 times 450 divided by 300 times 1. That gives 30 litres.
119296.m: For a fixed amount of gas, pV divided by T stays constant.

119297.q: What is the mass of 1 m³ of helium (M = 4 g/mol) at 0 °C and 101,325 Pa?
119297.e: n is 101,325 divided by 8.314 times 273.15, so about 44.6 mol. Times 4 g/mol, that gives about 178 g.
119297.m: Helium is about seven times lighter than air.

119298.q: 0.513 g of a gas takes up exactly 0.4 litres at 300 K and 100 kPa. Which gas is it?
119298.e: n is pV divided by RT, so 100,000 times 0.0004 divided by 8.314 times 300, about 0.016 mol. The molar mass, 0.513 g divided by 0.016 mol, gives 32 g/mol, which matches O₂.
119298.m: You can use the gas equation to find the molar mass of a gas.

119299.q: What is the law called which says that equal volumes of ideal gases at the same pressure and temperature contain the same number of particles?
119299.e: Amedeo Avogadro put forward this hypothesis in 1811. It follows directly from the equation of state, because the type of gas does not appear in it.
119299.m: Equal volumes of gas contain the same number of particles.

119300.q: In which unit must the temperature be put into the equation of state?
119300.e: The equation only works with absolute temperature. With degrees Celsius you would wrongly get a pressure of zero at 0 °C.
119300.m: Temperature always goes into the gas equation in kelvin.

119301.q: What does Boyle's law (the Boyle-Mariotte law) state for a fixed amount of gas?
a: At constant temperature, p·V is constant
At constant pressure, V/T is constant
At constant volume, p/T is constant
At constant temperature, p/V is constant
119301.e: At a constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional. If you halve the volume, the pressure doubles.
119301.m: At the same temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional.

119302.q: 6 litres of gas at 100 kPa are compressed to 2 litres at constant temperature. What is the new pressure?
119302.e: From p1V1 = p2V2 it follows that p2 = 100 times 6 divided by 2. That gives 300 kPa.
119302.m: A third of the volume means three times the pressure.

119303.q: A balloon holds 3 litres at the water surface (100 kPa). What is its volume 20 m deep (about 300 kPa) at the same temperature?
119303.e: For every 10 m of water depth the pressure rises by about 100 kPa, so at 20 m it is about 300 kPa. V2 is 100 times 3 divided by 300, so 1 litre.
119303.m: When diving, air is compressed as you go deeper.

119304.q: What shape is an isotherm of an ideal gas in a p-V diagram?
a: A straight line through the origin
119304.e: Because p = constant / V, you get a hyperbola. For higher temperatures it lies further from the origin.
119304.m: Isotherms in a p-V diagram are hyperbolas.

119305.q: Which scientist discovered the law independently of Robert Boyle a few years later?
119305.e: Robert Boyle published the relationship in 1662, the Frenchman Edme Mariotte in 1676. That is why in German and French the law carries both names, while in English it is usually just called Boyle's law.
119305.m: The law honours the Englishman Boyle and the Frenchman Mariotte.

119306.q: A 50-litre gas cylinder is at 200 bar. What volume does the gas take up at 1 bar and the same temperature?
119306.e: From p1V1 = p2V2 you get 200 times 50 divided by 1, so 10,000 litres. That is 10 m³.
119306.m: A compressed gas cylinder holds many times its own volume.

119307.q: How does the density of a gas change if the pressure is doubled at constant temperature?
119307.e: At twice the pressure the volume halves, while the mass stays the same. Density is mass divided by volume, so it doubles.
119307.m: At the same temperature, gas density grows with pressure.

119308.q: Why is a bag of crisps sealed in Zurich puffed up tight on the Jungfraujoch?
a: Because the outside air pressure is much lower there
Because the crisps give off gas at altitude
Because the air is warmer up there
Because the bag shrinks in the cold
119308.e: At about 3450 m the air pressure is much lower than in Zurich. The trapped air expands until the pressure inside and outside is almost the same.
119308.m: As the outside pressure falls, trapped air expands.

119309.q: What does Gay-Lussac's law state for a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure?
a: The volume is proportional to the absolute temperature
The volume is inversely proportional to the temperature
The volume does not depend on the temperature
The pressure is proportional to the volume
119309.e: At the same pressure, a gas expands evenly when it is heated. V divided by T stays constant if T is measured in kelvin.
119309.m: At the same pressure, gas volume grows with the absolute temperature.

119310.q: 3 litres of gas are heated at constant pressure from 27 °C to 127 °C. What is the new volume?
119310.e: In kelvin these are 300 K and 400 K. V2 is 3 times 400 divided by 300, so 4 litres.
119310.m: In gas laws, always convert temperatures into kelvin first.

119311.q: A gas is heated at constant pressure from 10 °C to 20 °C. How does its volume change?
a: It increases by about 3.5 per cent
119311.e: What matters are the absolute temperatures 283.15 K and 293.15 K. Their ratio is about 1.035, so the volume grows by about 3.5 per cent.
119311.m: Doubling the degrees Celsius does not double the temperature.

119312.q: Where does extending the volume-temperature line down to zero volume lead?
a: To the freezing point of water
To the boiling point of water
119312.e: If you extend the measured lines of different gases, they meet at the same temperature. This idea led to the Kelvin scale.
119312.m: The gas laws point to a lowest possible temperature.

119313.q: Which country did Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac come from?
119313.e: Gay-Lussac was a French chemist and physicist. In 1802 he published his measurements of the thermal expansion of gases.

119314.q: A balloon of 2 litres at 20 °C is put into a freezer at −18 °C at the same pressure. Roughly what is its volume then?
119314.e: V2 is 2 times 255.15 divided by 293.15. That gives about 1.74 litres.
119314.m: Cold air takes up less space than warm air.

119315.q: To what temperature must a gas at 0 °C be heated at constant pressure for its volume to double?
119315.e: The volume doubles when the absolute temperature doubles: from 273.15 K to 546.3 K. That is about 273 °C.
119315.m: Twice the volume needs twice the kelvin temperature.

119316.q: Which quantity stays constant in an isobaric change of state?
119316.e: “Isobaric” comes from the Greek “baros” for weight or pressure. Volume and temperature change, but the pressure does not.
119316.m: Isobaric means at the same pressure.

119317.q: How does an isobaric change of state appear in a p-V diagram?
119317.e: The pressure on the vertical axis stays the same; only the volume changes. The area under the line is the work done.
119317.m: An isobar is horizontal in a p-V diagram.

119318.q: Why does a gas need more heat at constant pressure than at constant volume for the same rise in temperature?
a: It also does work as it expands
119318.e: At constant volume, the heat only increases the internal energy. At constant pressure, the gas expands and gives off part of the heat as work.
119318.m: At constant pressure, heating also costs expansion work.

119319.q: How much heat does 1 mol of monatomic ideal gas (Cp = 20.8 J/(mol·K)) need to become 10 K warmer at constant pressure?
119319.e: Q is n times Cp times the change in temperature: 1 times 20.8 times 10 gives 208 J.
119319.m: Heat at constant pressure is amount of substance times Cp times change in temperature.

119320.q: How much work does 1 mol of ideal gas do when it is heated by 10 K at constant pressure?
119320.e: At constant pressure, p times the change in volume equals n times R times the change in temperature. 1 times 8.314 times 10 gives about 83 J.
119320.m: When heated at constant pressure, each mole of gas does about 8.3 joules of work per kelvin.

119321.q: Which state variable does the heat supplied at constant pressure correspond to?
119321.e: Enthalpy H is internal energy plus p times V. At constant pressure, the heat supplied equals the change in enthalpy.
119321.m: At constant pressure, the heat measures the change in enthalpy.

119322.q: 2 litres of gas at 300 K and 150 kPa are heated at constant pressure to 450 K. How much work does the gas do?
119322.e: The volume rises to 2 times 450 divided by 300, so 3 litres. The work is 150,000 Pa times 0.001 m³, so 150 J.
119322.m: At constant pressure, the increase in volume determines the work.

119323.q: A gas takes in 208 J of heat when heated at constant pressure and does 83 J of work in the process. By how much does its internal energy rise?
119323.e: According to the first law, the increase in internal energy equals the heat supplied minus the work given off: 208 J minus 83 J gives 125 J.
119323.m: The heat supplied is split into internal energy and work given off.

119324.q: Which quantity stays constant in an isochoric change of state?
119324.e: “Isochoric” means “same space”. The gas is enclosed in a rigid container, for example.
119324.m: Isochoric means at the same volume.

119325.q: How much expansion work is done in an isochoric change of state?
a: The same as the heat supplied
119325.e: Expansion work only arises when the volume changes. At constant volume no such work is done.
119325.m: Without a change in volume there is no expansion work.

119326.q: At what temperature would the pressure of an ideal gas in a rigid container fall to zero?
119326.e: At constant volume the pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature. At 0 K, which is about −273 °C, the motion of the particles and so the pressure would stop.
119326.m: At absolute zero the gas pressure would disappear.

119327.q: A bike tyre has an absolute pressure of 200 kPa at 20 °C. What is the pressure at 50 °C if the volume stays the same?
119327.e: p2 is 200 times 323.15 divided by 293.15, so about 220 kPa. You calculate with absolute temperatures.
119327.m: In the sun the pressure in a tyre rises.

119328.q: Why must you not throw an aerosol can into a fire?
a: The pressure in the can rises sharply with temperature
The volume of the can shrinks in the heat
The gas cools down in the fire
The pressure in the can falls to zero
119328.e: The can is a rigid container. When heated, the pressure inside rises until the can may burst.

119329.q: How does an isochoric change of state appear in a p-V diagram?
a: As a straight line through the origin
119329.e: The volume on the horizontal axis stays the same; only the pressure changes. There is no area under a vertical line, so no work.
119329.m: An isochore is vertical in a p-V diagram.

119330.q: A gas in a rigid container is at 100 kPa at 300 K. At what temperature is it at 300 kPa?
119330.e: Three times the pressure needs three times the absolute temperature, so 900 K. 900 minus 273 gives 627 °C.
119330.m: Twice the pressure in a rigid container needs twice the kelvin temperature.

119331.q: Which measuring instrument uses the change in pressure of an enclosed gas at constant volume?
119331.e: In a constant-volume gas thermometer, the pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature. For a long time it served as an accurate reference thermometer.
119331.m: A gas thermometer measures temperature through gas pressure.

119332.q: From the point of view of the particles, why does the pressure rise when a gas is heated at constant volume?
a: The particles hit the wall more often and harder
The particles attract each other more strongly
119332.e: Higher temperature means faster particles. They hit the walls more often and with more momentum, but the area stays the same.

119333.q: Which equation applies to an adiabatic change of state of an ideal gas?
119333.e: This Poisson equation contains the adiabatic index κ, the ratio of the heat capacities Cp to Cv. In an adiabatic change of state no heat is exchanged with the surroundings.
119333.m: In adiabatic processes, p times V to the power of kappa stays constant.

119334.q: Roughly what adiabatic index κ does dry air have?
119334.e: Air consists mainly of the diatomic gases nitrogen and oxygen. For these, κ = 7/5, which is 1.4.
119334.m: For air the adiabatic index is about 1.4.

119335.q: Roughly how much does dry air warm up per 100 metres as it sinks?
119335.e: Sinking air is compressed adiabatically by the rising pressure. The dry adiabatic lapse rate is just under 1 K per 100 m.
119335.m: Dry air gets about 1 degree warmer for every 100 metres it descends.

119336.q: Dry föhn air is at 4 °C on an Alpine pass 2100 m high and sinks dry-adiabatically into the valley at 500 m. Roughly what temperature does it reach?
119336.e: The difference in height is 1600 m. At about 1 °C per 100 m, the air warms up by about 16 °C, so from 4 °C to about 20 °C.
119336.m: Föhn brings warm air into the Alpine valleys.

119337.q: Why does a bike pump get warm at its lower end when you pump fast?
a: The air is compressed adiabatically and heats up
The air cools down as it expands
The valve produces heat with electricity
119337.e: When air is squeezed quickly there is no time for it to give off heat. The work of compression increases the internal energy and so the temperature of the air.
119337.m: Squeezing a gas quickly heats it up.

119338.q: How does an adiabat in a p-V diagram compare with the isotherm through the same point?
119338.e: In adiabatic compression the temperature rises as well as the pressure. That is why the pressure rises faster than at a constant temperature.

119339.q: Air (κ = 1.4) at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to a tenth of its volume in a diesel engine. Roughly what temperature does it reach?
119339.e: T times V to the power of κ minus 1 is constant, so T2 = 300 times 10 to the power of 0.4. That gives about 754 K, hot enough to ignite diesel fuel.
119339.m: In a diesel engine the heat of the compressed air ignites the fuel.

119340.q: A monatomic ideal gas (κ = 5/3) at 100 kPa is compressed adiabatically to half its volume. Roughly what is the final pressure?
119340.e: p2 is p1 times 2 to the power of 5/3. That gives 100 times 3.17, so about 317 kPa.
119340.m: Compressed adiabatically, the pressure rises more than isothermally.

119341.q: Why does a fine mist often form in the neck of a bottle of fizzy drink when you open it?
a: The gas expands quickly and cools down as it does so
The glass gives off water vapour
119341.e: When the bottle is opened, the gas above the liquid expands very quickly, with no time for heat exchange. It cools down so much that water vapour condenses into tiny droplets.

119342.q: Roughly what is the specific heat capacity of liquid water?
119342.e: Heating 1 kg of water by 1 K takes about 4.2 kJ. That is much more than for most other substances.
119342.m: Water stores a particularly large amount of heat.

119343.q: What is the SI unit of specific heat capacity?
119343.e: Specific heat capacity relates heat to mass and change in temperature. W/(m·K) is the unit of thermal conductivity.
119343.m: Specific heat capacity is measured in joules per kilogram and kelvin.

119344.q: Why do places on Lake Geneva often have milder temperatures in winter than places far from large lakes?
a: The lake water stores a lot of heat and releases it slowly
The lake water produces heat itself
There is no wind over lakes
The water reflects the sun back into the air
119344.e: Because of its high heat capacity, a large lake cools down only slowly in autumn. In winter it gives off heat to the air and softens temperature swings.
119344.m: Large lakes act like heat stores.

119345.q: A 2000 W kettle heats 1 kg of water (c = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K)) from 20 °C to 100 °C without losses. How long does it take?
119345.e: Q is 1 times 4180 times 80, so 334,400 J. Divided by 2000 W, that gives about 167 s.
119345.m: Time is the heat needed divided by the power.

119346.q: 0.5 kg of aluminium (c = 0.90 kJ/(kg·K)) takes in 9 kJ of heat. By how much does the temperature rise?
119346.e: Change in temperature is Q divided by m times c: 9 divided by 0.5 times 0.9 gives 20 K.
119346.m: You can calculate the rise in temperature from heat, mass and c.

119347.q: Equal masses of copper (c ≈ 0.39 kJ/(kg·K)) and water (c ≈ 4.18 kJ/(kg·K)) receive the same heat. How do their temperature rises compare?
a: Copper warms up about ten times more
Water warms up about ten times more
Copper warms up about twice as much
119347.e: The change in temperature is Q divided by m times c. Because c of water is about ten times larger, copper warms up about ten times more with the same heat.
119347.m: The smaller the specific heat capacity, the more a substance warms up.

119348.q: A piece of metal weighing 0.2 kg takes in 1.8 kJ and gets 20 K warmer. What is its specific heat capacity?
119348.e: c is Q divided by m times the change in temperature: 1800 divided by 0.2 times 20 gives 450 J/(kg·K). That roughly matches iron.
119348.m: Specific heat capacity helps to identify substances.

119349.q: How does the specific heat capacity of ice compare with that of liquid water?
a: It is about half as large
It is about twice as large
It is about ten times as large
119349.e: Ice has about 2.1 kJ/(kg·K), liquid water about 4.2 kJ/(kg·K). So the heat capacity also depends on the state of matter.
119349.m: Ice is easier to warm up than liquid water.

119350.q: What do you measure with a calorimeter?
119350.e: A calorimeter is a well-insulated container in which heat from reactions, mixing or burning is measured. The name comes from the Latin “calor” for heat.

119351.q: What does the water equivalent of a calorimeter tell you?
a: The mass of water with the same heat capacity as the container
The amount of water that fits in the container
The water pressure at the bottom of the container
119351.e: The container, the stirrer and the thermometer also take in heat. The water equivalent expresses this heat capacity as an equivalent mass of water.
119351.m: The water equivalent accounts for the heat the calorimeter itself absorbs.

119352.q: What is a bomb calorimeter used for?
a: To find the calorific value of substances
To measure explosive power in mining
119352.e: In a bomb calorimeter a sample is burned with oxygen in a pressure-resistant steel container. The calorific value, for example of foods, follows from how much the surrounding water warms up.
119352.m: In a bomb calorimeter, samples are burned to measure their calorific value.

119353.q: A calorimeter (C = 210 J/K) contains 0.5 kg of water (c = 4180 J/(kg·K)). By how much does the temperature rise when 9200 J of heat is supplied?
119353.e: The total heat capacity is 0.5 times 4180 plus 210, so 2300 J/K. 9200 divided by 2300 gives 4 K.
119353.m: With a calorimeter, you must include the container too.

119354.q: In a calorimeter with 0.2 kg of water (c = 4180 J/(kg·K)), 5000 J causes a rise of 5 K. What is the heat capacity of the container?
119354.e: In total, 5000 divided by 5 gives 1000 J/K. Of this, 0.2 times 4180, so 836 J/K, is for the water, which leaves 164 J/K for the container.
119354.m: You find the heat capacity of a calorimeter with a known amount of heat.

119355.q: Why do many calorimeters have a double wall with a vacuum in between?
a: So that hardly any heat is lost through conduction and convection
So that the water boils faster
So that the container is lighter
So that light can get in better
119355.e: In a vacuum there are no particles to conduct heat or carry it by flowing. Mirrored walls also reduce heat radiation, as in a vacuum flask.

119356.q: How many joules is one thermochemical calorie?
119356.e: The calorie used to be the heat needed to warm 1 g of water by 1 °C. Today it is fixed at exactly 4.184 J, but the SI unit is the joule.
119356.m: One calorie is just over four joules.

119357.q: What is the difference between the gross calorific value and the net calorific value of a fuel?
a: The gross value includes the heat released when the water vapour condenses
The gross value only applies to solid fuels
The net value is always twice as large
The net value includes the heat released when the water vapour condenses
119357.e: For the gross calorific value, the water vapour produced is condensed back into water and the heat released is counted too. That is why the gross value is larger than the net value.
119357.m: Condensing boilers also use the heat from the water vapour.

119358.q: Equal masses of water at 20 °C and 60 °C are mixed. What mixing temperature results without heat losses?
119358.e: With equal masses of the same substance, the mixing temperature is exactly halfway. 20 plus 60 divided by 2 gives 40 °C.
119358.m: Equal amounts of water give the average of the temperatures.

119359.q: 2 kg of water at 10 °C is mixed with 1 kg of water at 70 °C. What mixing temperature results?
119359.e: Weighted average: 2 times 10 plus 1 times 70 divided by 3. That gives 90 divided by 3, so 30 °C.
119359.m: The larger amount has more influence on the mixing temperature.

119360.q: 0.1 kg of iron (c = 450 J/(kg·K)) at 200 °C falls into 0.3 kg of water (c = 4180 J/(kg·K)) at 20 °C. Roughly what mixing temperature results?
119360.e: The mixing temperature is (0.3 times 4180 times 20 plus 0.1 times 450 times 200) divided by (0.3 times 4180 plus 0.1 times 450). That gives 34,080 divided by 1299, so about 26 °C.
119360.m: Water strongly resists changes in temperature.

119361.q: Which principle is the calculation of a mixing temperature based on?
a: The heat given off equals the heat taken in
119361.e: Without losses to the surroundings, energy is conserved. What the warmer body gives off, the colder one takes in.
119361.m: When mixing, no heat is lost; it is only shared out.

119362.q: After which physicist is the rule for calculating mixing temperatures named?
119362.e: Georg Wilhelm Richmann formulated the rule of mixtures in the 18th century in St Petersburg. It is called Richmann's rule of mixtures.
119362.m: The rule of mixtures bears Richmann's name.

119363.q: 0.1 kg of ice at 0 °C is put into 0.5 kg of water at 40 °C (latent heat of fusion 334 kJ/kg, c = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K)). Roughly what final temperature results?
119363.e: Melting takes 33.4 kJ. Heat given off equals heat taken in: 0.5 times 4.18 times (40 − T) = 33.4 plus 0.1 times 4.18 times T, from which T is about 20 °C.
119363.m: Ice cools especially strongly because it melts.

119364.q: How much water at 60 °C must you add to 50 litres of water at 15 °C to get a bath at 37 °C?
119364.e: The heat given off by the hot water must equal the heat taken up: m times 23 equals 50 times 22. So m equals 1100 divided by 23, about 48 litres.
119364.m: The mixing rule lets you work out the right amount of water.

119365.q: 30 litres of water at 50 °C are mixed with 10 litres of water at 10 °C. What is the temperature of the mixture?
119365.e: Weighted average: 30 times 50 plus 10 times 10, divided by 40. That gives 1600 divided by 40, so 40 °C.
119365.m: The mixing temperature is a weighted average.

119366.q: Why is the mixing temperature of 1 kg of hot water and 1 kg of cold copper much closer to the water temperature?
a: Water has a much greater heat capacity
119366.e: For the same mass, water stores about ten times more heat per kelvin than copper. So the water cools only a little, while the copper warms up a lot.
119366.m: The substance with the greater heat capacity sets the tone when mixing.

119367.q: How does the kinetic theory of gases explain the pressure of a gas?
a: By particles colliding with the container wall
By the weight of the particles at rest
By attraction between particles and wall
119367.e: The particles constantly hit the wall and transfer momentum. The sum of these impulses per area is the pressure.
119367.m: Gas pressure comes from countless particle collisions.

119368.q: According to the kinetic theory of gases, what is the temperature of a gas?
a: A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles
A measure of the number of particles
A measure of the size of the particles
A measure of the mass of the gas
119368.e: The faster the particles move on average, the higher the temperature. At absolute zero, thermal motion would come to a stop.
119368.m: Temperature measures how vigorously particles move.

119369.q: Roughly what is the root mean square speed of nitrogen molecules (M = 28 g/mol) at 300 K?
119369.e: v equals the square root of 3RT divided by M: the square root of 3 times 8.314 times 300 divided by 0.028. That gives about 517 m/s.
119369.m: Air molecules are faster than sound.

119370.q: How does the average particle speed change when the absolute temperature of a gas is doubled?
a: It increases by a factor of root 2
119370.e: The speed is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature. So double the temperature gives particles about 1.41 times faster.
119370.m: Particle speed grows with the square root of the temperature.

119371.q: Which distribution describes the speeds of the particles in a gas?
119371.e: James Clerk Maxwell and Ludwig Boltzmann derived the distribution in the 19th century. It shows that particles move at very different speeds.
119371.m: Not all gas particles are equally fast.

119372.q: Who explained Brownian motion in 1905 using the motion of molecules?
119372.e: Albert Einstein, who was then working at the patent office in Bern, explained the jiggling of small particles by collisions with molecules. This was important evidence that atoms exist.
119372.m: Brownian motion shows that molecules really exist.

119373.q: At the same temperature, how many times faster do helium atoms (4 g/mol) move on average than oxygen molecules (32 g/mol)?
119373.e: Speed is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass. The square root of 32 divided by 4 is root 8, about 2.8.
119373.m: Light gas particles are faster than heavy ones.

119374.q: How do the average kinetic energies of helium and oxygen particles compare at the same temperature?
a: Helium has eight times the energy
Oxygen has eight times the energy
119374.e: The average translational energy depends only on temperature, not on mass. Heavy particles are slower instead.
119374.m: At the same temperature, all gas particles have the same kinetic energy on average.

119375.q: Which scholar from Basel explained gas pressure in 1738 as a result of particle motion?
119375.e: In his work “Hydrodynamica”, Daniel Bernoulli described gases as a collection of moving particles. He is seen as a forerunner of the kinetic theory of gases.
119375.m: The kinetic theory of gases has roots in Basel.

119376.q: Roughly what is the value of the Boltzmann constant k?
119376.e: The Boltzmann constant is exactly 1.380649·10⁻²³ J/K. It links temperature and energy at the level of single particles.
119376.m: The Boltzmann constant is a very small number.

119377.q: Since which year has the numerical value of the Boltzmann constant been fixed exactly in the SI?
119377.e: With the revision of the International System of Units on 20 May 2019, several constants of nature were fixed exactly. Since then, k is no longer a measured value.
119377.m: Since 2019 the Boltzmann constant has been exactly defined.

119378.q: How is the Boltzmann constant related to the gas constant R?
a: k is R divided by the Avogadro constant
k is R times the Avogadro constant
k is R divided by the speed of light
119378.e: The gas constant refers to one mole, the Boltzmann constant to one particle. 8.314 divided by 6.022·10²³ gives about 1.38·10⁻²³.
119378.m: The Boltzmann constant is the gas constant per particle.

119379.q: Which SI base unit is now defined using the Boltzmann constant?
119379.e: The kelvin used to be defined by the triple point of water. Today it follows from the fixed value of the Boltzmann constant.
119379.m: The kelvin is now based on the Boltzmann constant.

119380.q: What is the average translational energy of a gas particle at 300 K (3/2·k·T)?
119380.e: 1.5 times 1.38·10⁻²³ times 300 gives about 6.2·10⁻²¹ J. Per particle, that is a tiny energy.
119380.m: A single gas particle carries only a tiny amount of energy.

119381.q: Roughly how many gas particles are there in 1 cm³ of an ideal gas at 100 kPa and 300 K?
119381.e: From p·V equals N·k·T, N equals 100,000 times 10⁻⁶ divided by 1.38·10⁻²³ times 300. That gives about 2.4·10¹⁹ particles.
119381.m: Even one cubic centimetre of air contains an unimaginable number of particles.

119382.q: Roughly what is the thermal energy k·T at 300 K in electronvolts?
119382.e: 1.38·10⁻²³ times 300 gives about 4.1·10⁻²¹ J. Divided by 1.602·10⁻¹⁹ J per eV, that is about 0.026 eV.
119382.m: At room temperature, k times T is about one fortieth of an electronvolt.

119383.q: What does the Boltzmann factor e^(-E/(k·T)) describe?
a: How likely a state with energy E is to be occupied
How fast light travels in the gas
How large a gas particle is
How well a gas conducts electricity
119383.e: The larger E is compared with k times T, the more rarely a state is occupied. This is why many chemical reactions run faster at higher temperatures.
119383.m: High energy states are rarely occupied at low temperature.

119384.q: How are the spores typically formed in basidiomycete fungi (Basidiomycota)?
a: On the outside of club-shaped basidia
In capsules at the ends of the hyphae
119384.e: In basidiomycetes the spores form on the outside of the basidium, usually four of them on small stalks (sterigmata). This is where the group gets its name.
119384.m: Basidiomycetes carry their spores on the outside of basidia.

119385.q: How many spores does a basidium of a typical basidiomycete carry?
119385.e: A typical basidium carries four basidiospores, each on its own sterigma. The number comes from meiosis, which produces four nuclei.
119385.m: A typical basidium carries four spores.

119386.q: Which group of fungi do most well-known cap mushrooms such as the fly agaric and the chanterelle belong to?
119386.e: Fly agaric, chanterelle and penny bun form their spores on basidia and are basidiomycetes. Ascomycetes include morels and truffles, for example.

119387.q: Which of these edible mushrooms belongs to the basidiomycetes?
119387.e: The penny bun forms its spores on basidia in its tubes and is a basidiomycete. Truffles and cup fungi belong to the ascomycetes.
119387.m: The penny bun is a basidiomycete.

119388.q: Which plant pathogens belong to the basidiomycetes?
119388.e: Rust fungi (for example stem rust of cereals) and smut fungi (for example corn smut) are basidiomycetes. Powdery mildews, scab and grey mould are ascomycetes, and water moulds are not true fungi at all.
119388.m: Rust fungi and smut fungi count as basidiomycetes.

119389.q: What is the spore-forming layer called that lies on the gills or in the tubes of cap mushrooms?
119389.e: The hymenium is the fertile layer with the basidia. Gills and tubes increase the area on which it lies.
119389.m: The fertile layer of a mushroom is called the hymenium.

119390.q: Which part of a basidiomycete often lives in the soil for years, while the fruiting body only appears briefly?
119390.e: The mycelium is a network of fine fungal threads, the hyphae. It can live in the soil for many years. The visible mushroom is only the short-lived fruiting body for producing spores.
119390.m: The real fungus is the long-lived mycelium in the soil.

119391.q: In basidiomycetes, where do the two nuclei of the paired-nucleus mycelium fuse?
119391.e: In the young basidium, the two nuclei fuse into one diploid nucleus. The meiosis that follows produces the four nuclei of the basidiospores.
119391.m: In basidiomycetes, the nuclei fuse in the basidium.

119392.q: In which structure do the spores of ascomycete fungi (Ascomycota) form?
119392.e: Ascomycetes form their spores inside a tube-shaped container, the ascus. This is also where the group's name comes from.
119392.m: Ascomycetes form their spores in the ascus.

119393.q: How many ascospores does a typical ascus contain?
119393.e: Meiosis is usually followed by one more mitosis, so eight ascospores form. The number can be different in some species.
119393.m: A typical ascus contains eight spores.

119394.q: Which group does the baker's and brewer's yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae belong to?
119394.e: Baker's yeast is a single-celled ascomycete. Under favourable conditions it forms asci, usually with four spores.

119395.q: Which fungus with a bright orange, bowl-shaped fruiting body is an ascomycete?
119395.e: The orange peel fungus forms its spore sacs on the inside of the bowl. Fly agaric, chanterelle and penny bun are basidiomycetes.

119396.q: Which ascomycete led Alexander Fleming to discover penicillin in 1928?
119396.e: In 1928 Fleming noticed that a Penicillium mould on his bacterial culture stopped staphylococci from growing. Penicillium moulds belong to the ascomycetes.
119396.m: Penicillin originally comes from a Penicillium mould.

119397.q: Which edible mushroom with a honeycomb-like cap is an ascomycete?
119397.e: The morel forms its asci in the pits of its cap. Chanterelle, trumpet chanterelle and parasol are basidiomycetes.

119398.q: Why do moulds spread so quickly in the kitchen?
a: They produce huge numbers of light spores
They actively crawl from one food to another
They only grow in the fridge
They are only spread by flies
119398.e: Moulds produce countless tiny spores without sexual reproduction. These float in the air and germinate on any suitable food.
119398.m: Mould spreads through the air with countless spores.

119399.q: Which partnership is most often formed by ascomycetes with algae or cyanobacteria?
119399.e: Around 98 per cent of lichen-forming fungi are ascomycetes. The fungus forms the body of the lichen, and the alga carries out photosynthesis.

119400.q: What distinguishes ectomycorrhiza from arbuscular mycorrhiza?
a: The hyphae do not enter the cells of the root cortex
The hyphae form little trees inside the cells
The fungus lives only in the cell nucleus
The fungus completely replaces the root tip
119400.e: In ectomycorrhiza, the hyphae only grow between the cells of the root cortex and wrap the root tip in a sheath. They do not enter the cells themselves.
119400.m: Ectomycorrhizal fungi stay outside the root cells.

119401.q: Why is the exchange of substances between fungus and tree root so effective in ectomycorrhiza?
a: A fine network of hyphae provides a large contact area
Fungus and root share one nucleus
The root completely digests the fungus
119401.e: Between the cortex cells the hyphae form the Hartig net. Across its large surface, fungus and tree exchange sugar for water and mineral salts.
119401.m: In the Hartig net, fungus and tree exchange substances.

119402.q: In ectomycorrhiza, what surrounds the fine root tips from the outside?
a: A slime capsule made of bacteria
119402.e: The fungus forms a dense sheath of hyphae around the root tip. Root hairs are often missing there, because the hyphae take over their job.
119402.m: In ectomycorrhiza, a sheath of hyphae wraps around the root tip.

119403.q: Which group of trees in Swiss forests typically lives with ectomycorrhizal fungi?
a: Only fruit trees in traditional orchards
119403.e: The pine family, the beech family and birches typically form ectomycorrhiza. Ashes and maples, by contrast, mainly live with arbuscular mycorrhiza.
119403.m: Many Swiss forest trees live with ectomycorrhiza.

119404.q: Which fungus is a well-known ectomycorrhizal partner of birches and spruces?
119404.e: The fly agaric lives in symbiosis with birches, spruces and pines. Button mushroom, oyster mushroom and shiitake, on the other hand, do not form mycorrhiza with trees.
119404.m: The fly agaric is a mycorrhizal partner of birch and spruce.

119405.q: What does the fungus get from the tree in an ectomycorrhiza?
119405.e: The tree passes some of its photosynthesis products, mainly sugar, to the fungus. In return the fungus supplies water, nitrogen and phosphate.
119405.m: The mycorrhizal fungus gets sugar from the tree.

119406.q: What does the word “mycorrhiza” literally mean?
119406.e: The term was coined in 1885 by the botanist Albert Bernhard Frank. It is made up of the Greek words for fungus (mykes) and root (rhiza).

119407.q: Why do penny buns and truffles hardly grow in pure culture without trees?
a: They depend on sugar from mycorrhizal partners
They constantly need temperatures below zero
They only feed on live insects
They can only germinate in sea water
119407.e: Ectomycorrhizal fungi usually only form fruiting bodies with a host tree that supplies them with sugar. That is why truffles are grown on plantations with inoculated trees.
119407.m: Mycorrhizal fungi usually need a partner tree to form fruiting bodies.

119408.q: What do plant and fungus exchange in arbuscular mycorrhiza?
a: The plant gives sugar, the fungus supplies mineral salts
The fungus gives sugar, the plant supplies mineral salts
The plant gives water, the fungus light
119408.e: The fungus cannot carry out photosynthesis and gets sugar from the plant. In return it brings mineral salts, especially phosphate, and water to the root.
119408.m: In mycorrhiza, the plant exchanges sugar for mineral salts.

a: Finely branched little trees of hyphae in cortex cells
Spore capsules on the surface of the soil
Thickened root hairs of the plant
Sheaths of hyphae around the root tip
119409.e: Arbuscules are hyphae branched like little trees inside the cortex cells. They stay wrapped in the plant's cell membrane, through which the exchange of substances takes place.
119409.m: Arbuscules are branched little trees of hyphae in the root cells.

119410.q: Roughly what share of land plant species forms arbuscular mycorrhiza?
119410.e: Arbuscular mycorrhiza is the most common form of mycorrhiza. It occurs in most herbs, grasses and many crop plants.
119410.m: Most land plants live with arbuscular mycorrhiza.

119411.q: Which nutrient do arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi mainly supply to the plant?
119411.e: Phosphate moves very little in the soil. The fine hyphae reach a much larger volume of soil than the roots and bring phosphate to the plant.
119411.m: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi mainly supply plants with phosphate.

119412.q: Which plant family usually does NOT form mycorrhiza?
a: Cabbage family, such as oilseed rape and cabbage
Grasses, such as wheat and maize
Legumes, such as pea and bean
119412.e: The cabbage family (Brassicaceae) usually does not form mycorrhiza. Cereals, legumes and tomatoes, by contrast, are good partners of arbuscular fungi.
119412.m: The cabbage family, such as oilseed rape, usually lives without mycorrhiza.

119413.q: Why can arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi not be grown on their own on a nutrient medium?
a: They are obligate symbionts and need a host plant
They only grow at over 60 degrees Celsius
They consist only of spores without hyphae
They are killed immediately by light
119413.e: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi get their carbon only from the plant. Without a living root they cannot complete their life cycle.
119413.m: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi only survive with a host plant.

119414.q: What do fossils such as the Rhynie chert in Scotland, around 400 million years old, show?
a: Arbuscules already existed in early land plants
Fungi only appeared after the dinosaurs
Mycorrhiza only exists in flowering plants
The first plants had no cell walls
119414.e: In the Rhynie chert from the Devonian, arbuscules are preserved in plant tissue. The symbiosis probably helped even the first plants to colonise the land.
119414.m: Arbuscular mycorrhiza is around 400 million years old.

119415.q: How does arbuscular mycorrhiza differ from the ectomycorrhiza of many forest trees?
a: The fungal hyphae enter the root cells
The fungi form large cap mushrooms above the ground
The fungi live only in the leaves
The fungi always harm the plant
119415.e: In arbuscular mycorrhiza, the hyphae grow into the cortex cells and form arbuscules there. In ectomycorrhiza they only wrap around the roots from the outside, and many of these fungi form cap mushrooms.
119415.m: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi grow into the root cells.

119416.q: What does the term “Wood Wide Web” mean?
a: A network of mycorrhizal fungi that connects trees
A radio network for foresters in the forest
A network of root runners of one plant species
A network of ant trails on the forest floor
119416.e: “Wood Wide Web” means a common mycorrhizal network. Fungal hyphae can connect several trees, including trees of different species.
119416.m: The Wood Wide Web is a fungal network between trees.

119417.q: What do trees get from the fungi in a mycorrhiza?
119417.e: The fine fungal threads reach into the soil much better than roots and supply water and mineral salts such as phosphorus. In return the fungi get sugar from the tree.
119417.m: Mycorrhizal fungi exchange mineral salts for sugar.

119418.q: Which researcher used labelled carbon in 1997 to show an exchange between birches and Douglas firs?
119418.e: The Canadian forest ecologist Suzanne Simard labelled trees with carbon isotopes. She found carbon that had passed from one tree species to another through fungal connections.
119418.m: Suzanne Simard studied the exchange of carbon between trees.

119419.q: With which method is the path of carbon through a mycorrhizal network traced?
a: With X-rays of the tree crowns
With noise measurements in the soil
With infrared photos from an aeroplane
119419.e: A tree is made to take up carbon dioxide containing carbon-13, for example. Then you measure whether the isotope turns up in neighbouring plants.
119419.m: Isotopes show where carbon travels in the soil.

119420.q: Which plant without chlorophyll taps into the mycorrhizal network of forest trees?
119420.e: The yellow bird's-nest has no chlorophyll and is mycoheterotrophic. It gets sugar through mycorrhizal fungi that are also connected to trees.
119420.m: The yellow bird's-nest lives on sugar from the fungal network.

119421.q: What criticism did researchers make in 2023 of popular accounts of the “Wood Wide Web”?
a: The evidence for mother trees deliberately helping others is weak
There are no mycorrhizal fungi in forests at all
119421.e: In 2023 a review by Justine Karst and colleagues showed that many field studies do not support the widely repeated claims. That mycorrhizal networks exist, however, is not disputed.
119421.m: How much trees help each other through fungi is disputed.

119422.q: Which book by the forester Peter Wohlleben made the fungal network of trees known to a wide public in 2015?
119422.e: In “The Hidden Life of Trees”, Peter Wohlleben describes, among other things, how trees are connected through fungal networks. Some of his descriptions are considered simplified by researchers.
119422.m: Peter Wohlleben wrote “The Hidden Life of Trees”.

119423.q: In technical language, what is a “common mycorrhizal network”?
a: A fungal network that connects at least two plants
A network of bacteria on leaves
All the fungi in a region together
119423.e: A common mycorrhizal network forms when one individual fungus is connected to the roots of several plants. It is the scientific basis of the catchphrase “Wood Wide Web”.
119423.m: A common mycorrhizal network connects several plants through one fungus.

119424.q: Which federal research institute found the large dark honey fungus in the Swiss National Park?
119424.e: Researchers from the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research WSL mapped the fungus in 2004 using many samples in the laboratory. It is considered the largest known fungus in Switzerland.
119424.m: The WSL found the largest known fungus in Switzerland.

119425.q: Roughly how large is the dark honey fungus in the Swiss National Park?
119425.e: The mycelium is about 800 metres long and 500 metres wide and covers around 35 hectares.
119425.m: The honey fungus in the National Park measures about 800 by 500 metres.

119426.q: How old is the dark honey fungus in the Swiss National Park estimated to be?
119426.e: From its size and growth rate, the researchers estimate its age at 800 to 2,000 years, and it may be even older. The fungus keeps slowly growing underground.
119426.m: The honey fungus in the National Park is many centuries old.

119427.q: Which part of the dark honey fungus in the Swiss National Park is so enormous?
a: The cap of a single fruiting body
The stem of a fruiting body
119427.e: The visible honey fungus mushrooms are only the fruiting bodies. The real fungus is a network of hyphae, the mycelium, which spreads over hundreds of metres in the soil.
119427.m: The real fungus is the mycelium in the soil.

119428.q: With which structures does the honey fungus spread underground from tree to tree?
a: With runners made of chains of spores
119428.e: Rhizomorphs are dark, root-like strands of hyphae, popularly known as “bootlaces”. With them the fungus grows through the soil to new roots.
119428.m: Honey fungus grows through the soil with rhizomorphs.

119429.q: How did the researchers check whether honey fungus samples from different places belonged to the same individual?
a: They let the mycelia meet in the laboratory
They compared the colour of the caps
They measured the size of the spores
119429.e: In these compatibility tests, mycelia of the same, genetically identical individual grow together without a boundary. Different individuals, by contrast, form a dividing line.
119429.m: Mycelia of the same fungus grow together in the lab without a boundary.

119430.q: How does the dark honey fungus live on living trees?
a: It is a parasite that can make trees die
It is a mycorrhizal partner that strengthens trees
It only lives on leaves on the ground
It feeds on insect larvae in the wood
119430.e: Honey fungus attacks the roots and the base of the trunk and kills weakened trees. Afterwards it lives on in the dead wood as a decomposer.
119430.m: Honey fungus can kill trees as a parasite.

119431.q: Where is the largest honey fungus known so far in the world?
a: In the Black Forest in Germany
119431.e: In the Malheur National Forest in Oregon, a dark honey fungus covers around 9 square kilometres. It is considered one of the largest organisms on Earth.
119431.m: The largest known honey fungus grows in Oregon.

a: Proteins in the cell wall of all fungi
119432.e: Mycotoxins are secondary metabolic products of moulds that are poisonous to humans and animals. They get into the body through mouldy food and animal feed.
119432.m: Mycotoxins are poisons made by moulds.

119433.q: Why does cooking hardly protect against mycotoxins in mouldy food?
a: Most mycotoxins are stable when heated
Cooking spreads the spores into the air
Mycotoxins only evaporate in the fridge
119433.e: Many mycotoxins survive boiling, baking and frying without much loss. That is why badly mouldy food belongs in the bin.
119433.m: Mycotoxins are usually not destroyed by cooking.

119434.q: Why should you throw away a mouldy loaf of bread completely instead of just cutting off the mouldy spot?
a: Fungal threads and poisons can spread invisibly through the whole loaf
Mould is only poisonous on the surface
Mould disappears when the bread is toasted
119434.e: In soft, airy foods, fungal threads grow deep inside, and mycotoxins spread. You only see part of the infestation.
119434.m: Mouldy bread belongs in the bin completely.

119435.q: Where can mycotoxins already form on cereals?
a: Already in the field and later in storage
119435.e: Moulds sometimes attack cereals while they are still flowering in the field. If the grain is stored damp, more poisons can form.
119435.m: Mycotoxins form in the field and in storage.

119436.q: Which human organ mainly breaks down many poisons such as mycotoxins?
119436.e: The liver is the most important organ for detoxification. That is why some mycotoxins such as aflatoxins damage it especially badly.

119437.q: What do you call an illness caused by mycotoxins?
119437.e: A mycotoxicosis is poisoning by fungal toxins. A mycosis, by contrast, is an infection in which the fungus itself grows in the body.
119437.m: Poisoning by fungal toxins is called mycotoxicosis.

119438.q: Why is animal feed also monitored for mycotoxins?
a: They harm the animals and can get into milk or meat
119438.e: Farm animals can become ill from fungal poisons. Some poisons or their breakdown products also pass into milk and so reach humans.
119438.m: Mycotoxins in feed endanger animals and humans.

119439.q: Which storage conditions most encourage the formation of mycotoxins?
119439.e: Moulds grow best in high humidity and warmth. Storing cereals and nuts dry and cool greatly reduces the risk.
119439.m: Damp warmth encourages mould and mycotoxins.

119440.q: What does an ergot look like on an ear of rye?
119440.e: The ergot sticks out of the ear as a dark purple to black, horn-shaped growth. It is clearly longer than a normal grain of rye.

119441.q: How is ergot poisoning from bread prevented today?
a: The grain is cleaned and checked before milling
The bread is baked for longer
Salt is added to the dough
119441.e: Modern mills sort out ergots with colour sorters, and maximum limits apply. That is why St Anthony's fire is very rare today.
119441.m: Cleaned grain protects against ergot poisoning.

119442.q: Which cereal is especially often infected with ergot?
119442.e: Rye is cross-pollinated, and its flowers stay open for a long time, so the spores can get in easily. That is why it is infected especially often.
119442.m: Rye is especially vulnerable to ergot.

119443.q: What was poisoning by ergot called in the Middle Ages?
119443.e: Ergot poisoning (ergotism) was called St Anthony's fire or holy fire. The Order of St Anthony cared for the sick.
119443.m: In the Middle Ages, ergot poisoning was called St Anthony's fire.

119444.q: Why did fingers and toes die off in severe ergotism?
a: The poisons narrow the blood vessels
The spores eat away the bones
The poison lowers body temperature to zero degrees
The fungus grows in the joints
119444.e: Ergot poisons such as ergotamine narrow the blood vessels a lot. The limbs get too little blood, and the tissue dies.
119444.m: Ergot poisons narrow the blood vessels.

119445.q: Which Basel chemist produced LSD from an ergot compound in 1938?
119445.e: Albert Hofmann synthesised LSD from lysergic acid at Sandoz in Basel in 1938. He discovered its strong effect by chance in 1943.
119445.m: Albert Hofmann produced LSD in Basel in 1938.

119446.q: Which group of substances is responsible for the effects of ergot?
119446.e: Ergot contains ergot alkaloids such as ergotamine and ergometrine, which are derived from lysergic acid. Some of them are used in medicine.

119447.q: What is the ergot compound ergotamine used for in medicine?
a: Against fungal infections of the skin
119447.e: Ergotamine narrows widened blood vessels in the head and was used for a long time against migraine attacks. Today newer medicines are usually used for this.
119447.m: Ergotamine from ergot is used against migraine.

119448.e: Aflatoxins come mainly from the Aspergillus moulds Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus. The name is made up of “A. flavus” and “toxin”.
119448.m: Aflatoxins come from Aspergillus flavus and related species.

119449.q: Which disease can long-term intake of aflatoxin B1 mainly cause?
119449.e: Aflatoxin B1 is one of the strongest natural cancer-causing substances and mainly damages the liver. The IARC places aflatoxins in Group 1.
119449.m: Aflatoxin B1 can cause liver cancer.

119450.q: Which event in England in 1960 led to the discovery of aflatoxins?
119450.e: Over 100,000 turkeys died of the mysterious “Turkey X disease”. The cause was mouldy peanut meal in their feed.
119450.m: Aflatoxins were discovered in 1960 after turkeys died in large numbers.

119451.q: In which foods are aflatoxins found especially often?
a: Milk, butter and cream fresh from the farm
119451.e: Aspergillus flavus grows well on products rich in oil and starch from warm regions. That is why nuts, maize, spices and dried figs are strictly checked.
119451.m: Nuts and maize are common sources of aflatoxin.

119452.q: How can aflatoxins in nuts or maize be made visible in the laboratory?
119452.e: Aflatoxins fluoresce blue or green under UV light. This is also where the names aflatoxin B (blue) and G (green) come from.

119453.q: How does aflatoxin M1 get into milk?
a: Cows convert aflatoxin B1 they have eaten
The fungus grows directly in the udder
It comes from the plastic of the milk cartons
119453.e: If cows eat contaminated feed, aflatoxin B1 is converted into M1 in the liver and passed out in the milk. That is why checking feed is important.
119453.m: Aflatoxin M1 forms in the cow from contaminated feed.

119454.q: Why have very low maximum levels been set for aflatoxins in food?
a: They cause cancer even in the tiniest amounts
They spoil the taste at once
119454.e: For cancer-causing substances that damage the genes, there is no amount that is definitely safe. That is why the principle is to keep exposure as low as possible.
119454.m: Very strict limits apply to aflatoxins.

119455.q: After being converted in the liver, how does aflatoxin B1 damage the cells?
a: It binds to the DNA and causes mutations
It only destroys the cellulose cell wall
119455.e: In the liver, aflatoxin B1 is converted into a reactive epoxide. This binds to the DNA, and mutations in the tumour suppressor gene p53 are typical.

119456.q: What do saprotrophic fungi feed on?
119456.e: Saprotrophic fungi break down dead wood, leaves, droppings and other remains. In this way they return nutrients to the cycle.
119456.m: Saprotrophic fungi live on dead material.

119457.q: Which animals grow a fungus in their nests that breaks down chewed-up leaf material and serves them as food?
119457.e: Leafcutter ants carry pieces of leaf into the nest, chew them up and use them to fertilise a fungus garden. The ants feed on parts of the fungus.
119457.m: Leafcutter ants grow fungi on leaf material.

119458.q: What do white rot fungi break down in wood that other living things can hardly decompose?
119458.e: White rot fungi can break down the tough lignin. What is left is pale, fibrous cellulose, hence the name white rot.
119458.m: White rot fungi break down lignin.

119459.q: What does wood look like after it has been broken down by brown rot fungi?
119459.e: Brown rot fungi mainly break down cellulose and leave the brown lignin behind. The wood shrinks and breaks into cube-like pieces.
119459.m: Brown rot leaves brown wood crumbled into cubes.

119460.q: Which wood-destroying fungus is especially feared in buildings?
119460.e: The dry rot fungus (Serpula lacrymans) causes brown rot in timber used in buildings. It can grow through brickwork and cause great damage.
119460.m: The dry rot fungus destroys wood in houses.

119461.q: Which cultivated mushroom grows as a saprotroph on compost made of straw and manure?
119461.e: The cultivated button mushroom breaks down fermented compost and can therefore easily be grown indoors in sheds. Tinder fungus and chicken of the woods grow on trees, the penny bun in the forest floor.
119461.m: Button mushrooms grow as decomposers on compost.

119462.q: Why is the old term “saprophyte” now considered inaccurate for fungi?
a: Fungi never live on dead material
The term only refers to bacteria
119462.e: The ending “-phyte” means plant, but fungi form a kingdom of their own. That is why today people speak of saprobionts or saprotrophic organisms.
119462.m: Fungi are not plants and are therefore called saprobionts.

119463.q: What role do saprotrophic fungi play in the forest's carbon cycle?
a: They release stored carbon as CO2
They store carbon only in spores
119463.e: As they break down wood and leaves, fungi use the carbon compounds for respiration. In this way the carbon returns to the air as carbon dioxide.
119463.m: Decomposing fungi release carbon into the air as CO2.

119464.q: What is the cell wall of true fungi mainly made of?
119464.e: Fungal cell walls contain chitin and glucans. Cellulose is typical of plants, murein of bacteria.
119464.m: Fungal cell walls are mainly made of chitin.

119465.q: Which building block is chitin made of?
119465.e: Chitin is a long chain of N-acetylglucosamine units joined by beta-1,4-glycosidic bonds. It is similar to cellulose but contains nitrogen.

119466.q: In which group of animals does chitin form the main part of the exoskeleton?
119466.e: Insects, spiders and crustaceans have an exoskeleton containing chitin. In crustaceans it is also strengthened with lime.
119466.m: Arthropods have an exoskeleton made of chitin.

119467.q: Which biopolymer is even more common in nature than chitin?
119467.e: Chitin is considered the second most common biopolymer on Earth. Only cellulose from plant cell walls is even more common.
119467.m: After cellulose, chitin is the most common biopolymer.

119468.q: Which element does chitin contain, but cellulose does not?
119468.e: Chitin is built in a similar way to cellulose. But its building blocks carry a group containing nitrogen, which cellulose lacks.

119469.q: Why do many plants produce the enzyme chitinase?
119469.e: Plants do not have any chitin themselves. With chitinases they can attack the cell walls of fungi that invade them.

119470.q: Which storage substance do fungi form instead of starch?
119470.e: Like animals, fungi store glucose as glycogen. Chitin and glycogen also show that fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.

119471.q: Where does the word “chitin” come from?
a: From the Greek word for garment or covering
From the Latin word for fungus
From the name of a French chemist
From the Arabic word for armour
119471.e: The word goes back to the Greek “chiton”, which means tunic or covering. The name suits its job as a protective covering.
119471.m: Chitin is named after the Greek word for garment.

119472.q: Which tree species in Switzerland is seriously threatened by the ash dieback fungus Hymenoscyphus fraxineus?
119472.e: The fungus causes ash dieback. Since the 2000s, many ash trees have been dying all over Europe.
119472.m: The fungus Hymenoscyphus fraxineus causes ash dieback.

119473.q: How does the ash dieback fungus spread from tree to tree?
a: By spores carried by the wind
By insects that bore into the bark
By root contact in the soil
119473.e: The small fruiting bodies on the ground release spores. The wind carries them onto the leaves of new ash trees, where the infection begins.
119473.m: Ash dieback spreads with wind-borne spores.

119474.q: Where does the ash dieback fungus originally come from?
119474.e: The fungus comes from East Asia, where it lives on the Manchurian ash without causing much damage. In Europe it meets ash trees that have no defence against it.
119474.m: The cause of ash dieback comes from East Asia.

119475.q: Why does the German name of the ash dieback fungus include the word “false”?
a: It looks very like the harmless native white stem cup fungus
It is not a fungus at all but a bacterium
It only forms false spores without a nucleus
It only grows on artificial trees
119475.e: The native white stem cup fungus can hardly be told apart from the outside. Only genetic studies showed that they are two species.
119475.m: The ash dieback fungus looks like a harmless native species.

119476.q: Where does the ash dieback fungus form its small fruiting bodies?
a: On fresh ash flowers in the crown
119476.e: In summer the little white cups appear on the previous year's leaf stalks in the leaf litter. From there the spores are carried by the wind onto new leaves.
119476.m: The little cups grow on old ash leaf stalks on the ground.

119477.q: Which fungus often also attacks the base of the trunk of ash trees weakened by ash dieback?
119477.e: Weakened ash trees often develop dead areas at the base of the trunk, where honey fungus settles. Such trees can fall over and become a danger on roads and paths.
119477.m: Weakened ash trees are often also attacked by honey fungus.

119478.q: Which group of fungi does the ash dieback fungus belong to?
119478.e: The fungus forms cup-shaped apothecia with asci. It therefore belongs to the ascomycetes.
119478.m: The ash dieback fungus is an ascomycete.

119479.q: What hope are researchers pursuing in the fight against ash dieback?
a: Finding and propagating less vulnerable ash trees
Felling all the ash trees in Europe as a precaution
Wiping out the fungus with cold in winter
Only growing ash trees in greenhouses
119479.e: A small share of ash trees shows hardly any damage. These less vulnerable trees are to be preserved and used for breeding.
119479.m: Resistant ash trees are the greatest hope against ash dieback.

119480.q: Which striking property does wood that has been penetrated by honey fungus mycelium show in the dark?
a: It heats up to over 50 degrees
119480.e: The mycelium of honey fungus is bioluminescent. Wood penetrated by it can therefore glow faintly at night, which used to be called “foxfire”.
119480.m: Wood penetrated by honey fungus can glow in the dark.

119481.q: Which tree species characterises the forests at the Ofen Pass, where the large honey fungus lives?
119481.e: Large mountain pine forests grow at the Ofen Pass. The honey fungus there mainly attacks weakened pines.
119481.m: Mountain pines mainly grow at the Ofen Pass.

119482.q: What is the sweet “honeydew” that the ergot fungus produces in infected flowers for?
a: It attracts insects that carry the fungal spores further
It protects the grain from frost
It serves the plant as a water store
It dissolves the leaves of the rye
119482.e: In its early stage, the fungus gives off a sugary juice containing asexual spores. Insects that feed on it spread the spores to other flowers.
119482.m: The honeydew of ergot attracts insects that spread the spores.

119483.q: When do plant roots release more signalling substances to attract mycorrhizal fungi?
a: When there is a lack of phosphate in the soil
119483.e: If phosphate is lacking, roots release strigolactones. These make the fungal hyphae branch out, and the plant gets more phosphate through the fungus.
119483.m: When phosphate is short, roots attract mycorrhizal fungi.

119583.q: What is the typical value of the resting membrane potential of a nerve cell?
119583.e: In most neurons the resting membrane potential is around -70 mV. So the inside of the cell is negatively charged compared with the outside.
119583.m: A resting neuron has a voltage of about minus 70 millivolts inside.

119584.q: Which ion mainly determines the resting membrane potential of a neuron?
119584.e: At rest, the membrane is mainly permeable to potassium ions. Their outflow along the concentration gradient charges the inside of the cell negatively.
119584.m: The resting potential is mainly a potassium potential.

119585.q: Which equation is used to calculate the equilibrium potential of a single type of ion?
119585.e: The Nernst equation links the ratio of an ion's concentration inside and outside with the voltage at which diffusion and electrical force balance out.
119585.m: The Nernst equation gives the equilibrium potential of a single ion.

119586.q: Which pump maintains the concentration differences of sodium and potassium at the nerve cell?
119586.e: Using ATP, the sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. Without it, the concentration differences would disappear.
119586.m: The sodium-potassium pump maintains the ion gradients.

119587.q: Where is the concentration of potassium ions higher in a resting nerve cell?
119587.e: Inside the cell, potassium is about 30 times more concentrated than outside. This gradient drives the outflow of potassium at rest.
119587.m: Potassium is plentiful inside and scarce outside.

119588.q: Where is the concentration of sodium ions higher in a resting nerve cell?
119588.e: Sodium is about ten times more concentrated outside the cell than inside. That is why it flows into the cell when sodium channels open.
119588.m: Sodium waits outside the cell membrane.

119589.q: Roughly what is the equilibrium potential of potassium in a neuron?
119589.e: The ratio of potassium inside and outside gives an equilibrium potential of around -90 mV. The resting potential is slightly more positive because a little sodium also flows in.
119589.m: The potassium equilibrium potential is more negative than the resting potential.

119590.q: Through which channels do potassium ions constantly flow out of the cell at the resting membrane potential?
119590.e: Potassium leak channels are open even at rest. They make the membrane at rest mainly permeable to potassium.
119590.m: Leak channels let potassium out even at rest.

119591.q: What happens during the action potential when the sodium channels open?
a: Sodium flows in and the inside of the cell becomes positive
Sodium flows out and the inside of the cell becomes more negative
Potassium flows in and the cell rests
119591.e: Sodium is much more concentrated outside than inside. When the channels open, it flows into the cell and briefly reverses the voltage.
119591.m: Sodium flowing in makes the inside of the cell positive.

119592.q: At what threshold is an action potential triggered in a typical neuron?
119592.e: If the membrane is depolarised from its resting value to about -50 mV, enough voltage-gated sodium channels open. The action potential then runs in a self-reinforcing way.
119592.m: Only when the threshold is reached does the action potential fire.

119593.q: Which ion flow causes depolarisation during an action potential?
119593.e: Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium flows into the cell. This makes the inside of the cell briefly positive.
119593.m: Sodium flows in and reverses the voltage.

119594.q: Which ion flow is mainly responsible for repolarisation after the peak of an action potential?
119594.e: Voltage-gated potassium channels open with a delay. Potassium flows out and makes the inside of the cell negative again.
119594.m: Potassium flows out and restores the negative voltage.

119595.q: What is the phase called in which the membrane is briefly more negative than at rest after an action potential?
119595.e: The potassium channels close slowly, so briefly too much potassium flows out. The voltage drops below the resting potential.
119595.m: In hyperpolarisation, the voltage briefly dips below the resting value.

119596.q: Which principle describes that an action potential is either triggered completely or not at all?
119596.e: Below the threshold no action potential arises; above it, it always runs at the same height. Stronger stimuli do not produce a bigger action potential.
119596.m: An action potential comes completely or not at all.

119597.q: Why can no new action potential be triggered during the absolute refractory period?
a: The ATP is completely used up.
119597.e: After opening, the sodium channels go into an inactivated state. Only after repolarisation can they be opened again.
119597.m: Inactivated sodium channels make the neuron briefly unexcitable.

119598.q: Where on a neuron is an action potential normally triggered?
a: at the tips of the dendrites
at the membrane of the axon terminal
119598.e: At the axon hillock, the density of voltage-gated sodium channels is especially high. There the incoming signals are added up, and when the threshold is reached an action potential is started.
119598.m: The axon hillock decides whether a neuron fires.

119599.q: Which scientists explained the mechanism of the action potential using the giant axon of the squid?
119599.e: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley measured the ion currents in the giant axon and described them mathematically. They received the Nobel Prize for it in 1963.
119599.m: Hodgkin and Huxley worked out the action potential.

119600.q: How does a neuron encode a stronger stimulus if all action potentials are the same height?
119600.e: Since the height of the action potential is fixed, the strength of the stimulus is passed on through the number of action potentials per second. This is called frequency coding.
119600.m: Strong stimuli show up as many action potentials per second.

119601.q: Which temporary chemical change does the protein of the sodium-potassium pump undergo during each transport cycle?
a: It is broken down into glucose.
It is moved into the nucleus.
119601.e: A phosphate group is briefly attached to the pump protein and later removed again. This changes its shape so that it opens alternately to one side of the membrane or the other.
119601.m: The pump changes its shape through phosphorylation.

119602.q: Where does the sodium-potassium pump get the energy for transport from?
119602.e: The pump is an ATPase. It works against the concentration gradients and therefore needs energy from ATP.
119602.m: The sodium-potassium pump runs on ATP.

119603.q: Why is the sodium-potassium pump described as electrogenic?
a: It moves one net positive charge out per cycle.
It conducts current along the axon.
119603.e: Three positive charges go out, only two come in. As a result, the pump directly contributes a little to the negative voltage inside the cell.
119603.m: The pump moves one positive charge outwards with each cycle.

119604.q: The sodium-potassium pump is a textbook example of which type of transport across the membrane?
119604.e: The pump moves ions against their concentration gradient and uses energy from ATP directly to do so. In diffusion and osmosis, by contrast, particles move without using energy.
119604.m: The sodium-potassium pump is an example of active transport.

119605.q: Which group of drugs blocks the sodium-potassium pump and is used for heart failure?
119605.e: Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin from foxglove block the pump in heart muscle cells. This indirectly raises the calcium in the cell, and the heart beats more strongly.
119605.m: Cardiac glycosides slow down the sodium-potassium pump.

119606.q: What happens in the long run if the sodium-potassium pump of a nerve cell is blocked?
a: The resting potential becomes more negative.
119606.e: Without the pump, leak currents gradually even out the concentrations inside and outside. This also removes the basis for resting and action potentials.
119606.m: Without the pump, nerve cells lose their ion gradients.
